items.question: In the book Backsliding, what are the signs that someone is falling away?
items.text:
The book names a number of symptoms that show a person may be sliding away, and it treats them as early clues worth noticing, the way a doctor reads signs in the body [1].

- **Bad company.** A Christian who keeps bad friends is a serious symptom, because bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33) and will eventually lead you to bad places [1].
- **Stubbornness.** A person who will not heed counsel but always does what he wants is a potential backslider; the backslider in heart is filled with his own ways (Proverbs 14:14), and Scripture says there is safety in the multitude of counsel [3].
- **Shock at "Christian surprises."** When believers are stunned by the failures they see in church or in leaders, they can easily fall away; we are told not to be afraid with any amazement (1 Peter 3:6), and to fix our eyes on Jesus rather than on men [3].
- **Praying less.** Prayer keeps us from falling, and a Christian who spends less time talking to God is unknowingly moving away from Him [4].
- **Not being committed.** Anyone who will not commit to a church will ultimately leave it; God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [4].
- **Coldness in worship.** The backsliding Christian becomes aloof, diplomatic and uninterested, yawning and glancing at his watch in the service; these are sure signs of imminent backsliding [5].
- **Foolish questioning.** Raising foolish and unlearned questions that only gender strife (2 Timothy 2:23) is another symptom, often a way of finding a reason to doubt the Bible [5].
- **Murmuring.** Complaining, grumbling and criticizing, whether at home, at work or in church, marks people who often leave their churches and eventually backslide [8].
- **Approval and admiration of wrongdoers.** Since people become attracted to something before they go for it, approving of someone doing wrong makes you likely to want to do the same [8].
- **Curiosity.** Some, like the prodigal son who had everything at home, are simply curious about what is "out there"; there is nothing new under the sun, and curiosity killed the backslider [8].

The book also says plainly that some Christians do not even know they are backslidden, and that this very attitude—"I can't see myself backsliding"—is itself a sign of being prone to it, since Scripture warns that he who thinks he stands should take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12) [2][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 2, 5 and 7 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 1:20; Proverbs 7:10; Proverbs 14:14; Ecclesiastes 1:9-10; Ecclesiastes 4:13; Jeremiah 2:32; Hosea 11:7; Matthew 10:22; Matthew 20:16; Matthew 25:1-46 and 7 more.

items.question: How should I respond when people I've loved and helped turn against me?
items.text:
That is a deep and painful thing to carry, and I'm sorry you're walking through it.

Jesus Himself was repaid with ingratitude and even killed by those He had helped, yet He never responded to that spirit of ingratitude [1]. So do not be surprised when it comes — every leader meets it, and people are often simply not grateful for what you do for them [1].

Do not look to people for your reward. The Scripture says that whatever good thing any man does, he will receive it from the Lord (Ephesians 6:8), so your rewards depend on God and not on the people you helped [1]. When you stop expecting men's approval, you find a real liberty and become accountable to the Lord rather than to them [1].

David's response to those who repaid his good with evil was to give himself to prayer and to ask God for judgment, praying that those who rejoiced at his hurt would be clothed with shame and dishonour (Psalm 35:19-26) [2][6]. And there is a warning here too: curses abound for those who repay good with evil, so learn to fear that sin and never become one of the unthankful yourself (Psalm 109:5-13) [3].

Some of the people a leader loves return that love with flatness, with hatred, or with treachery, and because they did not value the love shown them they end up cast away as profane branches [4]. Jesus went to the cross thinking of the purposes of God and not the treachery of Judas, and after He rose He never mentioned Judas again [7]. So do not let offences turn you away from your mission — keep moving, keep pressing on, and learn to forgive because you have been forgiven a lot [7].

Do not struggle when people are taken from you; sometimes it is in your eternal destiny that they be taken away and replaced [5]. God may allow people to leave so that you understand how our heavenly Father feels when His children leave Him, and walking in love and maturity toward those who desert or turn against you is part of becoming a father [5]. Move on and build new relationships, because there is a replacement for everyone who walks away — sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you, as it was when Saul's heart departed and David was revealed [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 11 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 5 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:1-2; Psalms 35:19-26; Psalms 109:1-13; Luke 15:11-13; John 10:32; John 21:15-17; Ephesians 6:8; 1 John 2:18-19.

items.question: What does the cross mean for me as a Christian?
items.text:
The cross is the true symbol of our faith, and it carries several meanings for you as a believer. Every time you see it, you are meant to be reminded of what it stands for [3].

- **It is the symbol of a death you must experience.** A person carrying a cross was on his way to die, so when Jesus told us to take up our cross daily and follow Him, He was telling us to go to a place where we lose our lives [3]. This death is not the physical end of your life but the disappearance of your own dreams, plans and future, and the emergence of God's plans for you [1].

- **It is the symbol of the price you must pay.** There is a price for becoming a Christian; Christ paid the greatest price to purchase your salvation with His blood, and you too will have to pay a price to follow Him [1].

- **It is the symbol of the love of God you must emulate.** Through the cross we perceive God's love, because He laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren [1].

- **It is the symbol of obedience.** Through the cross we see how Jesus was obedient even unto death, humbling Himself and becoming obedient to the death of the cross, so the cross is the greatest symbol of obedience [1].

- **It is the symbol of the sacrifice you must make.** Jesus gave Himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God, and the cross is the symbol of the sacrifice all of us must make to serve the Lord [1].

- **It is the symbol of humility.** In the cross Jesus humbled Himself to the uttermost, making Himself of no reputation and allowing Himself to be shamed and belittled by sinful men [1].

- **It is the symbol of the blood of Jesus.** The wooden cross broke the body of Jesus and shed His blood, so when we ask people to come to the cross we are asking them to come to the shed blood of Christ, through which peace was made and all things reconciled to God [1].

- **It is the symbol of the power that separates you from the world.** The cross released the power through which separation from the world takes place, so that a Christian will not mind being the odd one out, or a young person will not mind staying pure when everyone around them has not [2].

- **It is the symbol of true life.** Contrary to all expectations, the cross that seems to promise death actually brings life; if we have become united with Him in the likeness of His death, we shall also be in the likeness of His resurrection (Romans 6:5), and if we be dead with Him, we shall also live with Him (2 Timothy 2:11) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*.

items.question: How do I stop needing people's approval and praise after I preach?
items.text:
That's a real freedom to want, and the books speak to it directly.

**Look to God for your reward, not to people.** A leader looks to God for rewards, and Scripture says that whatever good thing any man does, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free (Ephesians 6:8) [1]. Your rewards depend on God, not on the people you helped, and God is the only one who can reward you adequately [1].

**Stop expecting people to commend you.** Many years ago I stopped expecting people to commend me after I had finished preaching; I do not care whether people commend me or not, because my duty is to preach from the Bible and I have done my duty [1]. When I decided not to look for man's approval, I felt a sense of liberty — free from men and accountable to the Lord [1].

**Seek God's approval instead of men's.** You do not need the approval of men; do not worry about what people think of you, just make sure that God thinks highly of you, and you will become a workman who is not ashamed (2 Timothy 2:15-16) [2]. People may congratulate you, but it is the Lord's approval that you really need [3].

**Expect ingratitude and don't be surprised by it.** Jesus Himself experienced ingratitude — He was killed by an ungrateful mob, exchanged for an armed robber — and He never responded to that evil spirit [1]. Every leader comes face to face with ingratitude, and if you begin to retaliate because of it, you will lose your place in the ministry [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 9 of *The Preparation of the Gospel* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:13; John 3:16; John 10:32; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 2:15-16; 2 Timothy 4:1-2; 2 Timothy 4:5.

items.question: How can I learn to pray early in the morning before my day gets busy?
items.book:
Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer
items.text:
Here are the ways our books point to for learning to pray early, before the day fills up.

- **Rise a great while before day.** Jesus Himself rose up a great while before day, went out to a solitary place, and prayed there (Mark 1:35), and if you are serious about prayer you must learn to do the same, because once the day begins in full you will not be able to pray much [1][2][5].

- **Go to bed early so you can wake early.** Learn to overcome sleep by going to bed early so that you can rise a great while before day — that was the life of Jesus [2].

- **Make it a repeatable habit.** Dawn prayer is something you can do tomorrow and every day of the year, in every season and even on your busiest days, so it becomes one of the most important habits of your life [1]. An action becomes a habit when it is repeated many times, and if you develop a habit of prayer you are developing a habit for success [4][6].

- **Let it feed your Bible reading.** When you pray at dawn you will find yourself praying much more than at any other time, and every time you pray you can read your Bible and meditate on the Word, so your knowledge of God's word will greatly increase [1].

- **Use it to fight prayerlessness and shallowness.** Any Christian who has not learned to rise a great while before day is most probably a prayerless believer, and it is the hidden part of you that gives you strength in public — if there is no hidden prayer, there will be no public strength [1].

- **Meet God before you meet the day.** Morning prayer is very good because you meet God before you meet the devil and before you meet the circumstances of life, and God anoints you to overcome every mountain you will encounter [3][7].

- **Expect it to steady you.** Praying at dawn helps you overcome the ups and downs most Christians experience, bringing consistency into your life, and it makes you ready for the battles of the day, so that God lifts you up and empowers you to overcome whatever has targeted you [1].

- **Keep praying through the rest of the day too.** There are four important times to pray — morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time — and you can pray on the bus, on your way to work, softly in the office, or in the shower, because God is happy when His children are constantly in touch with Him (1 Thessalonians 5:17) [7][8].

One more encouragement: a man once told Bishop Dag Heward-Mills that he had prayed three to five hours every day for over thirty years, and that waking up at night to watch and pray was the secret to his amazing prayer life [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 8 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 1 of *How to Pray* and chapter 10 of *Read your Bible Pray Everyday*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 6:10; Matthew 26:36-44; Mark 1:34-36; Mark 6:46; Mark 13:33; Luke 4:16; Luke 6:12-13; Luke 21:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that actually works is worth learning, and our books lay out clear ways to grow in it.

- **Pray strategic Bible prayers.** Let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the very prayers recorded in Scripture — Ephesians 1:17-19 is one of the most powerful a minister can pray, and Ephesians 3:15-19 prays to be grounded in love, which matters because a pastor may make great sacrifices yet, as 1 Corinthians 13:3 says, without love it profits nothing [1]. The Ephesians prayer topics have six components: giving thanks with a grateful heart, praying for wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, for the eyes of your understanding to be enlightened, to know your calling and the hope of your calling, the riches of the inheritance of the saints, and the power of God [4].

- **Pray fervently.** Fervent prayer is ardent, passionate, zealous, burning and eager — if someone watched you pray, they should be able to describe it with one of those words, and doodling and dawdling prayers are not fervent at all [1].

- **Pray in tongues.** Every minister should spend several hours praying in tongues, using the gift God has given rather than leaving it as an ornament; Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [1].

- **Have discussions with the Holy Spirit.** Prayer is meant to be two-way: speak to the Holy Spirit and hear His voice back, since He is to us what Jesus was to His disciples, teaching us all things and bringing all things to remembrance (John 14:18, 26) [1].

- **Pray for a long time.** Two-minute prayers differ from hours of prayer; Jesus rose a great while before day to pray (Mark 1:35) and continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12), and Paul spoke of night and day praying exceedingly (1 Thessalonians 3:10) [1]. Long prayer may not be an explicit command, but it is implicit throughout the Word [5].

- **Pray at set times, and all the time.** There are four important times to pray: morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time [3][5]. Morning prayer is good because you meet God before you meet the devil and before the circumstances of life [5]; afternoon prayer means recognizing God as most important in the thick of the battle [3]; night prayer is a different experience, and since the forces of darkness are called darkness, praying then tackles them differently [3]; and "pray without ceasing" (1 Thessalonians 5:17) means prayer is a never-ending stream of communication with your Father [3].

- **Watch and pray.** Watching means staying up at night to pray, and watching and praying is mentioned more in the Bible than fasting and praying

items.question: How can I make sure I'm not just saved but also living for God so I don't end up in the lowest place in heaven?
items.book: Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry
items.text:
It's good that you're asking this — the books speak to it plainly.

- **Be clear that salvation itself is not earned.** You are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so no one can boast; your best efforts could never qualify you for heaven [3]. As Romans 3:10 says, there is none righteous, not one [3]. So the question isn't how to secure your salvation — that is God's gift — but how to live well before the One who saved you.

- **Know that a judgment awaits every believer.** Even though you are forgiven and admitted into Christ, there is a judgment that awaits all believers — the Bema, the judgment seat of Christ, where each one is recompensed for his deeds in the body, whether good or bad [4]. This is distinct from the white throne judgment, which has to do with unbelievers [4].

- **Labour, and don't live a life of leisure.** Paul said he laboured so that he might be accepted of the Lord, and without hard labour you will never have a good experience at the judgment seat [4]. If you have been living a life of rest and comfort, you will be shocked there; Jesus told us to pray for labourers because the harvest is plenty but the labourers are few [4].

- **Make it your ambition to please the Lord.** Paul prepared for the judgment seat by seeking to be well pleasing to God, and anyone who lives by that rule will do well there [4]. You will not be afraid of that judgment if you live to please God [4].

- **Take seriously the bad things done in the body.** Many Christians live carelessly in sin, obeying neither the word of God nor living differently from worldly people, and at the judgment seat you will be held accountable for the bad things you have done [4]. You are washed and cleansed by the blood of Jesus and entitled to enter heaven, but you will still account for those deeds [4].

- **Do the good works God prepared for you.** You are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works which He ordained beforehand that you should walk in them [3][8]. The only reason you are still alive is to accomplish certain good works [8].

- **Refuse shortcuts.** Jesus was offered a quick and easy way to win the kingdoms of the world, and He was too wise to take it — He stayed on the path of righteousness [6]. There is no shortcut to heaven; it is only by accepting the Lord Jesus Christ as your personal Saviour and being born again [7]. The Kingdom of Heaven is like a mustard seed that must go through the long process of dying and growing before it yields fruit, and you cannot avoid the reality of fasting, praying, fellowshipping and witnessing [7].

- **Adapt and stay strong wherever you are.** You cannot put the Lord aside because you have moved to a new country

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 3 of *Church Planting*, chapter 5 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice* and chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:3; Isaiah 64:6; Matthew 4:8-9; Luke 9:24; Romans 3:10; 2 Corinthians 5:9-11; Ephesians 2:8-10.

items.question: How can I pray for the sick and be a source of healing?
items.text:
You're asking a good question, and our books have a lot to say about it. Here are the ways they describe.

- **Pray short, simple prayers.** Jesus prayed very short prayers for the sick — He sighed and said "Ephphatha, that is, be opened," and the man's ears were opened and his tongue loosed [3]. Short prayers are very powerful; don't be deceived into thinking you always need long, elaborate prayers [3].

- **Lay hands on the sick.** One of the ways God touches people is through the laying on of hands, and Scripture says "they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover" (Mark 16:18) [5]. Something wonderful happens when hands are laid on you by an anointed person, and many people are comforted when hands are laid on them [1][5].

- **Use anointing oil.** Praying for the sick with anointing oil is scriptural — the disciples "anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them" (Mark 6:13), and James 5:14-15 tells the elders to pray over the sick, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord [5]. If you can believe it is no more ordinary olive oil but the healing anointing of the Holy Spirit, it will heal every disease [5].

- **Believe for the anointing through garments and contact.** The woman with the issue of blood believed that if she could only touch Jesus' garment she would be healed, and she received that power [5][6]. The anointing can be transmitted through physical contact — even a hug or a handshake — and it is faith in the contact that activates it [5].

- **Rehearse your healing ministry.** Jesus sent His disciples out to cure diseases and cast out devils, letting them rehearse [2]. Every opportunity to pray for the sick is a rehearsal for greater days ahead — every testimony of headaches being healed is a rehearsal for bigger testimonies one day [2].

- **Overcome your fear.** Fear is a spirit that keeps you from using your gifts and callings, and fear was the greatest barrier to this ministry [4]. One man was terrified to pray for the sick outside his own church and battled the devil's taunts all day, but he overcame those fears and there were powerful testimonies that night [4].

items.question: How can I know my strengths and use them for God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and warmly. Here is what they counsel.

- **Know your temperament.** God has asked you to be strong in the grace He has given you, and the four temperaments — choleric, sanguine, melancholic and phlegmatic — reveal the natural strengths and weaknesses of your life, so everyone should know his temperament and learn to understand himself [1].

- **Flow in the grace that matches your temperament.** If you are phlegmatic, you have a grace to do the same thing repeatedly, so be a good teacher, pastor or headmaster and stay faithfully behind your screen [1]. If you are melancholic, you have a grace to be interested in detail, and your eye naturally picks out what is disorderly, so flow in that deep-thinking faithfulness [1]. If you are choleric, recognize the strength to be a driving personality, a finisher of projects and a natural manager, and walk in that leadership [1]. If you are sanguine, the grace is given you to be cheerful and pleasant in all circumstances — do not despise it, for you are the life of the group [1].

- **Give your temperament to the church.** To give yourself wholly to the ministry is to give your temperament — the choleric part can help you work with speed and take necessary decisions, and the melancholic part can help you structure a complicated network of churches [5].

- **Stay in your own course.** A true leader knows where his strength lies; do not be a pastor because everyone is pastoring, or a prophet because it is the latest fad, but do what God has called you to do [1]. Paul fought a good fight and ran his race, and it is time for you to run yours (2 Timothy 4:7) [1].

- **Make God your strength.** Trust in His mercy, for when you trust in other things you become weaker; the man who does not make God his strength but trusts in the abundance of his riches is contrasted with the one who is like a green olive tree in the house of God (Psalm 52:6-8) [2]. Receive counsel from God and let Him be your covering, for strengthening yourself with the world brings shame and confusion [2].

- **Translate willingness into strength through prayer.** There is a difference between being willing and being strong; many are willing and interested in the work of the Lord, but through prayer your weak flesh will be controlled by your strong spirit [6].

- **Learn the skills of a shepherd.** Relating with God is a skill you must learn, and a disciplined person with consistent prayer and personal Bible study shows a deep relationship with God [8]. Waiting on God is also a skill few have — if you do not wait on God you will not hear from Him, and they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31) [8].

-

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 6 of *The Determinants*, chapter 6 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 12 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities* and chapter 9 of *The Privilege*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 52:6-8; Ecclesiastes 9:11; Isaiah 40:31; Philippians 3:8; 2 Timothy 2:1; 2 Timothy 4:7.

items.question: How do I know my work for God is not a waste of time?
items.text:
It's a good and honest question to bring, and the books speak to it directly.

**Your labour in the Lord is not in vain.** Solomon called his own work vanity, but Paul described his work differently — "your labour is not in vain in the Lord" [2]. Working in the world is vanity; it is working in the Lord that is not vanity [2].

**Your work is the very reason God gave you new life.** These good works are why God gave us a new life in Him — so that we would live for Him and do His purposes, and He says, "I know thy works!" [3].

**Doing the work makes your personal problems smaller.** As you minister the Word of God, your problems become smaller; instead of focusing on your difficulties, you lift up your eyes to the Lord of the harvest [3]. God has never used perfect people — Noah had a drinking problem, Abraham had serious marital problems, Rahab had moral problems, yet God used them [3]. We carry this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Corinthians 4:7) [3].

**Your rewards are stored up in Heaven.** Ministry work expends energy and money, and you may get tired — but that tiredness is a sign the activity has entered the realm of work [5]. Your rewards and treasures will come one day in Heaven, as Matthew 6:20 says: "lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" [5].

**You have a limited season, which makes the work precious rather than wasted.** A short period is allotted for the work of ministry (Numbers 8:24-25), and some people delay unduly and lose their opportunity to work for God [4]. If you find yourself working in a church, be thankful and behave yourself wisely, because it is a privilege [4].

One caution worth holding alongside all this: God does not look on the outward appearance but on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), and no one is saved by religious works and good deeds — you are saved by grace through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9) [6]. So the worth of your work was never measured by how it looks to men.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 10 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapter 2 of *Church Planting*, chapter 10 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 30 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 8:24-25; 1 Samuel 16:7; Ecclesiastes 3:13; Ecclesiastes 5:10; Matthew 6:1-2; Matthew 6:20; Matthew 23:5; Luke 12:15; Romans 3:28; 1 Corinthians 15:10 and 3 more.

items.question: How can I motivate the people who follow me as a leader?
items.text:
Here are the ways our books describe for motivating the people who follow you.

- **Make them feel genuinely respected.** People naturally love those who respect them, and once a follower feels real self-worth and respect from you, you have gone a long way in winning their heart [1].

- **Turn your followers into great, distinguished people.** A true leader wants those he leads to become great; when people sense that following you will make them great and let them prosper in what you are building, they will stay close and be willing to obey [1]. Jesus did this with his followers, transforming them into the apostles we know, and promising them mansions and rewards — no wonder they died for him [1].

- **Sacrifice for them and give them a future and a hope.** You make people enthusiastic by sacrificing to make them happy; a congregation grows far more eager when they see their pastor building for them rather than only acquiring nice things for himself, so pay well and see that those who work for you have a home, cars and enough money [1]. A leader should aim for his followers to do well spiritually, as 3 John 4 says, and to do well financially, since Jesus himself promised his followers houses, lands and enough money [6].

- **Be real and speak from your heart.** The most successful leaders are those who are "real"; no one wants to follow a pretender, and people love hearing a leader speak naturally from his heart rather than reading a boring speech [2]. A leader without conviction is a lifeless, speech-reading, emotionless puppet whom nobody follows [8].

items.question: What does the Bible say happens to a society that stops being thankful to God?
items.text:
Our books speak to this directly, and the picture they paint is sobering.

When people know God but refuse to glorify Him or give thanks, their thinking becomes futile and their foolish hearts are darkened — as Romans 1:21 says, they become vain in their imaginations [1][2]. The books describe this unthankfulness as a kind of insanity, a madness that spreads: people fail to be grateful for the air they breathe, the water they drink, and the life God has given them, even while surrounded by so much destruction [1].

From there, the descent deepens. Because they were not thankful, God gave the human race up — three times over — to uncleanness, to vile affections, and to a debased mind, so that men and women turned against the natural use of one another [1][2]. The books trace the world's perversion and foolishness straight back to ingratitude, saying the human race is teetering on the brink of destruction because we are ungrateful both to men and to God [2].

And it does not stop with the society at large. Unthankfulness is listed among the terrible faults of the last days, alongside pride, blasphemy, and disobedience to parents, and we are told that in the last days men will grow more and more ungrateful [5]. The books warn that this is a high-ranking evil of our generation, a door that opens a person up to the most wicked spirits, and they urge us to be thankful [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 7 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 9:16-21; Luke 6:35; Romans 1:21; Romans 1:26-28; Colossians 3:15; 1 Timothy 4:3-5; 2 Timothy 3:1-5.

items.question: How do I know if I've been called by God to do His work?
items.text:
What a good question to bring — and one the books take seriously, because they say the call is the only real way into ministry [2]. Here is how they describe the signs.

- **A supernatural desire and interest in the work.** The books say that a genuine desire for ministry is itself a symptom of a divine call within you — it may not be a sensational experience, but it is a burden God has put there [3]. Paul's own words, "My heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved" (Romans 10:1), are given as an example of that desire being translated into practical ministry again and again [3].

- **A conviction that you are called, not a self-appointment.** No man can take this honour unto himself (Hebrews 5:4); no one should call himself, and ministry must wait until there is a definite call [2]. The book compares it to a girl getting married — she cannot propose to a man, she has to wait until a man proposes to her [2].

- **A specific commission that is yours alone.** The call of God is a specific commission He has for you; no one in the Bible had the commission Jonah had, as he was the only one sent to Nineveh [2]. You are to see yourself as someone with a specific mission that only you can accomplish [2].

- **A willing commitment to obey.** Some people know they are called and even have the desire, yet no commitment is seen in them [3]. Isaiah's response is held up as the true sign: "Here am I; send me" (Isaiah 6:8) — not "send him" [3].

- **Taking God's Word, dreams, visions and quiet times seriously.** The difference between those who seem called and those who seem to have no special calling is that those who believe they are called take a message from God's Word, their dreams, their visions and their quiet times more seriously than the average person [5].

- **A sense of destiny about it.** The call of God is no accident; it is the fulfilment of your predestination that caused you to walk into a church and hear about the call of God [5]. Whom He did predestinate, them He also called (Romans 8:30) [5].

- **Grace upon you.** To be called means the grace of God is upon you — kindness over and above the kindness that caused your salvation, so that you are well-favoured and precious because the call of God is upon you [4].

One more thing the books say plainly: don't take the call of God lightly, for you could pay with your life for disobeying the divine call [3]. And if you are unsure, remember that all born-again Christians have a supernatural calling to be saints — it may not be spectacular, but it is certainly supernatural [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapters 2 and 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 5 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 2 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 6:8; Jeremiah 1:7; Zechariah 2:8; Luke 4:18; John 1:6; John 4:34; Romans 1:7; Romans 8:30; Romans 10:1; 1 Corinthians 1:2 and 4 more.

items.question: One of my members says she has no reason to live anymore.
items.text:
That is a heavy thing to carry, and I am glad she has you near her in it.

What our books speak to most directly is the shortness of this life and the weight of the time we still have. One pastor was shown in a vision two dead ministers who had come back briefly and visited the churches they had built; they were grieved that their messages and their songs no longer moved anyone, and they told him plainly, "You have the best chance now. This is your time to be fruitful. Our time is past. Our chance is gone." He woke understanding that he could depart at any time, and that this present life is the chance to do God's will and finish His work [2]. The same warning is recorded again: this is our best chance, and soon we will be out of this world with no further chance to work for God [4].

So the counsel our books hold out to someone who feels she has no reason to live is not a list of reasons drawn from her circumstances, but this: her time is not past — it is now, and it is her best chance to be fruitful for the Lord and to finish her course [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Weeping and Gnashing* and chapter 9 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.

items.question: What happens in my life when I don't pray?
items.text:
When you don't pray, your life doesn't simply drift on its own — the books say it gets steered by forces you never chose.

- **Your life is directed by happenstance.** What looks like chance, luck, or fate is often governed by natural and spiritual factors working behind the scenes [1]. The story of King Ahab makes this plain: he disguised himself in battle, and a soldier drew his bow at random and struck him between the sections of his armor, and he died that evening — what looked like a random arrow was actually orchestrated by evil spirits [2].

- **Your life is governed by the major curses in this world.** The course of this world is largely determined by the curse on Adam, the curse on Eve, and the curse on Ham, and without prayer your life follows that stereotyped pattern [2]. Prayer, especially prayer for wisdom, is what changes this — curses are made bearable and defeated through wisdom, and Proverbs 3:13-16 says that length of days, riches, and honor come with wisdom [2].

- **Your life is governed by the god of this world.** Satan is called the god of this world, and he directs the affairs of this world into wars, conflicts, and countless sorrows [2]. This is why he could offer Jesus all the kingdoms of the world in the temptation — they were actually under his control [2][4]. When you don't pray, you don't call on God to legally intervene in your life here, and things simply go a certain way [4].

- **You fail to intervene in the spirit realm.** Spiritual beings and spiritual events cause things to happen in the natural — in Revelation 6:1-8, each seal opened and trumpet blown triggered events on earth [4]. When you pray, you enter the spirit realm and affect what goes on there; when you don't, you leave those events untouched [4].

- **Your life is governed by the wickedness of men.** The whole world lies in wickedness, as 1 John 5:19 says, and the will of man is often the will of Satan [4][5]. People around you are making decisions that affect you right now — a boss, a teacher, a spouse — and if you don't pray, the will of capricious and unreasonable men gets implemented in your life [3]. Jesus prayed long and hard in Gethsemane precisely so His life would not be governed by men's jealousies, greed, hatred, and disloyalty [5].

- **You miss the will of God being done.** Even though you may know God's will, it still must be prayed for — Jesus knew He had come to die, yet He still prayed for the Father's will to be done, three times, with the same words [3]. If you do not pray for the will of God, circumstances will direct you away from it [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to Pray*, chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer* and chapter 13 of *Read your Bible Pray Everyday*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 22:30-35; Proverbs 3:13-16; Ecclesiastes 4:14; Matthew 4:8-9; Matthew 6:6-7; Matthew 6:9-10; Matthew 16:22-23; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 John 5:19; Revelation 6:1-8.

items.question: How do I know if I'm ready to step into a bigger role in ministry?
items.text:
I'm glad you're asking this honestly rather than assuming — the books have a good deal to say about readiness.

- **Settle the deeper questions in your heart first.** Before stepping into something as challenging as full-time ministry, you must ask yourself some questions and settle certain issues in your heart forever — it is not a career move but a walk of faith in things not seen [1].

- **Be willing to leave familiar things behind.** Ask whether you're ready to leave old friends and acquaintances, since ministry separates you from many familiar things — your day off is usually Monday, which separates you from lay people and their lives [1].

- **Be ready to leave your own country, region, or neighbourhood.** Going away from your country is a real option for anyone coming into full-time ministry, and if we are ready to go to the nations there will never be enough people for the work [1].

- **Bring your whole family along.** It matters that your household follows you on this road, because some spouses reject the uncertainty of it all — a wise man will not marry someone who shows signs of allergy to uncertainty [7].

- **Don't enter too quickly.** Many ministries are frustrated because people entered full-time ministry too quickly, and there are people in full-time ministry who should not really be there; success requires both power and wisdom, as 1 Corinthians 1:24 says [3].

- **Let experience and proven service come first.** God does not put inexperienced people into the ministry — you need experience to be effective, and Scripture says not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6) [4]. There are four levels in the line of God's service: doing the work, having a gift, having a ministry, and occupying an office, as 2 Timothy 4:5 and Romans 11:13 describe [4].

- **Go the extra mile.** Christians who don't go the extra mile for fellowship, soaking in the Word, prayer, and fasting do not amount to much in the ministry — the five wise virgins in Matthew 25:4 made the extra effort, while the other five took the ministry for granted and were left out [5].

- **Be available for every experience God allows.** All the different experiences God allows you to have prepare you for the anointing — the churches you attend, the pastors you know, and the people you meet are divinely arranged, and to a believer there is no accident or coincidence [6].

- **Know that ministry moves in seasons.** God comes to you as the rain, the latter and former rain (Hosea 6:3), so there is a season of early rain that starts you off and brings you out of obscurity, a quiet season where you grow in faithfulness, endurance and persistence, and a later season where the rain falls again and things become much bigger [8].

One more

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapter 14 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 15 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 7 and 8 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 21 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 18:19; Psalms 1:1-3; Hosea 6:3; Matthew 25:4-5; Acts 1:3; Romans 11:13; Romans 12:6; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Timothy 3:6 and 1 more.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Disloyalty rarely announces itself; it grows quietly, so it helps to know what to watch for.

- **An independent spirit.** Watch for someone who becomes autonomous within the group — still part of it, but doing what he wants despite contrary instructions. If you call a fast on Friday, he quietly keeps his own Wednesday fast, and he attends only the meetings he judges important, obeying only the instructions he thinks really matter [1].

- **Absence in times of pressure.** Notice who disappears when the church is going through hard times; it is in pressure and crisis that true character shows. One leader tells of a crisis in his church when he urgently called some pastoral trainees to accompany him to see government officials, and they simply did not turn up — he felt depressed and let down in a time of war [2].

- **Inflexibility and stubbornness.** An inflexible person is defiant, unwilling to go beyond what is stipulated, always pointing out that work ends at 5 p.m., and sulking when asked to do something new. Such a person also refuses correction when confronted — as Saul argued with Samuel, insisting "I have performed the commandment of the Lord" even while the bleating of the sheep gave him away [3].

- **Silence and quiet satisfaction when things go wrong.** A disloyal assistant has no comment, good or bad, when you bring a new idea or vision, and when things go wrong he is quick to say, "I knew all along that this would not work" — glad that it failed [4].

- **A preoccupation with his own position.** He thinks, "I would be a better head if I had the chance," is unhappy about the differences that make him subordinate, and cares more about his own image than about raising yours [4].

- **Criticism, murmuring and fault-finding.** Where members criticise their leader, undermine their pastors, accuse, murmur and find fault, there is demonic activity at work; Jesus said of His own twelve, "one of you is a devil" (John 6:70) [7].

- **A warning about your own confidence.** Do not trust everyone's praises. Jesus did not commit Himself to those who seemed to praise Him, because He knew what was in man (John 2:24, 25), and even His own brothers gave Him advice that was not genuine (John 7:5) [2]. And remember that loyalty today does not mean loyalty tomorrow — one leader tells of a brother who proclaimed his commitment at meetings and condemned a rebel publicly, yet years later pulled out unexpectedly and kept some of the church's properties [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapters 4 and 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 5 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 1:5-7; John 2:24-25; John 6:70; John 7:3; John 7:5.

items.question: Why is the shepherd's ministry so important in the church?
items.text:
The shepherd's ministry matters because it is the ministry God uses to gather and keep His people. It is because there is no shepherd that the sheep are scattered—not because there is no prophet [1]. God will save His people through the shepherd, and the earth will yield her increase through him [1].

A shepherd's first duty is to feed the sheep, and the authority to lead is given to those with the ability to feed [2]. Jesus told Peter three times, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17), showing how important it is to the Lord that His sheep are well fed on the Word of God [2].

He also comforts them. Every sheep should be able to say, "Your rod and your staff comfort me" (Psalm 23:4), and God is angry with shepherds who have not ministered to the sheep under that comforting ministry (Ezekiel 34:4) [3]. The shepherd must genuinely love the sheep and stand by them in their greatest need and greatest joy [3].

He leads and rules them as well. A pastor is the head of the local church, and a head must take decisions; the sheep are looking for someone with direction, who knows where he is going [4]. And he builds a secure dwelling for them—a good shepherd builds church buildings so his sheep can be safely nurtured within its four walls [5].

items.question: What habits did Jesus have that made Him great?
items.text:
What a good question to sit with — the Lord's own habits are meant to be our pattern.

- **He went to church regularly.** The Bible says He had a custom of going into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, as Luke 4:16 records [1][2][3][4][5][6].
- **He went on prayer retreats.** He had a habit of going to a particular garden, a place He resorted to often, and everyone knew it — even Judas knew the place, as John 18:1–2 tells us [1][2][3].
- **He spent extended time alone with God.** He spent three days in the temple seeking God, and His parents only found Him after three days [8].
- **He asked questions about the ministry.** He was found in the temple hearing the doctors and asking them questions [8].

And Daniel stands alongside Him as an example: he prayed at specific times of the day, three times daily, as was his custom, and it was one of the greatest secrets of his life [1][2][3][5][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 8 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapters 8 and 9 of *The Secret*, chapter 44 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 1 of *How to Pray* and chapter 4 of *Ready@20*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 6:10; Luke 3:21; Luke 4:16; John 18:1-2.

items.question: How can I show God that I'm thankful for everything He's done for me?
items.text:
Gratitude to God is not something you can put in a letter — the books say the only way to say "thank you" is with your life [4]. Here are the ways they describe:

- **Give Him your whole life as a reasonable service.** Since He saved you, washed you, and gave you His best days, it is only reasonable to present your body as a living sacrifice, which is your reasonable service [1][2]. That means giving Him your youth and the best times of your life, not waiting until you cannot hear well or need glasses to read [1].

- **Labour more abundantly than everyone else.** Paul said he laboured more abundantly than all the apostles because he was conscious of the grace shown to him, and he did not want that grace to be in vain (1 Corinthians 15:10) [2]. There is no future for a lazy person in the church; you show that God's grace was not in vain by working harder than everyone else [2].

- **Be willing, fast, and complete in your obedience.** God foreknew you, predestined you, called you, justified you, and glorified you (Romans 8:29-30), so show your gratefulness by adjusting your life and humbly yielding to everything He asks [3]. You cannot tell Him, "Take it or leave it" — if you value the call, you adjust your life [3].

- **Be thankful for God's servants.** Appreciate those who diligently labour among you and have charge over you in the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5:12), because God's servants are His gift to you (Ephesians 4:11) [5]. When you are discontented and angry at His gift, you can imagine how God feels [5].

- **Thank Him in everything, and for everything.** Give thanks in every circumstance (1 Thessalonians 5:18), which is easier than giving thanks for everything (Ephesians 5:20) — thank Him for the good, the bad, and the ugly, and His power will be released in your life [5].

- **Let your thanks say that He is good.** Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good and His mercy endures forever (Psalm 107:1; 118:1, 29) [5]. Giving thanks sends God the message that you believe He is good and not a bad person in your life [5].

- **Avoid the opposite — murmuring and repaying good with evil.** The Israelites said "thank you" for their deliverance by murmuring against God in their tents (Deuteronomy 1:27), and unthankfulness is listed among the last-day evils (2 Timothy 3:2) [6][7]. Repaying good with evil brings a curse, so be a fir tree and a myrtle tree instead of a thorny brier (Pro

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3 and 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 5 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody*.

items.question: Where do demons come from?
items.text:
Our books describe demons as coming from a specific and terrible origin, not from God's good creation.

They teach that demons are the surviving spirits of the "para-humans" — the giants and hybrid creatures born when fallen angels had intercourse with human women. When those giant half-human, half-angel beings died, their spirits could not go to heaven or hell like ordinary human souls; instead they were confined to the earth and roam about as demons [1]. The Book of Enoch is cited for this: "Evil spirits have come out from their bodies because they are born from men and from the holy Watchers... they shall be evil spirits on earth" [1][6]. These spirits, the books say, "afflict, oppress, destroy, attack, war, destroy, and cause trouble on the earth" [6].

A related passage describes a further origin for what it calls unclean or animal spirits: fallen angels also sinned against birds, animals, fish and reptiles, and the offspring of those unions continued to interbreed, producing the strange wicked spirit-animal creatures known as unclean spirits [3].

The books are careful to distinguish demons from Satan and the fallen angels. Satan and the fallen angels are a separate order of beings; the angels were created good with free will, and some rebelled [2]. Demons, by contrast, are described as "another set of creatures" — the diamonion, distinct from the diabolos — that came into existence through the death of the para-humans [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies* and chapter 4 of *One of You is a Devil*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:31; Colossians 1:16; Jude 6.

items.question: How can I become a friend of God like Abraham was?
items.text:
Abraham's friendship with God wasn't a title he claimed — it was something God said of him because of how he lived. Here are the ways the books describe it.

- **Obey God completely, whatever it costs.** Abraham obeyed God even to the point of being willing to sacrifice his own son, and it was this obedience — the test of love — that made him God's friend [2][4]. God had told him to leave his country for a land he did not know, and he went at once; the blessing came on the condition that he obeyed [7].

- **Let nothing become a third party between you and God.** Abraham had no adviser, no friend lurking in the shadows, not even Sarah, coming between him and God [2]. God is jealous and warns us not to hearken to any voice — even a sincere one — that draws us away from Him, for He is proving whether we love Him with all our heart and soul (Deuteronomy 13:3) [2].

- **Be willing to give up your "Isaac."** God asked Abraham for his only son, and Abraham was ready to give up everything for Him [5]. Anything that becomes too precious to you becomes a potential idol, and God may ask for it; He wants to be the only God in your life [5].

- **Intercede for others.** Abraham pleaded with God for Sodom and Gomorrah, and God heeded him, even agreeing to spare the city if ten righteous men could be found [1]. When Job prayed for his friends, it was Job's own captivity that God turned (Job 42:10) [5].

- **Labour to be a blessing, not to be rich.** God told Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and you never find Abraham striving for wealth — you find him labouring to obey and please his Creator [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities*, chapters 2 and 11 of *If You Love The Lord*, chapter 5 of *The Art of Following* and chapter 7 of *Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich*.

items.question: How should I keep the Sabbath day as a Christian?
items.text:
The books speak to this in several ways, and they don't all sound the same note, so let me lay out what each says.

- **Set apart a day for rest from secular work.** The Sabbath is meant to be a day of rest for you, and it doesn't matter whether you choose Saturday, Sunday or Monday — what matters is that you have chosen a day to set apart for God and to rest from your ordinary work [1][3].

- **Go to church on that day.** The Sabbath is the day for going to church; Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath as His custom, and you cannot use the day for the stadium, the golf course, the night club, or sleeping in at home [1][5][6]. The book of Hebrews warns us not to forsake assembling together (Hebrews 10:25), and Judas is held up as a warning of what happens to a person who keeps avoiding fellowship for "legitimate" reasons [6].

- **Hear the word of God.** The Sabbath is a day for hearing the word of God — when Paul preached at Antioch, almost the whole city gathered the next Sabbath to hear the word of God (Acts 13:44), and the day is not for soccer, radio, or visiting friends instead [1].

- **Preach and teach the word.** Jesus honoured the Sabbath by preaching and teaching, entering the synagogue at Capernaum and teaching (Mark 1:21), and we are told to be like Him in this [1].

- **Let it test and grow your trust in God.** The Sabbath is a test of your ability to trust God and rest in Him — it takes faith to believe God will care for you even when you do not work (Exodus 20:10), and it brings out your willingness to rest, to be holy and special, and to be obedient [4]. The Jews' worldwide observance of the Sabbath has kept them a distinct and special people [4].

- **Remember what God brought you out of.** Righteous people remember their low points and how they came out of them; Israel was commanded to keep the Sabbath in remembrance that they had been servants in Egypt and the Lord brought them out (Deuteronomy 5:15) [7].

- **But do not let the day become a rule that overrides doing good.** Jesus healed a man with dropsy on the Sabbath and asked whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, pointing out that no one would leave an ox or donkey in a pit on that day (Luke 14:1-6); He said plainly that it is lawful to do well on the Sabbath days (Matthew 12:12) [2]. The book warns that Pharisee pastors become strict to the point of cruelty, critical in small matters, and blind — and that no rule or doctrine is truth; Jesus Himself is the truth (John 14:6) [

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Seven Great Principles*, chapter 25 of *Stir It Up*, chapter 4 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous*, chapter 1 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 10 of *Key Facts for New Believers* and chapter 6 of *Those Who Forget*.

items.question: How can I have a closer relationship with God?
items.text:
Wanting to be closer to God is a good desire, and our books speak to it plainly. Here are the ways they give.

- **Draw near to Him yourself, daily.** God does not come to you to build the relationship; it is up to you to draw near to Him, and He promises that when you do, He will draw near to you, as James 4:8 says [1][4]. The only way to know Him personally is a regular daily quiet time [1][4].

- **Be alone with Him.** When you are alone with someone you become close and intimate in a way a group meeting cannot produce, and you develop a bond and a knowledge of God you cannot acquire in public [6]. Paul's prayer was "that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection" (Philippians 3:10) [6].

- **Don't mistake public work for knowing Him.** It is possible to be a member, to prophesy and do wonderful works in His name, and still hear Him say, "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:21-23) [1]. Coming to church a thousand times, attending conventions and crusades, is different from personal, one-to-one interaction with the Lord [1][4].

- **Come through the blood.** You who were once far off have been made near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:12-16), so you can make advances toward God whenever you want, and He will relate with you as a child and a friend [8]. Through that same blood you can have communion with God [8].

- **Accept the doors He has given you.** People do not become close to God until they accept apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists; these are doors, and those too stiff to go through them will never experience a certain level of God's presence [7].

- **Take the little things seriously.** There are no meaningless details in the Bible, and little things often make a big difference; never trivialize an instruction or detail given by an important person, because to an important person a little detail is a very big thing [2].

- **Let go of the inferiority your sins create.** As we get closer to God we sense our unworthiness, and relationships break down when one party always feels inferior; to love God properly you must accept that you are forgiven and that everything in the past is washed away by the blood of Jesus [3].

- **Be prayerful.** Authority and closeness flow from your prayer life; the closer you are to a person, the more confidently you speak about him, and your private prayer will make people believe in you [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapters 2 and 18 of *Steps to God's Presence*, chapter 6 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 5 of *The Secret*, chapter 118 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 21 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent* and chapter 8 of *Blood Power*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:21-23; Matthew 12:36; Matthew 27:33-36; Matthew 27:50-51; Ephesians 2:12-16; Ephesians 4:3; Ephesians 4:11-13; Philippians 3:10; Hebrews 9:1-5; James 4:8 and 1 more.

items.question: How can a husband and wife make love in a way that is enjoyable for both of them?
items.text:
Lovemaking is meant to be a shared joy, not a performance, so the two of you can relax and learn this together as an art.

- **Make it a mutual pursuit of pleasure.** Sex was created by God as something beautiful and pleasurable for both husband and wife to enjoy, not just for procreation, and both partners should set out to give and receive maximum excitement [1]. It is not about scoring ten out of ten for your performance; it is about having fun with your partner and showing care [4].

- **Build the atmosphere before you ever reach the bedroom.** Be nice to each other during the day through small thoughtful acts like an intimate phone call or a bunch of flowers, and each of you should look nice, smell nice and be clean, perhaps wearing something your partner finds exciting [1]. items.question: How can I pray like Jesus did?
items.text:
Praying like Jesus is something the books describe in very practical ways. Here is what they hold out to you.

- **Pray short and bold in a crisis.** When Lazarus had been dead four days and everyone was watching, Jesus did not retreat for three hours; He prayed a short prayer and then acted boldly, and you can do the same and see one hundred per cent results [1][2].

- **Pray long when there is time.** Jesus went out to a mountain and continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12), and rose a great while before day to pray in a solitary place (Mark 1:35); develop the art of praying for several hours, starting with one hour and graduating to three, then five and seven [1][2].

- **Stay on the same topic for hours.** You do not have to change the prayer topic; praying on the same thing for hours is not useless repetition, it is praying like Jesus did [1][2].

- **Pray with strong cries and tears at times.** Jesus offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears (Hebrews 5:7); most of the time you can pray quietly, but there is a dimension of loud prayer you must get into, for some things will only happen when you pray like Jesus did [2].

- **Give thanks.** Apart from the usual "give me" prayers, God would love to hear "thank you"; in everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and as you thank Him you will experience many breakthroughs [2].

- **Pray to the Father, not to anyone else.** Jesus directed us to ask the Father in His name (John 16:23); begin your prayer by saying "Our Father," "Heavenly Father," or "Dear Father," and you will begin to experience better results [5].

- **Pray according to His will, led by the Spirit.** Jesus did nothing of Himself but only what He saw the Father do (John 5:19), and we have confidence that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us (1 John 5:14); many are unsuccessful in prayer because God is not leading them specifically [7].

- **Pray as a priest.** Jesus came as a priest and prayed as a priest (Hebrews 5:6-7), and God has washed us from our sins and made us kings and priests unto God (Revelation 1:5-6); as a priest you must offer sacrifices and prayers [8].

- **Set yourself targets and fast.** Set a target of hours to pray — ten, twenty, forty, fifty hours — and develop the art of waiting on God by praying with absolute fasting [6].

- **Pray in tongues for long periods.** Because the mind is unfruitful while the spirit prays, you can read the Bible

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 6 of *100% Answered Prayer*, chapters 7 and 9 of *How to Pray*, chapter 24 of *Church Growth* and chapter 21 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

items.question: What does it mean if God rewards my faithfulness with more work instead of rest?
items.book: WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work
items.text:
That's a good question, and the books speak to it directly.

The short answer is that God is the rewarding type, and one of His great rewards for hard work is to give you more work [2]. So when more work comes instead of rest, that is not God overlooking you — it is God thanking you. He will thank you for your efforts with the little church by giving you a big church to work with [1].

It helps to see that rest is also a reward, but it is not the only one. The books say hard work is often rewarded by lots of rest, and that God indeed has rest for His servants — yet they go on to show that God does not only give rest, but actually gives more work after the period of rest [2]. So more work is not the absence of reward; it is one of its forms.

The pattern runs all through Scripture. Joseph worked hard as Potiphar's overseer, and his reward was more work as the prison overseer; then his faithfulness in the prison was rewarded by being made overseer of all Egypt [4]. David was faithful with a few sheep, and God made him a national hero and then king of all Israel [3]. Jesus Himself said, "Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities" (Luke 19:17) [7]. And the Lord said of the good and faithful servant, "thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things" (Matthew 25:23) [8].

So the counsel is: do not expect holidays and restful seasons — expect more hard work [3]. Do not let your accomplishments lead you into retirement, leisure, or delusions; the reward for a hard-fought ministry is more ministry, the reward for being a good pastor is more pastoral work [5]. Keep pressing on, because God has plans to give you more hard work which He expects you to be faithful with [1].

And there is a further comfort in it: this does not end at death. The Bible says of His servants in eternity, "and his servants shall serve him" (Revelation 22:3) — the reward for all the obedience and ministry we have performed on earth will be to become His servants [6]. Let the revelation of "more work" guide you until you get into eternity [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work* and chapter 3 of *Be Thou Faithful Unto Death*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 15:1; Genesis 39:4-5; Genesis 39:20-23; Genesis 41:39-43; Ecclesiastes 12:12; Matthew 16:27; Matthew 25:23; Luke 12:42; Luke 16:10-12; Luke 19:17 and 6 more.

items.question: How can I grow and be more successful without becoming overconfident and setting myself up for a fall?
items.text:
It's good that you're asking this — the desire to grow and the fear of falling can live together, and the books speak to both.

- **Stay humble enough to keep learning.** Ministers stop learning at the rate at which they become proud, because pride takes away childlikeness and makes you unable to receive from people you despise — even someone from a different country, tribe or colour, someone with a funny accent, someone too young, someone you consider inferior [3]. When you are humble like a child you copy things easily, and copying is the divine method given to children to surge forward and catch up with adults [3].

- **Do not treat your position as foolproof.** If you regard yourself or your position in Christ as foolproof, you are in danger of backsliding — especially if you have had promotion in church or have been used by God in the past [2]. Where you are over-confident is where you can be the weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2].

- **Watch how you talk about others' weaknesses.** You can tell a Christian is over-confident by the way he talks about the weaknesses of others, criticizing them as though he could never make the same mistakes, overestimating his own ability and looking down on others [2]. When David heard that Saul was dead, he did not ridicule him or rejoice over his death, though he could have taken the opportunity to discuss what led to Saul's downfall [2].

- **Let past success feed gratitude, not presumption.** Recklessly advancing is caused by hubris born of success — the pride and confidence that comes because of your past successes, making you feel that what lies ahead will be defeated as easily as what you just conquered [4]. The children of Israel presumed to go up to the hilltop after God had said not to, and the Amalekites and Canaanites came down and smote them even unto Hormah [4].

- **Keep pressing forward rather than resting on the past.** Some Christians are hooked on the past, telling tales of the great exploits God used them to do years ago, but the time to minister to others is now [6]. The greatest blessing you can have is to become a blessing yourself, and a Christian should have the ambition to be useful in God's house [6].

- **Feed your faith by meditation.** Faith rises and falls depending on what you meditate on, and faith is a type of obedience that is not possible without meditating on the Word [5]. Joshua's only hope to prevent him from following the mistakes of his fathers was meditation, and God told him the book of the law was not to depart out of his mouth but he was to meditate in it day and night [5].

- **Do not become hard and stubborn.** A stubborn Christian who does not heed counsel can stray from the paths of righteousness, and stubbornness to God, to His Word, to His pastors and to biblical counsel

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 7 of *Backsliding*, chapter 2 of *Those who are Proud*, chapter 72 of *A Good General* and chapter 35 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 14:40-45; 1 Corinthians 10:12; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: How can I know the real number of people attending our church instead of just guessing?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and they are clear that the honest headcount is the place to start.

- **Count the people actually present.** The most informative figure is the headcount of human beings physically in the meeting — what the books call Type 1 counting — and it is usually the lowest number, which is exactly why it is the most useful [1][4]. Have your head usher or data officer do this count every Sunday [4][7].

- **Beware of the other ways of counting.** Counting everyone on the register, adding up attendance across the nights of a convention, estimating from how full the building looks, or giving a rough guess all produce figures that can mislead you [1]. There is even a kind of counting that simply aims to outdo everyone else in town, and the book calls that a spirit of lying and exaggeration [7].

- **Ask for the figures only after some months.** Counting every week and watching it closely can discourage you, because attendance fluctuates so much; the book's counsel is to keep counting each Sunday but only review the numbers after several months have passed, so you can see whether there is real improvement [7].

- **Let the true number do its work in you.** Knowing where you actually are helps you plan and move forward, and it stirs you to pray, fast, and seek God more [4]. The truth, as John 8:32 says, is what sets you free — it tells you where you are, where you are not, and where to go [2].

- **Keep the numbers in perspective.** Numbering is biblical, and God is interested in how much has been gained by trading (Luke 19:12, 15), but the danger is putting your trust in the numbers themselves; as 1 Samuel 14:6 says, there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 45 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 14:6; Proverbs 27:23-24; Luke 13:23; Luke 19:1-48; John 8:32; Romans 12:3; 1 Corinthians 3:13.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
Our books give a few ways to choose what to read.

- **Read through a book of the Bible a few verses at a time.** Pick a book and read a few verses every day, always remembering where you ended so you can continue from that same place the next day [3][4][5].
- **Follow a personality through the Bible.** Choose someone whose life story you follow, because a few verses from passages about Moses, for example, will give you much revelation for your life [3][4][5].
- **Use a daily reading guide.** Take the passage suggested in your reading guide; these guides are very helpful in developing a regular quiet time habit, and you will benefit from anointed teachers whose ministry helps you grow [3][4][8]. When he first became a Christian, Bishop Dag Heward-Mills depended on the *Our Daily Bread* devotional for his quiet time [3][4][8].
- **Go through a particular book, stopping where the Spirit speaks.** Decide to go through a particular book of the Bible every day, read a few verses of a chapter, and stop exactly where the Holy Spirit seems to be speaking — then stay there and meditate until the full revelation comes [6].

However you choose, read expecting God to speak to you, praying as Psalm 119:18 says, "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" [4][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 3 of *The Secret*, chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 34:6-8; Joshua 1:8; Psalms 119:18; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Timothy 2:7; Hebrews 5:14.

items.question: What will heaven and the new earth be like?
items.book: Who Is He That Overcometh the World
items.text:
Heaven and the world to come are the home we are heading toward, and the books describe them with real warmth.

- **It will be a brand-new world.** The world we know will pass away and be replaced by the world to come, the future world that God has prepared [1]. Everything we gathered and built here will be left behind, and we will be well established in another world [1].

- **The desires that pulled us from God will be gone.** When this world passes away, its lusts pass away with it, and the one who does the will of God abides forever, as 1 John 2:17 says [1].

- **God Himself will be with us, and every tear will be wiped away.** In the new world you will feel God's presence everywhere, and He will wipe the tears from our eyes; there will be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, for the former things will have passed away, as Revelation 21:1-5 says [1][2]. There will be no more curse, and His servants will serve Him, as Revelation 22:1-3 says [1][3].

- **It will be a beautiful city with life flowing through it.** The world to come has the New Jerusalem, a beautiful city where all nations walk in its light, with a river of life and a tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations [3]. No evil thing, no abomination, and no liar can enter it, and there will be no night and no need of sun or candle there [3].

- **The kingdoms of this world will become the Lord's.** The kingdoms of this world were handed to satan, but Jesus came to destroy the power of the god of this world and set many free, and the day is coming when the kingdoms of this world become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, as Revelation 11:15 says [1].

- **People we know as nobodies will rule.** In the world to come, those who seemed like nobodies on earth will become rulers, presidents, and heads of nations [1]. Appointments over the countries of the world will be given to those who do the work of the Lord, as Revelation 2:26 says [7].

- **There are rewards waiting that we cannot yet fully understand.** Those who overcome will be given hidden manna and a white stone with a new name written on it, whose value we will likely discover only when we arrive in Heaven, as Revelation 2:17 says [7].

So take heart: this world is not our home, and the world in view is far greater than this current one [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Who Is He That Overcometh the World*, chapter 31 of *Victory Secrets*, chapter 20 of *How To Neutralize Curses* and chapter 1 of *Tell Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 4:6; Ephesians 1:21; 1 John 2:17; Revelation 2:17; Revelation 2:26; Revelation 11:15; Revelation 21:1-5; Revelation 22:1-5.

- **God Himself will be with us, and every tear will be wiped away.** In the new world you will feel God's presence everywhere, and He will wipe the tears from our eyes; there will be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, for the former things will have passed away, as Revelation 21:1-5 says.

- **God Himself will be with us, and every tear will be wiped away.** In the new world you will feel God's presence everywhere, and He will wipe the tears from our eyes; there will be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, for the former things will have passed away, as Revelation 21:1-5 says.
There will be no more curse, and His servants will serve Him, as Revelation 22:1-3 says.
