- **It will be a beautiful city with life flowing through it.** The world to come has the New Jerusalem, a beautiful city where all nations walk in its light, with a river of life and a tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations.
No evil thing, no abomination, and no liar can enter it, and there will be no night and no need of sun or candle there.

- **The kingdoms of this world will become the Lord's.** The kingdoms of this world were handed to satan, but Jesus came to destroy the power of the god of this world and set many free, and the day is coming when the kingdoms of this world become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, as Revelation 11:15 says.
- **People we know as nobodies will rule.** In the world to come, those who seemed like nobodies on earth will become rulers, presidents, and heads of nations.
Appointments over the countries of the world will be given to those who do the work of the Lord, as Revelation 2:26 says.

- **There are rewards waiting that we cannot yet fully understand.** Those who overcome will be given hidden manna and a white stone with a new name written on it, whose value we will likely discover only when we arrive in Heaven, as Revelation 2:17 says.
So take heart: this world is not our home, and the world in view is far greater than this current one.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
This is a heavy thing to carry, and I'm glad you're asking rather than looking away.

The books speak to this directly. A Jezebel must not be allowed to operate freely in the church, and it angers God when she is [7]. One person identifying her and crying foul will not correct or control her; it takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with a Jezebel [3]. So this is not yours to handle alone — it needs the leadership standing together.

You must be willing to confront, not merely manage. Most pastors are too dignified and self-righteous to confront a pastor's wife or bring her to order, and many want to maintain good relations with everybody, so they will not rebuke and correct wives who are out of order [7]. But if a Jezebel is allowed to go uncorrected, you may lose everything [7]. Bishop Dag Heward-Mills tells of an assistant pastor who served his senior pastor faithfully for twenty-five years and helped build a church of thousands: the senior pastor's wife slapped a church member, the congregation rose up against her, the senior pastor resigned, and the ministry collapsed overnight. The assistant pastor's own conclusion was that their great mistake was allowing a Jezebel to operate freely because they thought they were showing respect to their senior pastor [7]. In another account, a man of God confessed that failing to confront the Jezebel in their midst cost him his life's work, his job, his church and his career, and that they should have fought against her openly no matter what it cost [8].

Be aware of how she works, so you are not caught off guard. Her aim is to isolate the man of God from other important people in his life, and she ministers constantly until she becomes a source of correction and direction for him [2]. She is a mistress of seduction and persuasion — gentle, sweet and seductive, so that it does not occur to anyone that they are being charmed and convinced [3]. And she often comes disguised as a spiritual person, a prophetess and a teacher of the Word, which disarms you and makes you unable to fight against it [6].

The counsel is plain: do not suffer that woman Jezebel [7]. Identify her, and refuse to let her operate unchecked [2][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4, 10, 17 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: How can churches grow in poor areas if they can't afford to pay pastors and workers?
items.book: Laikos Lay People and the Ministry
items.text:
This is a burden the books speak to directly, and their answer is the same in both places: the unpaid, working minister.

- **Let the ministry be carried by lay people who labour without pay.** The lay ministry is the sacrifice of pastors and evangelists who serve without being paid, and without that strategy very few churches will be planted [1][2]. It is virtually impossible for the church to employ all the people needed for the work of God [1][2].

- **See the poor harvest fields as the very reason for it.** Most of the ripened harvest fields are in the poor regions of the world, and most of those people cannot pay for the services of good pastors and evangelists — so the ministry of unpaid pastors and evangelists is the key to continued church planting [1][2].

- **Expect it to be unpopular, and press on anyway.** In some cultures everybody must be paid for his services — the organist, the guitarist, the sound controller — and the pastor constantly seeks a higher salary [1][2]. But where the sacrificial nature of Christianity is compromised, church planting comes to an end; the church was born on the sacrifice of Christ and grew through the sacrifice of the apostolic church [1][2].

- **Have the pastor get a job and pastor on the side.** A small church usually cannot afford to pay a pastor's salary, much less buy him a car, so the advice to anyone beginning a church is to find a job and start the church as a lay person [5][6]. When people see you are not ministering for financial gain, they will be more interested in your new church [5][6].

- **Do not become financially desperate.** Be careful not to become dependent on the church you are pioneering for your survival, or you will become a desperate man clutching at every straw [5][6]. Sixteen people cannot look after you, and twenty-one cannot support your upkeep and your children's school fees [5][6].

- **Keep the staff small and let the church's money build the church.** Keep your ministry staff as small as possible so you can pay them properly, and do not have idle, discontented people around you, since idleness leads to laziness, laziness to discontentment, and discontentment to disloyalty [4]. In the early stages, money is needed for equipment and rent; if you siphon out the lifeblood of the church, it will not develop normally [5][6].

- **Let lay people do far more than give money.** If pastors understood that their lay people can do much more than just give money, they would help themselves and their churches a great deal [8]. Doctors, architects, bankers, teachers, pharmacists, lecturers, accountants, students, nurses, army officers, civil servants, technicians, businessmen and lawyers have all become great lay pastors [8].

- **Remember the example of Paul.** Paul went to Corinth and

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapters 9 and 20 of *Church Planting*, chapters 3 and 6 of *Church Growth* and chapter 7 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Thessalonians 3:11; 1 Timothy 5:13.

items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Once you see it, the books are clear that you deal with it rather than let it sit — and they give several methods.

- **Teach, as a preventive measure.** The first method is to teach the Word of God regularly, because teaching fights deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [6]. A wise leader chooses preventive management over crisis management, constantly teaching and immunizing the people against the very problem he is trying to avoid [6].

- **Cast the scorner out.** The biblical remedy for scoffers is expulsion — to throw out, dismiss, expel, eject, banish, fire, sack, discard, unseat or lay off — because Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease" [2][7]. Failure to dismiss someone who must go is weak leadership; it is like allowing a snake to live under your children's bed [2].

- **Mark and avoid.** Romans 16:17–18 teaches that people who cause divisions must be noted and avoided at all costs — to mark means to brand or label so the person stands out and can be recognized from afar [2]. Bishop Dag tells of applying this in his own church: since he could not take a tin of red paint and brand the man, he called a meeting and told the people that this brother was unsafe and should be avoided, marking him sufficiently without even giving the details of his offences [2].

- **Dismiss even longstanding workers.** Disloyal, disobedient, non-compliant or offending bishops, pastors and workers should be dismissed completely, even if they have served for fifty years, because fellowship is a choice and no one must be forced to fellowship with those he despises or speaks maliciously about [5]. In keeping with mercy and compassion, financial provision should be made so they can live and work elsewhere without undue hardship, and they should be seen off properly to live and prosper under a leadership they love and respect [5]. This is based on Paul's warning in Hebrews 12:15 to avoid a root of bitterness that defiles many [5].

- **Act on questionable loyalty, not only open disloyalty.** A leader must refuse to lead people who are mysterious, secretive and questionable in their loyalty, and remove them from the fold, since failure to do so lets a root of bitterness grow until the whole church is destroyed [7]. Questionable loyalty is diagnosed when a person makes malicious, damaging or poisonous comments; has a spouse or close relative who is openly disloyal; has friendships, alliances or close ties with an openly disloyal person; or is known to communicate with persons who are openly disloyal [7]. This too rests on Proverbs 22:10, and such dismissal is not extreme hatred but a wise, calm, premeditated act of leadership

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 13:14-15; Proverbs 22:10; Romans 16:17-18; Hebrews 12:15.

items.question: What should I do if I've spread lies about someone in church and want to make it right?
items.text:
It takes real courage to want to make this right, and I'm glad you're asking.

The books speak plainly about what slander is and what it does, and that is where your repair has to begin. A slanderer is a revealer of secrets, and God sees that as evil — you must see it as evil too, because you were spreading the failings of a fellow brother who is as weak a person as you are [7]. The damage is real: it is difficult to erase from people's minds the impressions and feelings conveyed by slanderous stories, and once stories are spread, people do not forget them [1][3].

So the first thing is to stop. Lay hands on your tongue, if necessary, and make sure there is no poison in it — don't be a destroyer, because Satan is the one who comes to destroy [1]. Stop going from person to person; the Scripture says, "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" (Leviticus 19:16) [8].

Then remember what the person you spoke against is owed. People who fall into sin are to be helped to get up and walk again, not pushed further underground so they never rise again — how can a person rise again if you keep spreading his failings to everyone? [7]. The trustworthy man conceals a matter (Proverbs 11:13) [7].

And be honest with yourself about why you did it. Slander separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28), and it separates the sheep from their shepherd — through slanderers, loyal church members fall away [7]. If your words did that, naming it honestly before God is part of making it right.

One caution as you go: correcting someone does not mean disgracing them [4][5]. So as you seek to undo what you said, do it in a way that does not heap fresh shame on the person you harmed.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*, chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 7 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 119:21-24; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 16:28; Proverbs 22:10; Micah 7:8; 1 Corinthians 5:6-7; Jude 22.

items.question: What does it mean to be called by God?
items.text:
Being called by God is a tremendous privilege — far greater than any earthly appointment — and Scripture shows it carries several distinct meanings.

- **You are summoned distinctly.** To be called is to be identified, named, and selected by God — the Hebrew word *qara* means to call out and address by name [1]. Moses, Bezaleel, Samuel, and Zacchaeus were all called by name, as when God called, "Moses, Moses" (Exodus 3:4) [1].

- **You receive special mercy.** Your calling is an act of God's compassion and forbearance toward you — after salvation, it is His greatest act of kindness and clemency [4]. As 2 Corinthians 4:1 puts it, "seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not" [4].

- **You are appointed for a special purpose.** God has selected and assigned you for a particular position and work [4]. But be careful to seek out *why* He called you, not just *that* He called you — He may call you to plant churches when His purpose is for you to lay a foundation others will build on [5].

- **You are separated for God's purposes.** Your calling isolates you from the larger body of believers and from secular life, setting a boundary between you and others [2]. The Hebrew *badal* means to distinguish and make a difference between you and others [2].

- **You are sent out properly.** There is a difference between someone who was sent and someone who just went — God dispatches you on a journey to serve Him and to fetch souls from the grip of the devil [2]. The Hebrew *shalach* means to send someone away, often from family and friends [2].

- **You receive grace from God.** The grace upon your calling is kindness over and above the grace that saved you [6]. The Greek *charis* speaks of a divine influence on your heart that stirs up gratitude [6].

- **You receive a ministry, a talent, a gift, and an office.** Your calling brings you into the duties of a particular stream of Kingdom work [3][6]; it puts a tangible endowment in your hands to use for the Kingdom [3]; it gives you a natural capacity for certain things, so that called people do certain things effortlessly [3]; and it places you in a position of authority and responsibility from the Lord [3].

One more thing worth holding onto: your calling is no accident. As Romans 8:30 says, "whom he did predestinate, them he also called" — it is the fulfilment of your predestination, and those who believe they are called simply take God's Word, their dreams, and their quiet times more seriously [7]. And remember that many are called — this is not reserved for a spectacular few, but for ordinary saints, as when Samuel heard

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Many Are Called* and chapters 1 and 2 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:4; Exodus 29:1; Exodus 31:2; Deuteronomy 10:8; Deuteronomy 32:8; 1 Samuel 3:4; 1 Chronicles 15:16-19; 1 Chronicles 23:13; Jeremiah 1:7; Zechariah 2:8 and 26 more.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to think you're untouchable or indispensable in ministry?
items.text:
It's a real danger, and the books speak to it plainly.

**It hardens you instead of humbling you.** A person with the spirit of Absalom is not corrected by punishment or years of hard discipline; two years of exile and difficulty did not change Absalom's heart — he became hardened and even more dangerous [1]. Some people never apologize no matter what they go through, and such people are simply Absalom reborn [1].

**It is pride, and pride leads to destruction.** As soon as you begin to think of yourself as indispensable, you are becoming proud and deceived, and just like Absalom your delusions will lead to your destruction — pride always comes before a fall [1].

**It makes you a dangerous presence to have around.** Whenever a person feels indispensable, he is a dangerous person to have around; some feel they are untouchable and can never be dispensed with [1]. Absalom's own words — that if there were any iniquity in him, the king should kill him — reveal the mindset: "My father cannot sack me, cannot discipline me, cannot deal with me" [1].

**It can cost you your ministry.** Do not think you are indispensable: if you do not do what God wants you to do, your ministry will be taken away from you and given to another, as Luke 19:24 says — "Take from him the pound, and give it to him that hath ten pounds" [2]. If God gave you a pound, He can take it back when He wants to [2].

**It is a misuse of a special place.** Sometimes people sense they are special and loved and take advantage of that place — that too is a mistake, for there is always a Joab who will do the job the father doesn't want to do [1]. The same pattern appears with wives who feel they cannot be divorced and misuse the power of the marriage covenant, exploiting their untouchable status to the maximum [5].

**It grows into a takeover spirit.** Absalom desired to take over and replace his father, thinking himself as good as David — that is the spirit of Absalom, a "takeover" and "replacement" spirit, different from a son who humbly wishes to emulate his father [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons* and chapter 6 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 14:32; 2 Samuel 15:4; 2 Samuel 18:33-19:2; Luke 19:24; Romans 11:29.

**It is a misuse of a special place.** Sometimes people sense they are special and loved and take advantage of that place — that too is a mistake, for there is always a Joab who will do the job the father doesn't want to do.
The same pattern appears with wives who feel they cannot be divorced and misuse the power of the marriage covenant, exploiting their untouchable status to the maximum.

**It grows into a takeover spirit.** Absalom desired to take over and replace his father, thinking himself as good as David — that is the spirit of Absalom, a "takeover" and "replacement" spirit, different from a son who humbly wishes to emulate his father.

items.question: What happens when you pray for wisdom?
items.book: Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry
items.text:
Praying for wisdom is one of the most important prayers you can pray, and Scripture shows it changes a person deeply. Here is what the books describe as the effects of that prayer.

- **You receive a large heart.** Solomon was given a great depth of understanding and insight in response to his prayer for wisdom [3].

- **Your wisdom rises above the wisdom around you.** Solomon's wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt, so praying for wisdom gives you a higher level of wisdom than the prevailing wisdom of your nation and than your colleagues [1][3].

- **You become a person of proverbs and songs.** The wisdom received causes you to speak with proverbs and to write special songs, couching wisdom in ways that are hard to forget and that teach those who sing them [1].

- **You begin to appreciate nature.** Solomon spoke of trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things and fishes; the wonders of creation start to intrigue you as you grow in the wisdom God gives [1].

- **People travel from afar to hear you.** That someone would leave home, city or nation just to listen to your preaching is a sign that you possess God's great wisdom [1].

- **Kings and great men pay attention to you.** Kings reign through wisdom, and when you get their attention you have crossed an important barrier, as Proverbs 8:15 says, "By me kings reign, and princes decree justice" [1].

- **Curses are made more bearable and overruled.** Curses are defeated and minimised through prayers for wisdom; when you get wisdom, riches, honour, length of days and many blessings arrive and overrule the effect of the curse on man, as Proverbs 3:13-16 describes [2].

- **You receive the gifts and fruit of the Spirit.** Praying for the Holy Spirit brings the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, and gifts of healing, miracles, tongues and prophecy begin to flow, as 1 Corinthians 12:7-10 sets out [6].

- **You gain increasing wisdom, understanding, knowledge and counsel.** Praying for all the seven spirits of God makes you like Daniel, who had an excellent spirit, and most of the wrong moves of your life have come from lacking the wisdom to take the right decision [6].

- **You are given everything else besides.** God was so impressed with Solomon's prayer topic that He gave him riches and honour he did not ask for, as 1 Kings 3:12-13 records [4][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 26 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapters 3 and 4 of *How to Pray*, chapter 3 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer* and chapter 12 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 3:5; 1 Kings 3:9-13; 1 Kings 4:29-34; Proverbs 3:13-16; Proverbs 8:15; Isaiah 11:2; Matthew 6:33; Luke 11:11-13; 1 Corinthians 12:7-10; 2 Corinthians 4:4 and 1 more.

items.question: How can I avoid becoming too familiar with my leaders or with people I look up to?
items.book: Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar
items.text:
Here are some ways the books describe for guarding against familiarity with those you look up to.

- **Keep a sense of awe and admiration.** Familiarity is knowing someone so well that you lose your admiration, respect and sense of awe, and become presumptuous in a way that shows a lack of respect [5]. So guard your heart against that drift.

- **Don't let closeness breed contempt.** When you are too familiar with somebody you only see his ordinariness, forget he is also anointed, and gradually begin to despise him [2]. Remember that love is strong, as strong as death (Song of Solomon 8:6) [2].

- **Watch the subtle signs in yourself.** One sign is often sitting at the back of the church, no longer intrigued or excited, just observing from a distance [5]. Be quick to detect subtle indications of familiarity in yourself [3].

- **Never try to direct or correct your leader.** Familiarity is detected when a follower attempts to direct his leader; Peter thought his friendship with Christ gave him authority to direct and correct Jesus, and he was brought down to size [3]. The subordinate is not qualified to do this [3].

- **Maintain some distance and privacy.** Sometimes it is better to know someone from afar so you can keep receiving from his ministry [5]. A leader should keep a degree of mystique, because the less people know about his private realities, the more they can receive from him [4].

- **Cultivate thankfulness and reject presumption.** Presumption is the arrogant assumption that privileges must be given to you, and people who assume they are entitled complain and murmur about things that are great privileges to others [8]. Teach yourself to be thankful minute by minute, because thankfulness is a sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit [8].

- **Let teaching keep familiarity from growing.** Ignorance is the breeding ground of demonic activity, and teaching is the greatest tool that prevents familiarity from developing in the ranks [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 16 of *One Thousand Micro Churches*, chapter 95 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapters 8 and 10 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar* and chapter 13 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 41:9; Song of Songs 8:6; Matthew 16:22; Mark 1:37-39; Mark 6:2-3; Mark 6:5; John 6:10-11.

items.question: What does the anointing do for someone's ministry?
items.text:
The books describe many things the anointing does for a person's ministry. Here are the effects they name:

- **It brings supernatural help.** David saw his ministry as a king helped because of the anointing, and said, "I have given help to one who is mighty" (Psalm 89:19b) [1].
- **It raises you up to heights in ministry.** David saw his exaltation as a result of the anointing, for God said, "I have exalted one chosen from the people" (Psalm 89:19c) [1].
- **It establishes you.** There is a clear difference between a ministry established by God and one that is not; David became established because of the anointing, for God said, "With whom My hand will be established" (Psalm 89:20-21) [1].
- **It introduces strength.** Many ministers are weak in preaching and lack the power to change lives, but the anointing removes weaknesses; David said, "My arm also will strengthen him" (Psalm 89:21) [1].
- **It protects you from deception.** Deception develops into blindness and hypocrisy, and Jesus rebuked experienced ministers for their blind spots, saying, "You blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel!" (Matthew 23:24) [1].
- **It enables you to build and restore.** You gain the ability to raise up foundations, establish God's work, and lay brick upon brick, taking shattered and hopeless lives and making something out of them [2].
- **It reaches beyond your own borders.** It causes you to reach past your own country, tribe, and nation, breaking the barriers that keep people from responding to those of a different colour or accent, as Isaiah 61:5 says strangers shall stand and feed your flocks [2].
- **It makes you a priest.** Because of the anointing you will be a priest, called a Minister of God, as Isaiah 61:6 says, "ye shall be named the Priests of the LORD" [2].
- **It sets the bound free.** Logical teaching and systematic lectures cannot open prison doors; it is by the anointing that freedom comes to those you minister to [4].
- **It comforts those who mourn.** Comforting the mourning is part of the ministry of the Spirit, and when you are anointed people are encouraged just by seeing you, hearing you, or having you lay hands on them; this comforting is different from the healing anointing, and is a powerful alternative when there are legal reasons a person cannot be healed in this life [4].
- **It restores beauty and attractiveness.** The anointing makes you fresh, beautiful, and attractive, so that people are drawn to your church or crusades without knowing why, as Isaiah 61:3 speaks of giving beauty for ashes [4].
- **It affects your children.** You

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 15 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 89:19-21; Isaiah 61:2-3; Isaiah 61:5-6; Matthew 23:24.

items.question: What does the Bible say about the importance of skill for getting things built?
items.text:
Skill matters more than most of us realize when it comes to getting anything built. Here is what our books say about it.

- **Skill is the master key to building.** Failure to build reveals a lack of practical skills, and impractical "armchair leaders" build nothing [1]. When Solomon wanted the temple built, he asked for a man cunning to work in gold, silver, brass, and iron, and able to grave and cut timber [1].

- **Skill determines whether you build at all.** The ability to build a house is described as a specific blessing that came from God, as when He made houses for the midwives who feared Him (Exodus 1:21) [8]. It is also seen as a fruit of God's wisdom: "Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established" (Proverbs 24:3) [8].

- **Skill comes through humility and a determination to learn.** Solomon admitted there was no one among them who could hew timber like the Sidonians, and he hired them to teach his servants [1]. Skill requires the humility of associating with someone better than you in order to learn from him; without that humility you can never acquire the necessary skills [1].

- **Skill is often caught by watching, not just hearing.** In medical school they were taught to "Watch one, assist one, then do one" — the higher skills of surgery were not acquired by listening to lectures [6]. Most people build things they have seen, and most people minister like the people they have watched all their lives [6].

- **Skill is practical wisdom, not just theory.** The five wise virgins were called *phronimos* — the practical application of wisdom — because they made arrangements for extra oil (Matthew 25:1-2) [2]. Unrealistic theoreticians only propound theories about what must be done; it takes a practical person to lay a foundation and build something useful [2].

- **Building also requires courage and strength.** Scripture says, "Be strong and courageous, and act; do not fear nor be dismayed, for the Lord God, my God, is with you" (1 Chronicles 28:20) [3]. Building reveals that you are courageous and bold, and it reveals strength [3].

- **But skill is not the whole story — the anointing is.** Zerubbabel was building the temple, and the word to him was, "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6) [5]. The Church will be built by the power of the Holy Spirit, not by education, background, location, or strategy [5]. And unless the Lord builds the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1) [3].

So learn the skill, watch those who have it, stay

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Determinants*, chapter 64 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 3 of *The Mega Church*, chapter 34 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 9 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 9:25-26; Exodus 1:21; 1 Kings 5:5-7; 1 Chronicles 5:18; 1 Chronicles 28:10; 1 Chronicles 28:20; 2 Chronicles 2:7-8; 2 Chronicles 34:12; Psalms 33:3; Psalms 127:1 and 10 more.

items.question: What does The Mega Church say about why churches need many pastors?
items.text:
The book gives several reasons why a growing church needs many pastors and ministers.

- **A large church releases more workers into the harvest.** Jesus said the harvest is great but the workers are few, and He told us to pray for more laborers to be sent out (Matthew 9:37-38), so the larger the crowd, the more laborers are sent forth [2].

- **A large church produces more full-time ministers.** A ten thousand member congregation will produce more pastors than a hundred member church, and a smaller church's pastor is not likely to have enough people who want to be ministers of the gospel [2].

- **A large church appoints and releases more pastors and bishops into the field.** Through a mega church, more ministers of the gospel, full-time pastors and bishops are appointed and released into the harvest field [2].

- **A large church can finance the ministers it raises up.** The more laborers there are, the more easily you will be able to finance them [2].

- **A large church can meet the varied needs of its congregation.** In a large church you are likely to find a lawyer, a doctor, an engineer, a pharmacist or even a psychiatrist to serve the many different needs among the people [7].

- **A large church develops specialist ministries.** As the church grows it becomes more diverse, and this results in specialist ministries being developed, including ministries to the poor, refugees, and orphans [4][1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 41:1-2; Matthew 9:37-38; Mark 16:20; Acts 2:41-42; Acts 4:4; Acts 4:32-35; Acts 8:5-8; Romans 12:8; 1 Thessalonians 1:8; 2 Timothy 4:5.

items.question: How did Paul become equal to or greater than Peter as an apostle?
items.text:
Paul's rise alongside and ahead of Peter is something our books return to often, and they give several reasons for it.

- **He laboured more abundantly.** Paul himself said he laboured more than all the apostles, and he was bold enough to say he laboured more than Peter did, crediting it to the grace of God at work in him (1 Corinthians 15:10) [1]. The catching-up wisdom has two parts: walking in the grace of God, and working harder than those ahead of you [5].

- **He received an abundance of revelations.** Promotion and advancement in ministry come through the abundance of revelations a person receives, and Paul was promoted highly because of his abundance of revelations [4]. It was this grace of revelation that seemed to visit Paul rather than Peter [1].

- **He was a man of books.** Paul did not rely on visions and dreams alone; he read widely and quoted over 260 times from the Old Testament books, and even from prison asked for "the books, but especially the parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13) [4]. His ministry unfolded through the books he read [4].

- **He was given special wisdom.** Peter himself acknowledged that Paul wrote "according to the wisdom given unto him" (2 Peter 3:14-16), and it was this catching-up wisdom that let Paul bridge the gap with those who had walked with Jesus in person [5].

- **God raised up a replacement.** Just as Matthias was chosen to fill Judas's place, there was another replacement chosen by God rather than by casting lots — Paul, who described himself as "one born out of due time" and "the least of the apostles" (1 Corinthians 15:8-9) [2]. He saw himself as a full member of the apostolic family, saying he was "not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5) [1][2].

- **Even opposition served him.** Paul's greatest achievements were the letters he wrote, and he wrote them from prison; the wickedness of the Jews that put him there actually helped him [7]. The messenger of Satan that buffeted him kept him from pride, so that the power of Christ rested on him all the more (2 Corinthians 12:7-9) [7].

One caution our books add: Paul's writings, though greatly used by God, are not on the same level as the words of Jesus. Paul was a servant of Christ, not a second son of God, and the words of Jesus must remain the guiding post by which every ministry is assessed [3][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 13 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 5 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 7 of *WOM13. The Big Secret - Your Ministry Depends on Books*, chapter 13 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapter 3 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 6 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 37:26-27; Genesis 37:36; Exodus 34:7; Numbers 5:20-22; Matthew 18:1; Matthew 18:4; 1 Corinthians 15:8-10; 2 Corinthians 11:5; 2 Corinthians 12:7-9; 2 Corinthians 12:11-12 and 3 more.

items.question: What does it mean to make a C-turn toward Jesus instead of a U-turn away from him?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
That's a good question, and the books do speak to it directly.

A C-turn is not a reversal but a swerve to the side — a manoeuvre that takes you off the wrong course onto a better way [1][2]. A U-turn, by contrast, is a reversal of your former decisions, a turning back [2].

So a C-turn toward Jesus is a shift of direction that moves you deeper into Him rather than away. Jesus Himself made a C-turn when He left the country of the Gadarenes because the people asked Him to leave; He did not stop His ministry of casting out devils and healing, He simply shifted to where He was more welcome [1][2]. Peter made a C-turn when he left his nets as a fisherman and became an apostle [1]. Andrew and John made a C-turn when they moved on from following John the Baptist and followed Jesus — not a U-turn away from the ministry, but a turn that took them deeper and further into God and closer to Jesus [1].

A U-turn, on the other hand, is what the prodigal son made when he arose and went back to his father, reversing all his former decisions and humbly returning to his proper place [2]. Zacchaeus made a U-turn when he met Jesus, turning away from corruption and swindling and restoring fourfold what he had taken falsely [2][8]. That kind of U-turn is true repentance [2].

So the difference is this: a C-turn swerves you off a wrong course onto a better one, while a U-turn reverses decisions you made earlier and brings you back [1][2]. Both require flexibility — being malleable and capable of change in the hands of the Holy Spirit [1][2].

items.question: What does it mean to be a person of faith?
items.text:
To be a person of faith is really to be a person who obeys God — the two are equated in Scripture, so that an obedient person is the one who has faith, and obeying what God tells you to do is itself the exercising of your faith [1]. When Israel refused to go up and possess the land, their unbelief showed itself as rebellion against the commandment of the Lord, and to believe not was to disobey [1].

Faith also shows up in your attitude, not just your words. A person relaxes and grows negative toward those they hold in low regard, but brightens when they see someone they fear or respect — and God notices your face, your attentiveness when He speaks, even the loudness and fervency of your "Amen" [2]. So to have faith in God means to have a good attitude toward the Bible, toward the preaching of the Word, and toward every word from the Holy Spirit [2].

And faith is what keeps you on your knees. When you sit up all night speaking into the air to someone you cannot feel or touch, who does not answer back, it takes great faith to keep speaking — anyone who persists in prayer is a man of faith [3]. It is faith and patience together that produce the fruit; it was Benny Hinn's faith and patience that gave him his miracle crusades, and Fred Price's and Reinhard Bonnke's faith and patience that gave them their ministries, not money or connections or advertisements [4].

Faith is also the assurance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1), and God has dealt to every man a measure of faith (Romans 12:3) — you exercise it every time you sit on a chair or board a plane, trusting it will hold [5]. It is your faith in what God is telling you that lets you lead people through painful and tortuous routes, and a strong man of faith is a strong leader [7]. So do not be afraid to walk in risk and uncertainty — that is how you exercise your faith and please God; it is time to move forward into the new land, the new dimension, the new level He has set before you [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5, 10 and 15 of *Faith Secrets*, chapter 5 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities*, chapter 2 of *The Art of Following* and chapter 2 of *Name It Claim It Take It*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 9:22-23; Romans 12:3; Hebrews 11:1.

items.question: How do I become anointed by the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
Becoming anointed is really about drawing near to God Himself, and our books describe several steps along that road.

- **Be led by the Holy Spirit.** The Spirit leads you not mainly to places but to a spiritual destination — to become an anointed person — and Jesus Himself was led by the Spirit before His ministry began [1]. Learning to follow His voice is what sets a person apart, as Moses taught in Deuteronomy 28:1 [1].

- **Follow Him even when He leads you somewhere hard.** The Spirit led Jesus into a wild, barren desert, and Jesus went [1]. You must become someone who can follow the Spirit against your natural inclinations, because the anointing is not for your own interests or casual play [1].

- **Wait on God.** The disciples had to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father before the Spirit came [2]. Isaiah 40:31 promises that those who wait on the Lord gain new strength, mount up like eagles, and run without growing weary [2].

- **Pursue love and unity.** The Spirit fell at Pentecost only when they were all together in one accord [2]. God does not anoint a quarrelling, competing, bitter team; you will find the anointing where there is unity [2].

- **Soak in the Word by hearing with faith.** One man listened to Kenneth Hagin for ten years before he received the anointing to teach; one night as he played a tape while praying, something seemed to enter his belly and a voice said, "From today you can teach" [3]. Keep listening to messages you do not yet understand until you are saturated, for you receive the Spirit by the hearing of faith [3].

- **Relate to the Holy Spirit as a real person.** Talk with Him, greet Him, discuss things with Him, and recognize His thoughts and ideas [5]. Also recognize Him as wind — the gentle pressures, the sudden gusts, the sense of being enveloped [5].

- **Follow the Lord faithfully over years.** Everyone who received the anointing in the upper room had walked with Jesus for years; the apostles required a replacement to have been around at least three years [8]. Do not expect the greatest treasures of the kingdom after serving for a few minutes [8].

- **Remember that God decides.** The anointing is God Himself, and He hides Himself and is not accessed by seven simple steps; you must ask, seek, and knock [7]. No matter how hard you work, God sovereignly chooses whom He allows to come close to Him [7].

One more thing worth knowing: the number one way the Holy Spirit makes Himself visible is by teaching — Jesus promised a Comforter who would teach us all things and bring all things to remembrance, as John 14:26 says [6]. So when you read your Bible and deep understanding opens up, that is the Holy Spirit being manifest to you [6

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*, chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing*, chapter 1 of *Flow in the Anointing* and chapter 7 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 28:1; Isaiah 40:31; Isaiah 45:15; Matthew 4:1; Luke 4:1-15; John 14:26; John 20:22; Acts 1:4; Acts 1:8; Acts 1:21-23 and 2 more.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is a releasing of the heart, not just a feeling. To forgive is to release all hurts, bitterness and wickedness from your heart in such a way that satan stares in shock at a closed door to your heart — it is to deny access to a horde of demons that are waiting [6]. Concretely, that means dismissing the thorny and painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness toward them, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling any punishments you had planned for them [6]. As Ephesians 4:32 puts it, we are to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us [6].

It also means leaving vengeance to God rather than taking it into your own hands. Forgiveness must keep you busy, so that when you are busy forgiving you have no time to avenge yourself and take over God's work — and God is far better at avenging than you are [3]. Scripture says, "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19), and Jesus Himself taught us to pray night and day for God to avenge us, as in Luke 18:6-8 [3]. God has a repayment plan for all who harm you; He repays those who hate Him, and He will not be slack (Deuteronomy 7:9-10) [3].

Forgiveness is also something you walk out toward your offenders in love and prayer, blessing those who curse you and praying for those who despitefully use you [6]. And it carries real advantage: forgiveness makes you a great person, and through it you become more powerful spiritually, physically and emotionally [5]. Nelson Mandela is held up as one of the greatest men in the world because of forgiveness — imprisoned for twenty-seven years by the apartheid government and separated from his home, wife and children, he was able to forgive his white oppressors and form a reconciliatory government with them, and it was this apparent forgiveness that made him such a great person [5].

One more thing worth naming: forgiveness is not the same as a pardon. A pardon is the official granting of forgiveness for an offence, given by the church, a church council, or the highest executive position in the organization, and it may release a person from some or all of a punishment, sometimes after they have served part or all of a sentence [7].

items.question: How do I know God will take me back after I've turned away from him?
items.text:
That's a heavy question to carry, and I'm glad you asked it rather than sitting with it alone.

God is a God who rights the wrongs done to people, and He keeps a record of everything — He has a sheet of paper with the details of all that has happened, and He will visit the people one by one [2]. So nothing about your turning away is unseen or forgotten by Him.

The Scripture the book leans on says, "I will take revenge. I will pay them back," and also, "The Lord will judge his own people" (Hebrews 10:30) [2]. But the same passage goes on to tell the reader to remember the early days when they first learned about Christ, how they remained faithful even through terrible suffering, and it says, "So do not throw away this confident trust in the Lord. Remember the great reward it brings you! Patient endurance is what you need now, so that you will continue to do God's will. Then you will receive all that he has promised" (Hebrews 10:35-36) [2].

And there is this: God promises to forgive and forget the sins of those who love Him — mercy is shown to those who are loved, and God loves you back when you love Him [8]. The book tells of a man whose wife had been wretchedly unfaithful to him, and everyone was certain he would divorce her, but he forgave her and showed her much affection, and it became clear he truly loved her; the point was that mercy is always connected to love [8].

So the way back is not closed to you. Turn toward Him, and let your love for Him be real — that is where His mercy meets you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *TS2. Hope Secrets* and chapter 12 of *If You Love The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 7:9-10; Hebrews 10:30-36.

items.question: How can I grow spiritually and bear fruit as a Christian?
items.text:
Growing in Christ and bearing fruit is exactly what God has ordained for you, and the books lay out several ways this happens.

- **Get healthy spiritually.** Some Christians are unfruitful because of a spiritual sickness — laziness, pride, or living in sin, and nothing affects fruitful Christian living like sin does. The Bible tells us in 2 Peter 1:5-8 to add to our faith virtue, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness and charity, for if these things be in you and abound, they make you neither barren nor unfruitful [2].

- **Grow up into maturity.** A Christian without converts is immature, and an immature person cannot have children; after you are born again your main aim must be to grow, moving from childhood to adulthood [1]. When you are spiritually mature you are dominated by the Spirit rather than the flesh, and the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance — becomes visible in you, as Galatians 5:22-25 describes [5].

- **Stay planted and abide.** Jesus says in John 15:4-5 that the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide in the vine, and that he who abides brings forth much fruit [1]. You have to abide in the same place for some time to become productive there — a tree that is often transplanted will never grow to its full, fruit-bearing potential, and Psalm 92:13-14 promises that those planted in the house of the LORD shall still bring forth fruit in old age [3].

- **Stay connected to God in prayer.** Prayer is an opportunity to connect with the Father, and a prayerless person is a disconnected person; without this connection you cannot be a normal Christian and you cannot bear fruit [8]. Many people are unfruitful because they have lost connection with the head, as Colossians 2:19 puts it [8].

- **Set spiritual goals and press forward.** Christians who have no spiritual ambition tend to become fruitless, so aim higher than just being happy to be a Christian; Paul said in Philippians 3:13-14, "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind... I press toward the mark" [4]. The time to minister to others is now, and Hebrews 5:12 warns against still needing someone to teach you when you ought by now to be teaching others [4].

- **Get active.** Passive Christians bear no fruit; if you want to be a fruitful Christian you must engage in the activity that makes you fruitful — witnessing, teaching, and helping in the church [3]. The Lord has chosen and ordained you to go and bring forth fruit that remains, as John 15:16 says [4][7].

- **Guard against the cares of the world.** The cares of this world, the deceit

items.question: How can a young person deal with sexual desires and stay pure?
items.text:
You're asking a question the books speak to very directly, and with real sympathy for how strong those desires are.

- **Respect the desires instead of denying them.** Your sexuality is something to be respected, and a proper respect for youthful lusts—rather than a denial of them—will save you from them; desires are real forces that guide the events of life [4]. If you do not respect these animal instincts they will overwhelm you, override you and lead you away from God's plan for your life [2].

- **Flee, don't fight.** Nowhere in the Bible are you taught to fight lust; you are taught to flee from it, as 2 Timothy 2:22 says, "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" [2][4]. When you sense strong desires for a woman or a man, you must run away from it [2].

- **Guard yourself from being under anyone's influence.** To be sober is to be free from outside influences that direct, manipulate and guide you; any boy under the influence of a girl is not sober [2]. Young people are supposed to keep themselves from influences that steal them away from the influence of the Holy Spirit [2].

- **Know God's will for your sexual life and build your own plan around it.** The will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality, as 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 says, and since that is one of the clearest directions of the Lord, make it one of your clearest and most energetic goals to practically live a sexually pure life [5]. Everyone has a different way by which he keeps himself from fornication—it may be God's will for you never to read certain books or watch certain films, never to have certain friends, never to work with women or have female secretaries, or to marry young—so find out what God's will is for your own journey of staying away from fornication [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 10, 13 and 20 of *Ready@20* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

items.question: Why should we not boast about our own strength or willpower when we survive something?
items.text:
That's a good question, and our books speak to it plainly.

- **Boasting takes glory that belongs to God.** When people credited a man's survival to his resilience and willpower, the book points out that God does not like it when we boast about things He has given us as though we did not receive them — "What hast thou that thou didst not receive? If thou didst receive it then why dost thou boast as though thou didst not receive it?" (1 Corinthians 4:7) [1].

- **Boasting invites testing.** When a Christian keeps boasting about his strength, Satan hears him and decides to test him; where you are over-confident is where you can be weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2][3]. The book tells of a brother who kept telling his pastor with great conviction that he would never leave the church — and a few months later he walked out and never returned [2][3].

- **Willpower alone cannot sustain you.** The book tells of a man who survived being buried underground for a long time; his wife and his doctors all attributed it to his strong willpower and determination. A week later he had a heart attack and died suddenly — showing that his willpower was unable to sustain him [1].

- **Over-confidence about your own strength is a setup for falling.** If you regard yourself or your position as foolproof, you are in danger of backsliding, especially if you have had promotion or been used by God in the past — "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12) [3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, not by your own strength [2][3].

- **Boasting often shows itself in how we talk about others.** You can tell an over-confident Christian by the way he criticizes others as though he could never make the same mistakes, overestimating his own ability and looking down on them [2][3]. David, when he heard Saul was dead, did not ridicule him or rejoice, but said, "Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon" (2 Samuel 1:20) [2][3].

- **Strength itself is a gift, and God keeps us humble.** When God blesses a person with abundance of grace and gifts, there is a great tendency to be lifted up with pride — Lucifer was lifted up this way and it destroyed him — so the Lord often allows unpleasant "agents of humility," what Paul called a thorn in the flesh, into our lives [6]. Paul wrote that God's grace is sufficient, for His strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7-10) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 12 of *Those who are Proud*, chapter 3 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 5 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 1:20; Proverbs 30:8-9; 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 10:12; 2 Corinthians 12:7-10.

items.question: How should a pastor plan church finances when people don't pay the money they pledged?
items.text:
This is a real and common burden, and the books speak to it plainly.

- **Never budget on pledges.** A wise pastor should not expect more than about 30% of pledged money to actually come in, because most members will not pay what they promised, so you must never plan your finances around what the congregation has pledged [1][2][3][4].

- **Save toward the project before you fundraise for it.** It is wise to put money aside for a project before you even begin raising funds, so that the project can go ahead whether or not people honour their pledges [1][2].

- **Keep the pledge window short.** The shorter the time given to pay a pledge, the higher the returns tend to be, since many forget their promises soon after making them; a period of one week to three months is recommended [1][2].

- **Let tithes and offerings be your real foundation.** Fundraising is only meant to boost the regular tithes and offerings, and if that basic income is not established, fundraising will never achieve its intended effect; God has determined that the church be financed through regular tithes and offerings [1][2].

- **Plan around the reality of your members.** Financial planning must take into account that most members are irregular in attendance and therefore give irregularly, which accounts for the unpredictable and low income of churches [3][4].

- **Handle the money with wisdom and avoid debt.** Managing money takes a lot of wisdom, and over-spiritualizing financial issues is the number one cause of the financial confusion that plagues churches; avoid debt, for debts have closed down many churches [8].

- **Be blameless in the money itself.** Do not receive money on behalf of the church, do not personally count the offerings, and do not take the offering to your house, so that no one has grounds to speak against you [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 9, 12 and 14 of *Church Growth*, chapters 2 and 6 of *Church Administration* and chapter 11 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Philippians 2:15; 1 Timothy 6:10; Titus 1:5.

items.question: How can we grow our church like the early church did?
items.text:
The early church gives us a clear picture of growth under God, and our books point to several ways you can pursue it.

- **Make growth a deliberate ambition, not an accident.** Many pastors think their churches will grow by osmosis, as if crowds will mysteriously appear, but your church will grow through a series of campaigns [4]. Achieving church growth is one of the most difficult things to do, so let it be one of the great ambitions of your life [2].

- **Set up a Church Growth Office.** A bishop must create a Church Growth Office, an administrative office that measures church growth and monitors data like attendance, income, number of branches, lay pastors, full-time pastors, shepherds, small groups, active members, weekly converts, and even the number of cars each week [3]. It monitors the growth of the church and takes decisions to ensure the church increases rather than decreases [3].

- **Run systematic, aggressive campaigns with a specific purpose.** A church growth campaign must be systematic, must consist of a series of aggressive activities, and must have a specific purpose [4]. You are in a war to achieve church growth, and God wants you to set up a campaign of systematic aggressive activities that lead toward that singular goal [4].

- **Grow your naturally forming groups.** Take your tangerine segments — the easily defined groups like the choir, the ushers, or the people who live near the church — and make them grow bigger, because if your choir is very large, your church will be very large [6]. Instead of fighting the air and not knowing what to target, emphasize growing these naturally forming groups as engines of growth [6].

- **Start small and don't be in a hurry.** Two or three is enough to start a church, for where two or three are gathered in His name, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20) [5][7]. There isn't any tree that grows from a seed into a large tree overnight, so if you have a hasty spirit you will not be successful; do not expect much within a year, and don't be surprised if you only have twenty people after two years [5][7].

- **Pray for and recruit pillars.** Pray for labourers, ask God to give you helpers, then go out and recruit pillars, just as Jesus called individuals — Simon and Andrew, then James and John (Mark 1:16-20) — who later became pillars in the church (Galatians 2:9) [5][7]. Be extra careful that you do not break down somebody else's church in the process of building your own [5][7].

- **Love and keep your Group B members.** Group B members are the once-a-weekers and the less involved, and in a large church many people fall into this group; love them anyway, preach sermons they can appreciate, pray for them, and use social events

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 62 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapters 4 and 26 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 28:22; Jeremiah 30:19; Matthew 13:31-32; Matthew 18:20; Mark 1:16-17; Mark 1:19-20; Acts 2:41; Acts 2:47; Acts 4:4; Acts 13:44 and 3 more.

items.question: Why do some pastors keep moving from place to place or stay far from home?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Our books give several reasons why a pastor might keep moving or stay far from home, and they do not all agree on whether it is good.

- **He is searching for the place God has planted him.** Blessings are tied to particular locations, and a man may move from place to place until he finds the spot where God has made room for him, as Isaac did when he named the well Rehoboth and said, "now the Lord hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land" (Genesis 26:22) [1]. A leader may transfer pastors precisely to find their Rehoboth, the place where they will flourish [1].

- **He is being corrected or set in order.** A bishop is to move and transfer pastors to set things in order and improve the life of the pastor and the church, as Paul left Titus in Crete to "set in order the things that are wanting" (Titus 1:5) [7]. Transfers are also used to break a cycle of barrenness in a church that will not grow, or to break cycles of immorality by moving a man out of a town where he cannot live in purity [7].

- **He is running from trouble at home.** Some men move hoping each new house will fix a terrible marriage, one man of God lived a seven-hour flight away from his wife to stay away from his marital home, and another abandoned his church for years and moved abroad while everyone thought he was pioneering a mission — he was on the run, like Elijah [8]. A "Jezebel wife" can cause a man of God to become the exact opposite of what he wants to be [8].

- **He is unstable, and it harms him.** People who move from church to church often do not flourish; they experience stunted growth, and some backslide [2]. One prophet told of a dream in which a pastor who kept moving from church to church had backslidden and become a Rastafarian — a warning to the unstable pastor [2]. Those planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish (Psalm 92:13), so a member should stay in one place, develop roots, and flourish [2].

- **He is separating himself from fellowship and covering.** Some deliberately move to where their history is not known [3]. Separation cuts a man off from the voice of God and right advice, exposes him to evil thoughts, and is given as a reason so many branch pastors rebel and become wasteful [3]. A lay pastor must not become independent of the source of his authority, and those who struggle with being transferred are often agitated by spirits of rebellion, like Absalom, who did not want to be where he was placed [4].

- **He is avoiding idleness or an unsustainable post.** Some pastors become idle and lazy waiting for Sunday, and a man may need to take a secular job and pastor on the side

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 11 of *The Mega Church*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapter 59 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 18 of *The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 26:22; Genesis 28:16; 2 Samuel 14:31-32; 1 Kings 21:18-19; 1 Chronicles 12:33; Psalms 92:13; Psalms 104:24-27; Matthew 16:26; Titus 1:5.

items.question: How old were Jesus' disciples when he called them?
items.text:
The books give us some clues about the ages of the disciples when Jesus called them.

- **They were likely around twenty years old.** The Mishnah, the oldest authoritative collection of Jewish oral laws from the time of Jesus, says that at twenty years a young man is fit for pursuing a vocation, and the disciples were apprentices in their family businesses when Jesus called them [1]. Since Peter was married and the others were not, Peter was probably older than the rest, though not by much, since Andrew his brother was also unmarried [1].

- **Most of them may have been under eighteen.** According to the Mishnah, at eighteen a young man is fit for the bride-chamber, and Peter is the only disciple known to have been married, since the Bible mentions his mother-in-law in Matthew 8:14-15 [1]. If the others had no wives, they were likely below eighteen, with some perhaps as young as fifteen [1].

- **Peter started his ministry at about twenty.** When Jesus was challenged about paying tax, He sent Peter to catch a fish and pay for Himself and Peter only, not the other disciples, because they were not yet over twenty, the age at which the tax was required according to Exodus 30:12-14 [3]. Peter received his calling in his twenties and it took him well over thirty years to finish it [3].

- **They were young men, and spiritual age is not tied to natural age.** Peter, James, John and the others became apostles when they were young men, and your spiritual age is not determined by your natural age [2]. Do not assume that because a person is older he is wiser spiritually, and do not believe you cannot become great spiritually because you are young [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *The Word Of My Patience* and chapter 6 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 30:12-14; Matthew 8:14-15; Matthew 17:24-27; Luke 5:10; Luke 7:28; Acts 4:13; 1 Corinthians 4:1; Revelation 3:10.

items.question: How can I deal with people in my church who criticize the pastor behind his back?
items.text:
It's a heavy thing to carry, and the books speak to it plainly.

- **Don't be surprised or offended by it.** Jesus Himself said, "Tonight, you will be offended because of me" (Matthew 26:31), and it is normal and expected for God's servants to go through fiery trials and temptations [3]. When people speak against you, remember that the stories out there are often far from the truth, and those who love you will never believe bad things about you [3].

- **Recognize what you're dealing with.** A church full of critical and faultfinding people is one of the highest kinds of demonic infiltration in the church [7]. Criticism of the pastor behind his back is a serious matter, not a small one.

- **Check whether it's immaturity before you treat it as rebellion.** Often a person is critical because he is inexperienced — assistant pastors are sometimes critical of the senior pastor because they have never been head pastors themselves [5]. If you are a senior pastor, it is important to check this before it grows into a serious rebellion [5].

- **Consider the school of hard knocks.** One of the best ways to deal with mild disloyalty is to allow the individual to go through certain experiences himself — let him pioneer a church or become a senior minister, and he will mature in no time [5]. Jesus did not rebuke the disciples for abandoning Him; He understood them and sent them out into the world to preach the gospel [5].

- **If it is scorning, the remedy is different.** Scorners are people who mock at you and do not believe in you or in what you are doing, and the Bible says we are not even to sit in the same chair with the scornful (Psalm 1:1) [4]. The biblical remedy is not prayer or fasting but to cast the scorner out, for Proverbs 22:10 says that when the scorner is cast out, contention goes out and strife and reproach cease [4].

- **Bind up a Judas.** If someone is disloyal and spreading bad stories, you must restrict him rather than let him operate freely — God Himself bound the devil, put him in a bottomless pit, shut him up and sealed him [8]. A pastor who left his church of several thousand with a disloyal associate came back to find the associate had spread bad stories and left with almost the whole church, reducing it to about twenty members [8]. If you make mistakes with the handling of a Judas, you will only live to regret it [8].

- **Watch your own tongue toward others.** Secret criticism kills relationships, so do not criticize or ridicule guest ministers, and do not entertain negative comments about them while they are with you or after they are gone — speak evil of no man, as Titus 3:2 says [1]. The way you speak will set the stage for others to criticize

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Church Growth*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended*, chapters 4 and 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 10 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 1:1; Proverbs 3:7; Proverbs 22:10; Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27-31; Romans 13:1; Titus 3:2.

items.question: What does the Bible say about people who were born and raised in the church?
items.text:
What a gift it is to have grown up in the house of God. The books speak warmly of this.

The eighty-seventh psalm is the heart of it: those born in the house are destined to be greatly established, and the Highest Himself shall establish them (Psalm 87:5) [1][2]. It is far easier to be established in the things of God when you were born in the house, and being born and raised in a church to become a leader in that same church is itself a prophetic blessing [1][2].

Those born in the house have their foundation in the holy mountains (Psalm 87:1), which means a foundation of holiness — and without holiness no one will see the Lord, as Hebrews 12:14 says [1]. Growing up in the house means you can grow up without the unholy excursions of the world, without the habits and addictions and patterns that are so hard to break later [1].

Glorious things are spoken of those born in the house (Psalm 87:3) — beauty will be found in their ministry, and they will accomplish what grown-ups could not [1]. The Lord shall count them among the great when He writes up the people (Psalm 87:6); they may not appear on the world's honours lists, but God will include them among His great men [1]. And the singers and players on instruments shall be there (Psalm 87:7) — the children of the church grow up loving Christian music and are never polluted by the music of the world [1].

One picture from the book stays with me: the author describes going to the horse races, where the horses stood behind a net that was suddenly raised for the race to begin. Some horses were not lined up at the right spot, or were even facing the wrong direction, and had to turn around before they could start — and a bad start usually decided the race. Only very special horses could overcome it. That, he says, is what being born in the house gives you: a good start for your life and ministry [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Ready@20*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 87:1-7; Romans 1:4; Hebrews 12:14.

items.question: How can I show appreciation to the people in my life before it's too late?
items.text:
That's a good and tender question, and our books have a good deal to say about it.

- **Do it now, while there is still time.** Honour is something to rush toward, not postpone; most people only recognize a person's greatness after they are gone, so if you want to honour someone, do it quickly [3]. The books urge you to look into your life and see whether there is anyone you need to value, and to make amends while it is hopefully not too late [1][2].

- **Find a concrete way to express it.** It is not enough to feel appreciation; locate the people you need to value and find a suitable way of expressing it to them [1][2]. Bishop Dag tells of a time he felt convicted to honour Archbishop Idahosa while he was visiting Ghana: he found out which hotel he was staying in and presented him with a special offering, and the archbishop laid hands on him and prayed for him. Two weeks later, the archbishop died suddenly, and Bishop Dag realized God had urged him to honour him before it was too late [3].

- **Say what you would want to have said.** At the funeral of Ron Brown, the American Secretary of Commerce who died in a plane crash, his son gave a tribute carried live on CNN, saying he had no regrets because he had said everything he could have said to his father and had kissed him goodbye on his lips the day he travelled. He had little to regret after losing his father [1][2].

- **Give your life, not just your words.** The deepest way to say thank you is with your life, not merely with songs or words you have learned from others; give Him something genuine that comes from you [5]. Say thank you to God by giving Him your reasonable service, being transformed by the renewing of your mind, as Romans 12:1-2 says [8].

- **Give yourself while you are still able.** Jesus gave Himself for you when He was agile, strong and young, and the books ask why you would wait until you are half dead, needing medicine daily, to give yourself to Him; this is the time to love and serve the Lord [5].

One caution worth carrying: beware of people you feel under pressure to show appreciation to, because such people will not be satisfied with any show of love anyway [4][6]. And do not look to people for gratitude in return; a leader looks to God for rewards, as Ephesians 6:8 says [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 4 of *Frugality*, chapter 13 of *Those Who Honour You*, chapter 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 8 of *The Privilege* and chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: John 10:32; Acts 1:21-22; Acts 28:3; Romans 12:1-2; Ephesians 6:8; 1 Timothy 3:2-6.

items.question: How do I experience God's presence when I don't feel Him near?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question — wanting Him near and feeling nothing. Let me share what our books say about this.

- **Look for freshness and refreshing, not just feeling.** People who are stale and unable to walk in newness prove they lack the presence of God, and when you come back from church feeling refreshed, that is because you experienced His presence [1]. So watch for where your spirit is actually revived rather than waiting on a sensation.

- **Learn to know Him as Jehovah Shammah.** Jehovah Shammah means "The Lord is there," the God whose presence can be felt, and it is possible to grow in your ability to experience Him — in your room, in your meetings, at home [2]. You can become someone who knows when God is there and when He is not [2].

- **Believe in the blood and the cross.** You can practically invoke the presence of God by believing in the atoning blood of Jesus, and His presence comes where redemption and salvation are prominent [4]. The wisdom of men, laced with scriptures, cannot replace the wisdom of the cross of Jesus Christ [1].

- **Stay under a covering.** A man of God who has no covering will not experience the presence of God in his ministry, and the presence of God is not felt in a certain way when there is no covering [3]. Do not be a loner; be humble and relate with whoever God places over you [3].

- **Deal with sin, especially pride and the flesh.** Many people have lost the presence of God because of sins of the flesh and sins of pride [5]. It is dangerous to walk in sin or play the fool in the presence of God [7].

- **Create the right environment.** A shabby, dirty, poverty-stricken environment does not encourage the presence of God; you must create a royal environment if you want to experience His presence [8]. Churches with buildings and roofs are more likely to experience God's presence [3].

- **Draw close to understand His purposes.** When you go near the presence of God, you understand His purposes; it takes closeness to God to understand what He has purposed [7]. Much of our confusion comes from not understanding His purposes [7].

One more thing worth holding onto: the presence of God is often like dew — invisible rain. You cannot see dew, but you can see its effects, the watering and growth it brings [2]. So even when you do not feel Him, look for the growth.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 13 and 18 of *The Anointing and the Presence* and chapters 7, 11, 14 and 25 of *Steps to God's Presence*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 25:21; Exodus 33:14-15; Ezekiel 48:35; Hosea 14:5-6; Zechariah 11:12; Matthew 27:8-9; Luke 5:17; 1 Corinthians 1:27-29.

items.question: How can I keep from becoming bitter and turning away from God when I go through hard times?
items.text:
Hard seasons can wear a soul down, and it is a good and honest thing to want to come through them without bitterness. Here is what our books counsel.

- **Expect the bitter waters as part of the journey.** God knows the way to sweet waters, yet He deliberately led Israel to the bitter waters of Marah, and that place was a test for them and will be a test for you too [4]. On the road to ministry, one of the very first stops is Marah, and it is there that many fall away [4].

- **Let the test reveal rather than ruin you.** Suffering is a test that brings out what is in you, the way correction exposes a person's true nature [1]. The things a person has survived speak volumes about him, and the credentials of survived tests are greater than the credentials of any educational institution [2].

- **Refuse bitterness when you meet the "contradiction of sinners."** Hebrews 12:3 speaks of Jesus enduring the contradiction of sinners — receiving the opposite of what you expected after doing good [1]. Do not turn against God when that happens; Jesus showed us how to endure it, so do not become bitter [1].

- **Guard your spirit and your words.** A minister once said it is important to always maintain a sweet spirit, and we must learn to live without bitterness [2]. Murmuring reveals a bad attitude and keeps you from the call of God, so do not complain about your work or anything else, but learn to work peacefully and be cheerful [5].

- **Put on the new nature, where bitterness is replaced.** In Christ you are a new creature, and the new man lays aside all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor and slander, being kind and tender-hearted and forgiving others just as God in Christ forgave you [6]. Instead of bitterness there will be forgiveness and love [6].

- **Walk in forgiveness, because bitterness shuts you off from God.** God allows all Christians to be offended and then watches whether you will obey His Word and forgive [2]. When you walk in forgiveness you attract God's mercy — blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy — but if you fail the test of hurts and offences you exclude yourself from that mercy, and with bitterness in your spirit you no longer receive from God and He no longer answers your prayers [2].

- **Do not let bitterness move you away from God.** Hebrews 12:15 warns lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and thereby many be defiled [3]. Bitterness is an advanced, deep-seated form of offence, and many who walk out of a church are offended Christians whose wounds never healed [3]. It is perhaps the greatest thing that keeps a person from being faithful unto death, and an analysis of rebellious and fallen pastors shows a consistent strain of bitterness and unforgiveness in them [8].

- **Hold on and keep pressing in

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*, chapter 10 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapters 26 and 30 of *Why Few Are Chosen*, chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers* and chapter 4 of *Be Thou Faithful Unto Death*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 8:2; Hebrews 12:3; Hebrews 12:15.
