items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
This is a question the books speak to directly, and they give several reasons why tithing seems not to work for some people.

- **Wrong desires.** If a person's heart is set on killing, fighting, and consuming what they get on their own lusts, God cannot bless them; as James 4:2-3 says, they ask and receive not because they ask amiss [1].

- **Not at peace with the brethren.** The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace (James 3:18), and faith works by love, so strife with brothers and sisters is not something God will bless [1].

- **Bad marital relationships.** Strife, bitterness, unforgiveness, and hatred in a marriage can neutralize the prayers of the saints; as 1 Peter 3:7 says, husbands are to dwell with their wives in honour so that their prayers be not hindered [1].

- **Hidden sins.** Proverbs 28:13 says that he who covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy; hidden sin fights against the blessing a person invokes by tithing [1].

- **The tithe is not ten percent.** The tithe simply means ten percent; nine percent is not a tithe, nor eight, nor seven, nor any less. God honours ten percent of your increase [7].

- **The tithe is not given first.** The tithe is the first fruits of your increase, not the last fruits of your surplus; it changes in its very nature when it is not done first, and that may be why someone gives ten percent but sees no increase [7].

- **The offering is not acceptable.** Money entering the offering bowl does not mean it was accepted in Heaven; offerings can be unacceptable because of the unrighteous life of the giver, the secret worship of idols, or not giving in proportion to what was received [7].

Alongside these, the books also describe what tithing does work in those who practise it: it fulfils the law of humility, since wealth and promotion come from God (Psalm 75:6-7) [3]; it fulfils the law of sowing and reaping, since the tithe is a seed sown in the house of God, and they that sow in tears shall reap in joy (Psalm 126:5) and give and it shall be given unto you (Luke 6:38) [3]; and it fulfils the law of prioritisation, seeking first the kingdom of God (Matthew 6:33) [3]. It also flows with the seasons of life, since there is a time to plant and a time to harvest (Ecclesiastes 3:1-2) [2], and it develops a willing attitude, for if ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land (Isaiah 1:19-20

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 14 and 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 12:43-44; Psalms 75:6-7; Psalms 126:5; Proverbs 28:13; Ecclesiastes 3:1-2; Isaiah 1:19-20; Matthew 6:33; Luke 6:38; James 3:18; James 4:2-3 and 1 more.

items.question: If I do good things for others, how will I be rewarded?
items.book: He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath
items.text:
The books speak to this in a few ways, and they don't all say the same thing, so let me lay them out for you.

**Look to God for your reward, not to people.** A leader should not look to people for gratitude, because your rewards depend on God and not on the people you helped; as Ephesians 6:8 says, whatever good thing any man does, the same shall he receive of the Lord [2]. Do not expect much from people — expect your rewards from God [2]. This matters because people are often ungrateful and forgetful; Paul warned that in the last days men shall be unthankful (2 Timothy 3:1-2), and Jeremiah asked, "Shall evil be recompensed for good?" (Jeremiah 18:20a) [5].

**Expect ingratitude, and don't be surprised by it.** Jesus Himself did many good works and was rewarded with hatred and stoning (John 10:32), and He never responded to that evil spirit of ingratitude [1][2]. If you begin to retaliate because of ingratitude, you will lose your place in the ministry [2].

**Faithfulness with what belongs to others leads to being given your own.** A great qualification for reward is to be constant and faithful with things that are clearly not your own; as Luke 16:12 asks, if you have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own? [4]. God sees your faithfulness as an assistant, a driver, a worker, and rewards you not with rest but with more hard work in your own ministry [4].

**Blessing is meant to flow through you to others.** God does not bless us so that we will multiply silver and gold to ourselves, but so that we will be a blessing to others [8]. The four lepers were blessed so they would tell the others there was food, and they knew they would not "do well" if they did not tell the news; remembering others is the key to doing well [8].

One caution sits alongside all this: doing good deeds can become a clever substitute for simple obedience. God will not reward you because you did many good things but because you obeyed Him, and obeying God will often not bring you honour from men [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 26 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 5 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work*, chapter 5 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 15 of *Others*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Chronicles 20:10-12; Proverbs 26:27; Jeremiah 18:19-20; Luke 14:26; Luke 16:12; John 10:32; John 15:24-25; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 3:1-2.

items.question: Why do the people closest to a pastor, like family and his wife, often have a hard time receiving from his ministry?
items.text:
This is a painful thing to watch, and the books speak to it directly.

The heart of it is familiarity. Jesus Himself could do no mighty work in His hometown, because the people there knew Him too well to receive Him as the Son of God — they had questions about His parents, His family, and His background (Mark 6:1-3, 5) [6][8]. Moses, who commanded a pillar of fire by night and a pillar of cloud by day, could not impress his own sister Miriam; she criticized him about his marriage and suffered for it [6][8].

The books name the groups who most easily fall into this. Colleagues and friends who have been around a man of God for so long, and seen his ups and downs, slip into familiarity — when Bishop Dag started his church as a medical student, very few of his colleagues could receive from him, saying in their hearts, "Is this not Dag? We know him and we know his class. We saw him struggling at an exam last week" [6][8]. Relatives say, "Is this not Azoyzoy's son? We carried him when he was a baby" [8]. And pastors' wives often suffer severe familiarity — like Michal, they are not impressed with their husbands when everyone else is impressed, saying, "I know you. No one knows you better than I do" [8].

The books describe the effect plainly: familiarity carves out a road of ministry for anointed people, directing them away from their colleagues, friends, and family, and toward the non-familiar, the poor, the forgotten, and the neglected — which is where the outsiders come in, often to replace those who have become too familiar with the anointed one [6][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Church Planting* and chapter 13 of *Ministerial Barrenness*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 6:1-3; Mark 6:5.

items.question: How can I stay close to God and keep bearing fruit in my life?
items.text:
That's a good and honest question, and our books have a great deal to say about it.

- **Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.** Closeness is a law of fruitfulness — a branch cannot bear fruit unless it stays in the vine, and the closer you get to God, the closer you are to bearing fruit [1]. So take time to go and wait on the Lord; as James 4:8 says, draw nigh to God and He will draw nigh to you [1].

- **Stay connected to Jesus as your master key.** Any fruit you bear comes from your close connection to Him, and human effort can never substitute for being deeply connected to Jesus [2][6]. As John 15:5 says, without Him you can do nothing [2][6].

- **Abide — stay, remain, be planted.** Abiding means staying in God rather than being in and out of Him, and the longer you stay, the more fruitful you become [1]. A tree that is often transplanted will never grow to its full fruit-bearing potential, so be stable and permanent where God has planted you [8].

- **Stay close to the spiritual tree and the people God has given you.** Your key to flourishing as a branch is to stay attached to your spiritual tree, and disconnection and detachment are the master keys to withering [3]. God Himself gives you pastors after His own heart (Jeremiah 3:15), and your survival is connected to maintaining the closest connection to the apostles and prophets He has given you [3].

- **Let the Word abide in you and obey the Lord.** If you want answers to your prayers, stay in the Word, for God does not do anything outside His Word [5]. And as 1 John 3:22 says, we receive from Him because we keep His commandments and do what pleases Him [5].

- **Bear fruit, and keep bearing it.** God has linked answered prayer to fruit bearing — as John 15:16 says, He chose and ordained you to go and bring forth fruit that should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in His name He may give you [5]. Do something in your church rather than sitting and watching, for the blessings are for Christians who bear fruit [5].

- **Guard against the distractions and the drift.** Slow deterioration and withering is the sign of those who no longer bear fruit [1], and the confessions of the fruitful life include overcoming the distractions that prevent people from bearing fruit — reading your Bible, praying, and keeping your quiet time every day [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Fruitfulness (2022)*, chapter 6 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 14 of *Victory Secrets*, chapter 26 of *Name It Claim It Take It*, chapter 3 of *100% Answered Prayer*, chapter 5 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

items.question: How can I be sure I really know the Lord and won't be turned away from heaven?
items.text:
It's a question worth asking soberly, and our books speak to it plainly.

- **Know Him personally, not just publicly.** It is possible to be a member of a church and do great things for God without actually knowing Him, and Jesus' own words in Matthew 7:21-23 warn that He will say "I never knew you" to people who prophesied and did wonderful works in His name [3][4]. Meeting someone in public and shaking his hand is not the same as knowing him; knowing about someone is different from knowing the person [4][7].

- **Let your daily quiet time be the place of that relationship.** A daily quiet time is what gives you a personal, one-to-one relationship with the Lord, and nothing else can produce it; coming to church a thousand times is not the same as personal interaction with Him [3][4]. Draw near to God and He will draw near to you, as James 4:8 says [4][7]. One of the books puts it bluntly: a daily quiet time may actually be your passport to heaven [7].

- **Come to Him through the blood of Jesus.** Through the blood of Jesus you are cleansed from your sins and can get to know God; His blood and supreme sacrifice paid the price so that we can know Him [2]. He stands at the door and knocks, and if you open, He will come in and sup with you, as Revelation 3:20 says [2].

- **Follow the One who actually knows the way.** Jesus Christ knows the way to heaven because He has been there before, and He said in John 14:6 that He is the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him [8]. Follow someone who knows the way to heaven [8].

- **Let your life bear fruit.** After you are born again you must become fruitful, because the Holy Spirit is poured out to make you fruitful and to make you a soul winner; Jesus said every branch in Him that bears no fruit is taken away, as John 15:2 shows [5].

- **Don't be thrown off by opposition.** Expect persecution and rejection — Jesus said in John 15:20 that if they persecuted Him they will persecute you, and in John 16:2 that people will even think they do God service by killing you — so steel your heart and don't let offence turn you away from the ministry [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 28 and 30 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 5 of *The Secret*, chapter 7 of *Seven Great Principles* and chapter 19 of *Those Who Are Offended*.

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
It's a hard thing to watch your own words wound the people you love, and I'm glad you're bringing it into the light.

**Recognize that the tongue is beyond your own strength to tame.** Scripture says the tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison, and that no man can tame his tongue — it takes the Holy Spirit to help a believer control it [3]. So this isn't a battle you win by sheer willpower alone.

**Understand that your words carry real power, for death or for life.** Death and life are in the power of the tongue, which means your angry words are not harmless venting — they are doing something [3]. The words you speak are spiritual creatures coming out of your mouth, performing things in the physical realm, so you must watch your mouth and watch what you hear [7].

**Refuse to give your anger a foothold.** Scripture says, "Neither give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:27), and the counsel is to give no opportunity to your flesh [6]. Be aware of the potential for evil that is in your flesh, spend time fasting regularly, and stay far from the enticements that trip you up — when God says run, you run, you don't stand and fight [6].

**Let no corrupt communication come out of your mouth.** Ephesians 4:29 says to let nothing corrupt proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for edifying, so that it may minister grace to those who hear [1]. And Ephesians 4:26 says, "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" — deal with the offence rather than letting it fester [1].

**Deal with the root, which is often unforgiveness.** Wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking are all signs of lingering unforgiveness, and Scripture says to put them all away and instead be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven you (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5]. A Christian is commanded by God to forgive, and walking in forgiveness is how you get the offence off your chest [1].

**Guard your heart from bitterness.** Beware of becoming bitter after bad experiences, because when a bitter person speaks, it affects, influences and poisons others [5]. Keep your heart pure and free of hurts, and forgive those who wound you, even when it costs you [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 60 of *Model Marriage*, chapter 1 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 5 of *Why Few Are Chosen*, chapter 4 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*, chapter 2 of *Seven Great Principles* and chapter 13 of *Victory Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:21; 2 Corinthians 10:5; Galatians 5:13; Ephesians 4:26-27; Ephesians 4:29; Ephesians 4:31-32; James 3:8; Revelation 16:14.

items.question: What does the wind of the Holy Spirit do in a person's life?
items.text:
The books describe the wind of the Spirit as active and real in a believer's life, and they name several things it does.

- **It withers what displeases God.** The wind of the Spirit can cause anything displeasing to God to wither, just as the thin, blasted ears of grain in Pharaoh's dream were withered by the east wind (Genesis 41:22-23) [1].

- **It drives away demonic powers.** The wind of the Spirit can blow away demonic powers, as when the Lord turned a mighty strong west wind that took away the locusts from Egypt (Exodus 10:16-19) [1].

- **It blows away death.** The wind of the Spirit can blow away the plague of death, as when God made a wind to pass over the earth and the flood waters assuaged in Noah's day (Genesis 8:1-3) [1].

- **It makes a way for you.** When Israel was trapped between the Red Sea and the Egyptians, God caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind and made dry land (Exodus 14:21-22), and He promises to make men go over dryshod by His mighty wind (Isaiah 11:15-16) [1].

- **It dries up evil things.** The wind of the Spirit can dry up the evil springs of the enemy, and the book says this is how deeply rooted habits—especially sexual ones—are dealt with, by being dried out rather than simply stopped (Hosea 13:15) [1].

- **It destroys the enemy's forces.** Whatever is fighting you can be destroyed by the mighty Holy Spirit, who is a mighty rushing wind that can destroy enemies and empty their land (Jeremiah 51:1-2; Psalm 35:5) [3].

- **It brings in the supplies you need.** Through the wind of the Spirit, Moses was able to feed two million people every day, and the book tells us to expect mighty financial miracles of provision through the rushing wind of the Spirit [3].

- **It brings life, feeling, sight, sound, activity, and growth.** When the breath of God comes into you, you receive life: life has feelings, sight, and sound; life has activity; and life has growth, so a church or ministry that is alive will show growth (Genesis 7:21-22; Psalm 104:29) [4].

- **It is the evidence of the Spirit's presence in soul winning.** Where the Holy Spirit is present there is soul winning and an emphasis on the Great Commission, and the great evidence of His presence is the harvesting of lost multitudes to Jesus Christ [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Flow in the Anointing* and chapter 9 of *Make Yourselves Saviours of Men*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 7:21-22; Genesis 8:1-3; Genesis 41:22-23; Exodus 10:16-19; Exodus 14:21-22; Psalms 35:5; Psalms 104:29; Isaiah 11:15-16; Jeremiah 51:1-2; Hosea 13:15.

items.question: What can I learn from Esther about helping others even when I'm comfortable?
items.text:
Comfort can quietly make us forget the people outside our own walls, and Esther's story speaks directly to that. Here is what the books draw out of her life.

- **Your comfort is not an accident — it is a assignment.** You have come into your position for a reason, and that reason is to deliver others; God raised you up so you could help them [1]. Perhaps the very reason God made you a queen was so you could help others [1].

- **If you hold back, God will use someone else — and you will lose what you were given for.** Mordecai warned Esther that if she kept silent, deliverance would arise from another place, but she and her father's house would be destroyed [1][2]. God can and does raise up people to supply the needs of the church, and enlargement can come from many other sources [2].

- **Neglecting others can cost your family too.** Just as you neglect the "others" who are important to God, God may neglect the "others" who are important to you [1]. The warning to Esther was not only about her own life but about her father's house [1].

- **Remember where you came from.** Esther remembered who she was and where she came from, and because of that she was used to save an entire nation [5][8]. A daughter of destiny does not quickly forget where she came from; she remembers her father and helps him, not knowing the price he paid to care for her [3].

- **Be willing to lay down your life.** Esther said, "if I perish, I perish," and went in to the king though it was not according to the law [2][3][5]. No one becomes anything great unless he is ready to give up his life for his beliefs — and Esther is remembered eternally because she gave up her life for hers [5].

- **Stay small enough to receive counsel.** Esther remained small in her own eyes and kept listening to Mordecai even after she became queen, doing what he told her as she had done under his care [7]. Every novice and newcomer must desire counsel and hold on to it, learning survival skills from experienced people [4].

- **Let serving others pull you out of yourself.** When you help others, you take the focus off yourself and your problems, and that is a cure for self-centredness and self-pity [6]. Learn to comfort others with the comfort you have received [6].

- **Do not grasp at your privileges.** Esther was prepared to give up the treasured position of living in the king's house, ready to lose her privileges and recognition for the sake of her high calling [7]. Do not lose your relevance by neglecting the divine reason for which God raised you up [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Others*, chapter 33 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*, chapter 4 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 14 of *The Art of Following* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:32; 1 Samuel 15:17; Esther 2:10; Esther 2:20; Esther 4:13-16; Esther 7:3-4; Proverbs 17:22; Proverbs 31:20; Isaiah 51:1; Luke 22:24-27 and 3 more.

items.question: Why is it so hard to leave a church that feels like family?
items.text:
It's hard because a church that has become family is exactly what Jesus made it to be. When Jesus was told His mother and brothers were outside, He stretched out His hand toward His disciples and said, "Whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Matthew 12:48-50) — He made those who obey God's word His family [1]. That is why people sometimes criticize such churches as cults, saying no one can leave; the truth is that no one leaves a family, and it is difficult to leave a church that has become a family [1]. Faithfulness unto death is simply the natural occurrence for families — no one leaves a family until they die [1].

The books also describe the church as a building and a garden. We are God's building (1 Corinthians 3:9), and you cannot easily remove the blocks of a building; blocks are a permanent part of the structure [2]. We are also like a garden, and if you uproot a plant and replant it elsewhere, you endanger its life — do it repeatedly and you will kill the plant [2]. And every family has its problems: conflicts and misunderstandings come, but a misunderstanding with your uncle does not lead you to change your name, so hurts should not make members change their churches [2].

One more thing worth naming: leaving is also hard when leadership itself is the difficulty. It is very difficult to live under oppressive leadership, and if someone does not feel important and appreciated, he often begins to look elsewhere — it is the duty of the head to make everyone feel important and appreciated [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Be Thou Faithful Unto Death*, chapter 11 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 2 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:5; Matthew 12:48-50; 1 Corinthians 3:9; Ephesians 5:31.

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
That is a heavy thing for a young person to carry, and I'm glad you're walking with him in it.

The books speak directly to this. The madman of Gadara, fully under the influence of Satan, cut himself with stones — he systematically destroyed himself, and this is described as a very important manifestation of the presence of Satan: self-destruction [8]. The demonized man of Gadara tried to kill himself by cutting himself with stones [1]. So what this boy is doing is not a small thing to be explained away; it is a sign of a spiritual battle.

The books also say that what makes people so sad that they give up on life and become suicidal can only be demons [3]. They point to Jonah, who was depressed and very suicidal and prayed that he would die [6], and to Elijah, who after great victory became depressed, retreated from his ministry into the wilderness, and asked God to take his life [6]. Social withdrawal is named as one of the most common and telling signs of depression, because depressed people feel miserable, worthless, ashamed, misunderstood and hopeless, and do not like to spend time with others [6].

The counsel that follows from this is to know the source of the problem and tackle it at its root, rather than only treating the surface [3]. The books urge deliverance: "Perhaps evil spirits are making you depressed and sorrowful. Receive your deliverance today in the name of Jesus!" [3]. And they warn plainly: be careful that demons do not cause you to behave like a mad man in the ministry of the Lord Jesus Christ [1].

One more thing the books name, which may matter for a teenager carrying hurts: unforgiveness and bitterness are a demonic foothold, and there is nothing more self-destructive than bitterness and hurts [8]. God will forgive every sin we commit, but He will not forgive us when we do not forgive others [8].

So stay close to him, do not let him isolate, and pray for his deliverance — and please, alongside that, make sure he is also under proper medical care, since the books themselves note that depression patients are prone to suicide and that many mental health conditions lead to it [1][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7, 14 and 22 of *Those who are mad* and chapters 9 and 11 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; 1 Kings 19:2-4; Isaiah 61:3; Ezekiel 28:16-18; Jonah 4:1-9; Mark 5:5.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.

items.question: Can God heal emotional wounds and mental problems that medicine can't fix?
items.book: Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit
items.text:
Yes — and the books speak to this very tenderly. God is not against medicine; the wisdom to develop medicines is itself a gift from Him, and the two streams of healing are not contrary to each other [3][6]. But there are wounds medicine simply cannot reach, and God can.

The Word of God has a way of healing us of our pain and wounds, and a daily dose of it brings healing to every inner wound [1]. Jesus Himself said He was anointed to heal the broken-hearted, and that healing comes through the Word of God [1]. The broken-hearted are people with deep disappointment — shattered dreams and hopes — and Christ came to save men from exactly that [2]. As Psalm 147:3 says, "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds" [2][4].

The books are honest that this is the hardest ground. Spiritual, emotional and psychological problems are the most difficult to solve, and doctors often struggle with them to no avail; the psychiatrist is described as the doctor with fewest answers, often only able to calm and sedate a patient [2]. But God knows everything and reaches to the innermost parts of our being [2]. He is Jehovah Rophe — the Lord who heals, repairs, restores and mends what is broken, damaged or torn, and who makes us happy again [5]. He restores the soul (Psalm 23:3) [2][7].

This covers more than sadness. The healing anointing heals the will of men — the inability to say "no" to things that destroy you is a sign of a diseased will [7]. It heals the souls of men, so that people who cannot love anyone, or cannot receive love, can be restored [7]. It heals those oppressed by evil spirits, who are described in Luke 6:17-18 as being healed [7]. And it heals depression, which is a common and serious illness — God can heal it through His power [7].

One thing worth holding onto: while God's grace is available for your emotional healing, you are the key to your own recovery, and how soon you heal depends on you [4]. The path the book describes moves through shock, fear, guilt, hurt, anger, acceptance, forgiveness, and finally healing, where the Holy Spirit is like oil and balm for your wound [4]. And we should stay humble here — the secret things belong to the Lord (Deuteronomy 29:29), and for now we see through a glass darkly (1 Corinthians 13:12) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapters 1, 14, 15, 17 and 18 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 29:29; 2 Kings 2:19-22; Psalms 23:3; Psalms 107:20; Psalms 147:3; Jeremiah 17:14; Mark 5:2-3; Mark 6:31; Luke 4:18; Luke 6:17-18 and 3 more.

items.question: How can I tell if someone is really a Christian or just going to church?
items.text:
You're asking a question the books speak to directly, and their answer is simpler than we often fear.

- **Look at their fruit, not their appearance.** Jesus said, "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them" (Matthew 7:20), and that is how we distinguish genuine Christians from counterfeit ones — by what their lives actually produce [1][2]. Bishop Dag Heward-Mills tells of a patient he once saw in the gynaecology department at Korle-Bu Hospital: a young person in her early twenties who had never had a menstrual period, and on examination turned out to have hidden male reproductive organs. Outwardly she looked like a woman, but she could never bear children because she was not one. In the same way, some people cannot bear spiritual fruit because they are not real Christians [1][2].

- **Ask whether they are bringing others to the Lord.** If, by your spiritual activity, others just like you are brought to the Lord and discipled, that fruit shows you are real; but if there are no converts to show for your Christianity, something is missing [1][2]. A person who has genuinely been changed will go about joyfully telling others, and no one will have to urge them on — it happens naturally [1][2].

- **Watch for the signs of a merely outward faith.** Church membership does not prove anyone is a genuine Christian at all; some come to church for reasons other than a deep desire to seek God, or simply follow a family member or friend, and they fall away when certain things happen because they were never really what they claimed to be [1][2]. Real Christianity takes place outside the church after Sundays — each weekday has its share of prayer, worship, Bible reading and labouring for the Lord [1][2].

- **Remember the counsel to examine yourself.** The books press this home with 2 Corinthians 13:5: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" [1][2]. And be careful not to be moved by foolish questions and suspicions about others, which only gender strifes (2 Timothy 2:23) [4].

One caution, pastor: this is a test we are told to apply honestly to ourselves far more than to sit in judgment over others. If you are trying to discern in a particular person, look patiently for the fruit, and let your own life bear it too.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Many Are Called*, chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind* and chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:20; 2 Corinthians 13:5; 2 Timothy 2:23.

items.question: Why can't I get to heaven by being a good person?
items.text:
It's a question many sincere people carry, and the books speak to it directly.

Being a good person and doing good works is not the way to Heaven; good works will not take you there, because the only way is through the blood of Jesus [1][2][6]. Our own righteousness does not qualify us — as Isaiah 64:6 says, all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and as Romans 3:10 says, there is none righteous, no, not one [1][3]. Salvation is by grace through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9) [3][6]. You cannot be good enough to qualify for Heaven; our best is not good enough [3].

There is also only one door. There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and there is no other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved (Acts 4:12) [1][2]. Jesus said plainly, "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" [6]. And there is no shortcut — the only way is accepting the Lord Jesus Christ as your personal Saviour and being born again [7].

One thing worth holding alongside this: the same Scripture that says we are saved not by works also says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has ordained that we should walk in them (Ephesians 2:10) [3][4][8]. So good works are not the way to Heaven, but they are the reason we are left here after we are saved — we are alive to accomplish the good works God prepared for us [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 65 and 111 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 1 of *Tell Them*, chapters 2 and 3 of *Church Planting* and chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 11:16; Proverbs 11:4-5; Isaiah 42:17; Isaiah 64:6; Matthew 7:21-22; Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6-7; Luke 9:24; Acts 4:12; Romans 3:10 and 3 more.

items.question: What happens if I dishonour my husband?
items.text:
This is a heavy thing to carry, and I want to speak gently with you about it.

The books describe dishonour as a seed that grows into more dishonour, and they trace several results. Dishonour opens the door to a demonic invasion of your life — Jesus said He had no devil because He honoured His Father, and Judas received Satan into his soul when he dishonoured the appointment Jesus gave him [2]. It also brings obscurity: the Scripture says the one who curses his father has his lamp put out in obscure darkness (Proverbs 20:20), and the book applies that to those who dishonour the ones who raised them [1]. Dishonour leads to being replaced, as Vashti lost her place as queen when she refused to honour her husband, and her royal estate was given to another [1]. And it leads to being lightly esteemed, for God says, "them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed" (1 Samuel 2:30) [1].

The book also names what dishonour looks like in a marriage. A wife who stops adapting herself to her husband — no longer washing, cleaning, anointing herself, or caring what she wears at home — is dishonouring him, because a woman in awe of her husband carefully presents herself to him [3]. Stubbornness, resistance and rejection of authority are ways disobedience shows itself [5]. Pretending or being a hypocrite is also a sign of dishonour, for the Lord said of such people, "This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me" (Matthew 15:7-9) [5]. And opposing your husband publicly is dishonour — a daughter of destiny supports her husband publicly and brings her disagreements to him in private, for the virtuous woman's husband is known in the gates (Proverbs 31:23) [4].

One book speaks to the cost of standing on your rights in marriage. It tells of a woman whose disobedience led to divorce, and it weighs two bad options: humble yourself, obey, and preserve your marriage, or stand up for your rights, refuse to be bullied, and lose your marriage. It counsels that it would be wise to retain your God-given position, and that in some cases fighting for your human rights may be more expensive than enduring moments of indignity [4]. It also says that when your husband is disgraced, you are disgraced as well, for when his face is dragged in the mud, so is yours [4].

If you would like, tell me more of what is actually happening between you and your husband, and we can look at it together.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 6, 9 and 11 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 31 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 32:17; Ruth 3:1-4; 1 Samuel 2:30; Esther 1:15-20; Proverbs 20:20; Proverbs 31:23; Matthew 15:7-9; Luke 22:3; John 8:49-50.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
When someone you've trusted turns against you, that wound is real, and the books speak to it directly. Here is what they counsel.

- **Dismiss them outright.** God's own pattern with Lucifer was to cast him out — not to pray for him, counsel him, or rehabilitate him — so rebellious people must not be given access to the church they rebelled against, and opening your doors to them is not love but foolishness [1]. The biblical remedy for a scoffer is to cast them out, as Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [6][7].

- **Wipe out their associates too.** No friendship with a disloyal person is neutral, so those who are friends of your traitors should be released to join the enemy camp openly, just as God cast out the angels associated with Lucifer [3].

- **Teach your people constantly.** This is the preventive method — regularly teaching the Word fights deception, since it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer, and the devil is called "that old serpent who deceives the whole world" [4].

- **Restrict them.** Binding a "Judas" means restricting him; letting a known disloyal person operate freely because you don't want to restrict anyone is making yourself wiser than God [8].

- **Be fierce and resolute.** Disloyalty has the power to end a church and a ministry, so you must not deal with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence [5].

- **Watch for the signs.** Scorners mock you and don't believe in you, and you shouldn't even sit in the same chair with them [6]; inflexibility — stubbornness, refusing correction, unwillingness to go beyond the contract — is itself a manifestation of disloyalty [6].

- **Recognize what they are.** A disloyal person is unfit for the work of God, worthless to your cause, dangerous, unreliable, and an impostor — so you must protect yourself from them rather than try to use them [7].

One caution the books give: handle a "Judas" God's way, with knowledge and wisdom, because if you make mistakes in handling him you will only live to regret it [8].

items.question: Why does the Bible warn against trying to get rich?
items.book: Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich
items.text:
The Bible's warnings about pursuing riches are many, and they all point in the same direction — that riches make a dangerous master. Here is what our books say about why we are told not to labour to be rich.

- **Ill-gotten riches can cut your life short.** Those who gain riches the wrong way may have their days cut off, as Jeremiah 17:10-11 says — the one who gets riches and not by right shall leave them in the midst of his days [1].
- **Riches can turn you into a fool.** Jesus told of a rich man whose ground brought forth plentifully; he planned to pull down his barns, build greater ones, and tell his soul to take its ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said to him, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee," and asked whose those things would then be — so is he who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God (Luke 12:15-21) [1].
- **Riches can keep you from taking up your cross and following Jesus.** A man who had kept the commandments from his youth went away grieved when Jesus told him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him, for he had great possessions; and Jesus said how hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God (Mark 10:17-23) [1].
- **Riches are deceptive.** The deceitfulness of riches, along with the cares of this world and the lusts of other things, chokes the word so that it becomes unfruitful (Mark 4:19) [1].
- **Riches are linked to many temptations and traps.** Those who will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts which drown men in destruction and perdition, for the love of money is the root of all evil; some who coveted after it have erred from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:9-10) [2][3].
- **Riches are laden with foolish and hurtful desires**, and those who aim to be rich are drowned in destruction and perdition [2].
- **Riches cannot be taken with you.** As Ecclesiastes 5:14-16 asks, what profit has he that has laboured for the wind, since in all points as he came, so shall he go [2].

The heart of it is that God's word says plainly, "Labour not to be rich" (Proverbs 23:4), and calls us instead to cease from our own wisdom and labour to be blessed, since the blessing of the Lord makes rich (Proverbs 10:22) [4][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 4 of *Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 23:4; Ecclesiastes 5:14-16; Jeremiah 17:10-11; Matthew 1:21; Mark 4:19; Mark 10:17-23; Luke 12:15-21; 1 Timothy 6:9-10.

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
That is a heavy thing to carry, and I'm sorry you're walking through it.

The first thing the books would have you do is refuse to let fear take over. Slander spreads fear and panic through a congregation, and fear is not from God — as 2 Timothy 1:7 says, God has given us a spirit of power, love and a sound mind, not fear [1]. So you can trust Him to steady you rather than being swept up in the alarm the stories create.

Remember that God sees this and will deal with it. The psalmist, surrounded by people taking counsel together against him, said, "But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God" [1]. The books promise that God will cause you to trample over satan and his slanderers, and that in time those who spread the stories will be caught in the very fuel they meant to burn you with [1].

Guard your own tongue in the middle of it. Slandering is evil because it spreads the failings of a fellow brother who is as weak as you are, and people who fall are to be helped up, not pushed further down [6]. The counsel is to lay hands on your tongue if necessary and make sure there is no poison in it [3].

And know that this is not a small thing in God's eyes — He hates a lying tongue (Proverbs 6:16, 17), and liars are disloyal people [5]. A slanderer is a devil and an accuser, and there is never a day when it is good to be one [6]. You are not imagining the wrong done to you.

If the lies are coming from someone in leadership, that carries particular weight, because the authority of a pastor gives credence to the stories being peddled [1]. And if the person is actively campaigning — going from one person to another to turn hearts against you — the books call that the sin of "going up and down" as a talebearer (Leviticus 19:16), and it is a sin to be an active spreader of lies [6].

One more thing worth holding onto: slanderous stories are hard to erase from people's minds once they've heard them [3]. That is a real grief, and it is why the books urge you not to be a destroyer yourself, since Satan is the one who comes to destroy [3]. Keep your hands clean, keep trusting God, and let Him be the one who vindicates you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*, chapter 9 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue* and chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Numbers 16:12; Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 119:21-24; Proverbs 6:16-17; Proverbs 6:19; Proverbs 11:13; 2 Timothy 1:7.

And if the person is actively campaigning — going from one person to another to turn hearts against you — the books call that the sin of "going up and down" as a talebearer (Leviticus 19:16), and it is a sin to be an active spreader of lies.
One more thing worth holding onto: slanderous stories are hard to erase from people's minds once they've heard them.
That is a real grief, and it is why the books urge you not to be a destroyer yourself, since Satan is the one who comes to destroy.

items.question: How do I meditate on the Bible and get something out of it during my quiet time?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
Meditation is where the quiet time comes alive — it's the thinking through and soberly reflecting on what you've read, and without it you lose a major blessing of the Word [1][2][3]. Here are the ways the books lay out:

- **Read slowly and keep it short.** Read the passage slowly, and don't take a very long passage unless it's necessary [1][2][3]. The goal isn't volume; it's depth.

- **Stop where a verse strikes you.** When a verse stops you, stay there and think about it — God's Word is so powerful that a single word in a verse is enough to change your life, so each quiet time is a search for that one word [1][2][3]. Turn it over in your mind until the full revelation comes [4].

- **Chew on the words themselves.** Think about the meanings of the words you're reading [1][2][3]. A dictionary helps here, because you'll be surprised at the meanings of words we assume we know [6][7].

- **Ask how it applies to your generation.** Think about how the Scripture applies to life in your own day, not just in Bible times [1][2][3].

- **Ask the Holy Spirit to open it.** Whisper to the Holy Spirit, "Help me, Holy Spirit, to understand your Word. Father, give me the Spirit of wisdom and revelation" [1][2][3] — the prayer Paul prayed in Ephesians 1:17 [1][2].

- **Decide on a practical way to do it.** Without thinking of a way to apply the Scripture directly, you will often not benefit from your quiet time [1][2][3]. Paul told Timothy to think about the Word of God, as 2 Timothy 2:7 says [1][2][3].

- **Go deeper when God ministers to you.** Sometimes you'll need a longer quiet time, so be prepared to study further with a good reference Bible, looking for what the passage teaches about God, a promise to believe, a command to obey, a warning to heed, or a prayer to pray [1][2].

- **Write down what He tells you.** Develop the habit of writing the things God speaks to you about — the very fact that you have a notebook shows faith in an invisible God, and without faith it is not possible to please God [1][2]. Moses was told to hew two tables of stone and write the words on them (Exodus 34:1) [6][7].

- **End in prayer.** The last step is to pray and listen to the voice of the Holy Spirit; at times it will be short, at other times long, and as you keep the habit your prayer time will grow longer and longer [1][2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 12 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapters 3 and 11 of *The Secret* and chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 34:1; Joshua 1:8; Psalms 119:18; Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44; 2 Corinthians 3:18; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Timothy 2:7; 2 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 1:1-2 and 1 more.

items.question: How can I cooperate with the anointing for dreams and visions?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is simple: God gives the dreams, and your part is to receive them with respect and act on them.

- **Believe that God will speak to you this way.** The key to cooperating with the anointing is to accept, believe in, and flow with the visions and dreams God gives you; most people never walk in this anointing simply because they do not value the dreams they are given [1]. Daniel believed in dreams and visions, and that made him one of the greatest prophets [1].

- **Write them down right away.** When Daniel had his dream, he wrote it down, and writing something shows how seriously you take it [1]. Show respect to the Holy Spirit by writing your dreams and visions down immediately, and do not disregard even the smallest kind of dream or vision [7].

- **Obey them, even when they seem vague.** Most of us have dreams and visions we do not obey, and if we obeyed them we would experience the anointing; the drive to obey these visions is the drive toward the anointing [2]. Cornelius obeyed the vision and met Peter, Peter obeyed a vision and met Cornelius, and as Peter preached, Cornelius and his whole household received the anointing — one thing leads to another until you are standing in the river of the anointing [2].

- **Ask God for understanding of what you see.** Zechariah was known for his understanding in the visions of God, and as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper (2 Chronicles 26:5) [4]. A person can have many dreams and not understand anything he sees — one young man dreamed he was caught up in a tree by his hair, insisted it meant jealous people were holding him back, and weeks later fell into rebellion exactly like Absalom, manifesting what his dream had warned him about because he had no understanding of it [4].

- **Do not be moved by dreams that come from your own needs.** Hungry people dream about food and thirsty people dream about drink, so do not be moved by the visions and dreams you generate out of your needs and desires; wait on the Lord and He will speak to you through genuine dreams and visions [5].

- **Expect the Holy Spirit to be the source of them.** When people received the Holy Spirit they began to have dreams, and dreaming is an ability that comes from the anointing; without the influence of the Spirit you will never have dreams, visions, or direction [7]. The anointing oil in your life brings guidance — the oil for light is the coming of the Holy Spirit and the giving of visions, dreams, and revelations of the Word [8].

- **Let them guide you, because they carry real weight.** Visions are God's way of speaking to His anointed, to those with understanding, and to His servants in their sleep [4][5]. Where there is no vision

items.question: How do I get angels to intervene in my situation when I pray?
items.text:
The books speak directly to this, and they give several ways.

- **Pray — that is the main way.** Jesus said He could pray to the Father and be given more than twelve legions of angels, and the book says prayer is the greatest and most definite way of securing angelic participation [1][2]. Where there is prayer there is angelic intervention; prayer activates and releases angels [2]. Daniel was told, "from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand... thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words" [3], and at the beginning of his supplications the commandment came forth and Gabriel was sent [6].

- **Expect angels to come to the place where you pray.** When Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, an angel appeared to Him from heaven, strengthening Him [3][7]. When He prayed in the wilderness, the angels ministered to Him [3]. Angels are drawn to prayer; they will come to the room you are praying in, and you can never be truly alone when you are praying [3].

- **Keep praying, even when the answer is delayed.** Daniel's angel was withstood by the prince of the kingdom of Persia for twenty-one days before Michael came to help [3]. Do not stop praying; prayer secures angelic activity [8].

- **Pray over the situation itself, not only for angels.** Prayer brings God into every situation [7], brings a supernatural element into it [7], and brings a blessing into it — as when Jesus looked up to heaven and blessed the five loaves and two fishes, and five thousand were fed [7]. Prayer also brings the Holy Spirit into the situation, as when the disciples prayed and the place was shaken and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost (Acts 4:31) [7].

- **Pray against what opposes you.** Prayer destroys demonic power that is against you in every situation; no one can spoil a strong man's house unless he first binds the strong man (Matthew 12:29) [7]. Angels contend against those who contend against you, as when an angel was sent because of Hezekiah's prayer and destroyed his mockers [8].

- **Add hospitality.** The book names entertainment and hospitality as the first well-known way of bringing angels into your life: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" [5]. Lot pressed the two angels to stay, made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate — and they later turned out to be his saviours [5]. Abraham hurried to provide water, bread, butter, milk and a good calf, and his guests turned out to be angels who helped him and Sarah have a child [5]. Manoah, Samson's father, cheerfully hosted visitors and provided food, and angels were attracted to his residence [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Prayer Changes Things* and chapter 1 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 18:1-8; Genesis 19:1-3; Exodus 23:20-22; 1 Kings 19:1-7; 2 Kings 1:2-3; Proverbs 3:5-6; Daniel 9:21-25; Daniel 10:1-15; Matthew 12:29; Matthew 26:52-54 and 9 more.

items.question: How should I respond when people constantly accuse and criticize me for serving God?
items.book: One of You is a Devil
items.text:
It's a heavy thing to carry, and you're not imagining it — the books speak plainly about how relentless and real this attack is. Here is what they counsel.

- **Know who the accusers around you are.** Every good leader must understand the principles of accusation, because ministries cannot prosper once a finger-pointing person is allowed to flourish nearby [1]. Accusations are what Scripture calls "the pointing of the finger," and much of the darkness in the body of Christ comes from brother accusing brother, sister accusing sister [1].

- **Recognize the source behind it.** Watch out for anyone who constantly ridicules preachers, accuses men of God of being dishonourable, or questions their motives while they preach — this is what Satan does, for he is an expert at questioning motives and suspecting good people of ulterior motives [3]. Jesus Himself was accused until His life was snuffed out, and He was crucified by principalities working through the Pharisees, Scribes and Jews who accused Him and organized His execution [3][5].

- **Expect it, and don't be shaken by it.** Everyone who takes up the call of God is truly an honourable person, yet in spite of this great effort ministers are vilified and denigrated constantly [5]. You will receive innumerable accusations as you serve the Lord [3].

- **Answer decisively, as David did.** When Michal accused David of uncovering himself before the handmaids, he refused to accept her re-description of his worship — he said it was before the LORD who chose him, and he would play before the LORD [7]. That was the end of Michal, and it would be the end of many accusations if ministers responded that decisively [7].

- **Weigh accusations rightly rather than swallowing every tale.** Loyalty demands continuous analysis in the face of constant accusations, rumours and slanderous stories [6]. Scripture says, "Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses" (1 Timothy 5:19) [6].

- **Don't let fault-finding take root in you either.** The servant with one talent did nothing because he found fault with his master, calling him a hard man; fault-finding is a common characteristic of fruitless and inactive people, and those who criticize pastors will weep and gnash their teeth [2]. Protect yourself from fault-finding and criticizing, for it will be an eternal point of regret [2].

- **Keep encouraging the accused, including yourself.** Most of the people trained in ministry were discouraged and accused by the devil, but constant encouragement to serve God and trust Him silenced the voice of the accuser, and weak, incapable people received salvation, power and strength to do God's work [1]. When the accuser is cast down, salvation, strength, the kingdom of our God and the power of His Christ are released (Revelation 12:10)

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 8 of *Those Who Accuse You*, chapter 5 of *Weeping and Gnashing*, chapter 17 of *One of You is a Devil* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 6:20; Isaiah 58:8-9; Daniel 10:13; Matthew 25:24; 1 Corinthians 2:8; Ephesians 6:12; 1 Timothy 5:19; Revelation 12:10.

items.question: Can a pastor lead a group of people he pulled away from their church into a new one?
items.text:
This is a heavy question, and the books speak to it directly.

The answer they give is no. A pastor who has led people away from their rightful leader cannot truly lead them, because they have learned rebellion from him and will practice it again when the chance comes [1]. He will not be able to silence their murmuring, quench their grumbling, or prevent the conspiracies around him, and he will never have the stability he desires, because he has sown the very seeds of instability he now reaps [1].

The books show this working out in real life. Bishop Dag tells of a 747 pilot he trained as a pastor, a humble and effective church member, who broke away to start an independent ministry near the church he had led; a few years later other pastors followed his example one after another, until the city was dotted with splinter churches and hundreds of confused members who did not know which group to belong to [2]. He also tells of a pastor who left, took about eighty percent of the congregation with him, and then appointed eleven new pastors a few months later — men of no evident training or calling, much like Jeroboam appointing priests from the lowest of the people [3].

The books also warn that such a leader is known by his fruits, not his words: if the fruit is division, disloyalty, and the subtle destruction of someone else's ministry, that tells us who he is [2]. And they note that people who leave send a message that others should not give their money to your ministry, which is why departing leaders so often redirect the finances of loyal followers to themselves [8].

One more thing the books add: those who have suffered this kind of betrayal often react defensively afterward — some refuse to appoint assistants, some refuse cell groups, some give up expansion altogether — and the counsel is simply to make sure your response is not influenced by bitterness [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5, 6 and 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 12:28-31; Daniel 1:1-21.

items.question: Why are Jesus' words so much greater than the words of other great teachers?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
The books give several reasons why Jesus' words stand above every other teacher's.

- **They are the words of the Son of God, not merely a servant's words.** Paul, Peter, James and John were servants of Christ, and though God used their writings to bless the church, their words cannot substitute for the words of the Son of God himself; Jesus' words must be taken more seriously and are the ultimate and final statements of truth [2].

- **They are revelation, not enquiry.** After reading Plato, Socrates or Aristotle, the difference we feel between their words and Christ's is the difference between an enquiry and a revelation [1][4].

- **They answer the questions that throb in the human breast.** Their greatness lies in dealing clearly, definitively and authoritatively with who God is, whether He loves me, what I should do to please Him, how He looks at my sin, how I can be forgiven, where I will go when I die, and how I must treat others — and no other man can answer those as Jesus answered them [1][6].

- **They are anointed and full of love.** Jesus' words were so anointed that they changed the lives of those who heard them, and they contain great kindness — He taught forgiveness not just seven times but seventy times seven, as Matthew 18:21-22 records [4].

- **They are inexhaustible and never obsolete.** Christ's message is inexhaustible, each generation finding it new and exciting, and there is no reason any of His words should ever pass away or become obsolete [1][3][6].

- **They are backed by His own person.** When Jesus uses the personal pronoun "I" — "but I say to you, amen, I say to you" — He stands and backs every word with personal fidelity and intentionality, so His words are of permanent value because of His person; they endure because He endures [1][4].

- **They have outlasted and outshaped all others.** His words have passed into law, doctrines, proverbs and consolations but have never passed away, and no revolution in society compares to that produced by the words of Jesus [1][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 5 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*.

items.question: How do I know if God has hidden a gift in me that others can't see yet?
items.book: Lord I Know You Need Somebody
items.text:
What a tender question, and one the books speak to directly. Here is how you can know and what to do with it.

- **Expect that the gift is concealed by God's design.** God has hidden the potential He placed in you, so people cannot see the treasure yet; every great man of God is like a hidden treasure waiting to be revealed [1]. Your ministry is like a mustard seed sown in a field — the least of seeds, but when it grows it becomes the greatest among herbs, so that the birds of the air lodge in its branches (Matthew 13:31-32) [1].

- **Don't be shaken when those closest to you can't see it.** Even Mary could not see the gift of God in Jesus, so do not be surprised if your own mother cannot see it in you [2]. His own brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:1-5), so do not be amazed or angry when your relatives miss the apostolic or prophetic gift in you — with time they will find out what God placed there [2].

- **Take heart when a parent doesn't recognize it.** Joseph's father rebuked him for his dream, unable to understand how he and the family would one day bow to Joseph, though God had put commanding wisdom in him (Genesis 37:9-10) [3]. Your biological father may not see what God sees, so do not be sad or worried that he does not notice who you are [3].

- **Look for the hidden things God is growing in you.** God wants you to focus on the inner, deep, hidden aspects of your life, because it is the hidden, unseen part that determines the level to which you will go [4]. Ask yourself what hidden aspect is missing or faulty — jealousy, hatred, unforgiveness, bitterness, sin — for though no one can see them, they are the very things that will destroy your life and ministry [4].

- **Give yourself to the hidden disciplines.** Hidden prayer, where you go into your closet and pray to your Father in secret, is one of the hidden things that must be present if you are to do well in God (Matthew 6:6) [4]. Hidden fasting and hidden giving are the same — done secretly before your Father who sees in secret, and He will reward you openly (Matthew 6:17-18; Matthew 6:2-3) [4].

- **Press on, because having some gift makes you a candidate for more.** If you already have some anointing, you become a candidate to receive even more, for whoever has, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance (Matthew 13:12) [6]. If you perceive God has given you a gift, open your heart to receive more, because that is the law of the kingdom [6].

- **Ask God for eyes that see and ears that hear.**

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody*, chapter 12 of *Why Few Are Chosen* and chapter 12 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 37:9-10; Matthew 6:2-3; Matthew 6:6; Matthew 6:17-18; Matthew 13:11-12; Matthew 13:16; Matthew 13:31-32; Matthew 13:44-46; John 7:1-5.

items.question: Why does God allow trials and suffering in the lives of believers?
items.text:
The books give several reasons God allows His people to walk through trials and suffering.

- **Because it pleases Him.** It pleased the Lord to bruise His own Son, and the cross was called a sweet-smelling savour to God, so suffering is not outside His good purpose [2].

- **To follow the example of Jesus.** We are called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example that we should follow His steps (1 Peter 2:21); even Jesus, who had all faith to heal and raise the dead, set an example of suffering [1].

- **To break the power of sin.** He that has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin (1 Peter 4:1); suffering has power to break sin's influence, and where there is no suffering, sin increases [1].

- **To prove you are a good Christian.** Paul laboured and suffered reproach because he trusted in the living God (1 Timothy 4:10), and all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2 Timothy 3:12) [1].

- **Because it goes with your specific calling.** Paul was appointed a preacher and suffered for it (2 Timothy 1:11), and the Lord said of Paul that He would show him how great things he must suffer for His name's sake (Acts 9:15-16) [1].

- **To humble you and test you.** God led Israel forty years in the wilderness to humble them and to prove them, to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2); Paul was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet him, to keep him from exalting himself (2 Corinthians 12:7) [5][8].

- **To reveal what is in your heart.** No one knows what is really in your heart, but God allows circumstances that bring it out [8].

- **Because affliction is part of the call.** By faith Moses chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season (Hebrews 11:24-25); faith makes you able to endure the afflictions God has chosen for you to experience [6][7].

- **To produce endurance and completeness.** Consider it all joy when you encounter various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing (James 1:2-4) [8].

One caution the books give: it matters that you suffer according to the will of God, entrusting your soul to a faithful Creator in doing what is right (1 Peter 4:19); there are two possible reasons for what you are experiencing — you may be suffering according to His will, or you may be suffering the fruits of your own disobedience, so it is important to seek God about why you are

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*, chapter 31 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 41 of *Church Growth*.

items.question: How can I know what my calling from God is?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
Discerning your calling is something God means for you to see and know, not something you have to guess at blindly. Here are the ways the books describe.

- **Watch what works as you serve.** You discover your calling by observing what the Lord does with you and through you — where there is a stronger anointing and more success, and where nothing seems to work [2]. The Bible says you "see" your calling, so you watch it and flow with what God is doing rather than waiting for a voice thundering from Heaven [2].

- **Pay attention to a supernatural desire.** A genuine desire or interest in the work of the ministry is itself a symptom of a divine call within — it may not be sensational, but it is a burden God has put there [8]. Paul spoke of his heart's desire and prayer for Israel to be saved, and that desire was translated into practical ministry time and again [8].

- **Let your calling become more specific as you mature.** You may start with a general sense of calling, but as you mature your ministry becomes more specific, and it grows more dangerous to stray into areas God has not called you to [4]. Paul repeatedly introduced himself as an apostle "by the will of God," and over the years your understanding of how God intends to use you increases [4].

- **Seek the purpose within the call, not just the call.** Your calling is according to God's purpose, and you must find out the purpose for which He called you [3]. God may call you to be an evangelist, for instance, but His purpose in that call may be to set an example in soul winning or to teach others how to do the work of God [3].

- **Be sure you are called, and don't call yourself.** No man can take this honour unto himself, as Hebrews 5:4 says, so ministry must wait until there is a definite call [5]. Once you have been called, you are standing on a solid foundation [5].

- **Take your quiet times, dreams, and visions seriously.** Those who believe they are called take a message from God's Word, their dreams, their visions, and their quiet times more seriously than the average person [6]. The author tells how he took a major step when he read "Give thyself wholly to these things" (1 Timothy 4:15) and believed with all his heart that God was speaking to him [6].

- **Don't depend on outward signs.** When God calls you, you may feel utterly powerless and inadequate, even sensing an absence of miracle and healing power, and you may be tempted to ask for signs to confirm the call [1]. If you depend on the presence of miracles to confirm your calling, you may never enter the ministry — God may have planned for you to see the first miracle after twenty years in ministry, so depend on the voice of the Holy Spirit [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Many Are Called*, chapter 5 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapters 1 and 2 of *Predestination*, chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 10 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry* and chapter 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 6:13; Jonah 1:1-3; Matthew 10:6; Romans 1:1; Romans 8:30; Romans 10:1; 1 Corinthians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 1:26; 2 Corinthians 1:1; Ephesians 1:1 and 6 more.

items.question: How can I be a good shepherd to the people in my church?
items.text:
That's a question every pastor should keep asking, and our books have a great deal to say about it. Here are the ways they lay out.

- **Lead them by going first.** A good shepherd is practically available for his sheep to see and learn from him in every area of life and ministry; anything you want your sheep to do, you must do it yourself first, as Jesus said, "he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him" (John 10:4) [1][2]. If you want your people to pray, lead them into prayer rather than sending them off alone [2].

- **Let them know your voice and know you.** A true sheep learns to recognize his own shepherd's voice and discovers that all shepherds are not the same [1]. Open up your life to the sheep so they can know about you; don't be a mystery figure, but let them see how real you are and how you face the same problems and temptations they do [3].

- **Know your sheep and keep them.** Jesus said a good pastor knows his sheep, and He kept saying of those the Father gave Him, "those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost" (John 17:12) [3]. Work with junior pastors and shepherds so that none of the sheep slip away, because God will hold us accountable for every single sheep that is lost [3].

- **Be a door for them.** A good shepherd provides an entrance for the sheep to move forward — a way into marriage through teaching and counselling, a way into a prosperous life through guidance, and a way into the ministry [1]. Jesus said plainly, "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved" (John 10:9) [1][5].

- **Do the work of an evangelist.** According to Jesus, to be a good shepherd you must leave the ninety-nine and go after the one lost sheep (Luke 15:4-7) [4]. A good shepherd starts by bringing people to Christ and then pastors them, and those saved through your ministry tend to be more stable and faithful to you [5]. Paul told Timothy to "do the work of an evangelist" (2 Timothy 4:5) [7].

- **Give them life, and give your life.** Through a good pastor the sheep experience a better kind of life, since the teachings that bring wisdom and understanding give the sheep a better life [5]. And the shepherd actually lays down his life so the sheep may have a better life; Jesus said, "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep" (John 10:11) [5][6]. The rank of a shepherd is carved out by the sacrifices he makes for his congregation [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Shepherding*, chapter 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 8 of *Church Growth* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

items.question: How can I serve closely in ministry without missing the spiritual blessings?
items.text:
Serving close to a man of God is a great privilege, and the books speak directly to how to keep it from becoming a hollow privilege.

- **Serve to be with him, not just for a task.** The Lord took the twelve on so that they would be with Him, and only afterward sent them out to preach; personal servants pass through a "be with me" phase before a "sending out" phase [1].

- **Choose the good part.** Martha was close to Jesus but busy and troubled, while Mary chose the one needful thing; the good part of personal ministry is not the physical advantage but the spiritual treasure, and the fact that a spiritual leader likes you does not mean you will do well on the Day of Judgement [1].

- **Beware of familiarity.** Jesus' own brethren did not believe in Him, and seeing the human side of God's servant can tempt you to think you are not dealing with the power of God — all personal servants must be careful of becoming another Judas [1].

- **Soak in his words.** The disciples soaked in the words of their master until He left them, because the anointing is in the words; Elisha stayed in constant conversation with Elijah, and you should decide to stay close to the very end until the anointing you desire is flowing through your ministry [4].

- **Draw near and stay near.** Being close is both an art and an act of humility; pride creates a gap and guilt keeps people away when they should be close by, helping in the ministry — you are loved, wanted and needed, so come closer and be as involved as you can [7].

- **Keep growing in the Word yourself.** Meditation is thinking deeply about God's Word, and the lack of it is the cause of a lack of personal conviction; sharing the Word with others grounds you in the truth and grooms you for ministry [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapter 6 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapter 5 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*.

items.question: How can I protect my church from wolves?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and they give you real weapons for it.

- **Be aggressive toward them.** You are told to fight the good fight of faith, as 1 Timothy 6:12 says, and to show every wolf that attacking you and your church will be costly and painful [1]. Teach, explain, and repeat the teaching against disloyalty until every wolf lurking around your life and ministry is exposed and defeated [1].

- **Fight with fire.** Wolves hate fire, and Jesus baptizes with the Holy Ghost and fire, as Luke 3:16 says [1]. Be a pastor on fire — your passion and zeal for the Lord alone will drive wolves away, and churches that have lost their zeal are the ones ravaged by them [1].

- **Climb out of reach.** Wolves cannot climb trees, so go higher in God; the higher you go, the less access wolves can gain to you, and they can only devour those who have not gone higher and deeper with God [1]. John the Revelator was told, "Come up hither" (Revelation 4:1) [1].

- **Expect them and prepare.** Be sober and vigilant, because your adversary the devil walks about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, as 1 Peter 5:8 says [4]. Wolves are real and they will come, so every church must prepare for them, and churches that do not teach loyalty and faithfulness will struggle to survive a wolf attack [4].

- **Identify sympathisers of the "departee" and send them away.** There are always people who sympathise with the one who left, and they will always be a source of instability; it is often wisdom to send away people who cannot be made to believe in you [3]. Abraham sent Ishmael and the sons of the concubines away from Isaac while he was still alive (Genesis 25:5-6), because separation is often the only way to instil stability and harmony after someone has polluted the church with his venom [3].

- **Do not curse randomly.** Be careful of issuing random curses on people who hurt you, since you also sometimes hurt others without knowing it, and Paul said, "Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not" (Romans 12:14) [2]. Some who turn against you do so out of immaturity, and God in His mercy gives them room to grow, as the prodigal son came to his senses (Luke 15:17) [2].

- **Use curses to protect your congregation.** There are times the Holy Spirit directs you to speak a curse; when you lead a congregation and cannot physically protect them, you place spiritual barriers to protect the sheep [2]. Paul, unable to do anything but write, spoke a curse against anyone bringing a new and false doctrine to the congregation (Galatians 1:8

items.question: Why do I need to hear from God for myself instead of just listening to my pastor?
items.text:
You're asking something every minister has to settle, and the books speak to it directly.

You need to hear from God for yourself because hearing Him directly is how you come to know Him — you get to know someone as you talk with him and he talks with you, and some people think they can live on tapes and read-out sermons, but you need to know God for yourself and not only through a second person [1]. The children of Israel were brought to Mount Sinai to hear God's voice for themselves, and they refused, and so failed that test; if you do not hear from God directly you will get disconnected, and even in a good church with a good pastor leading the flock you still need to hear His voice for yourself [1]. This is also a test of self-discipline: you have to build good habits of regularly going to seek His face, and as you fail to go away to seek Him, you end up failing the test of hearing [1].

That said, the books do not set your own hearing against listening to your pastor. One passage teaches that pastors should listen to the messages of their leader in order to learn how to preach, following those who through faith and patience inherit the promises, as Hebrews 6:12 says, and to have resource material to preach from [2]. Another says hearing means listening to the preaching of God's word and the teachings God has for you, and that the art of listening to preaching messages is one of the most important skills you can develop [3]. And another urges you to assemble a large collection of preaching materials, letting the Holy Spirit lead you to what you listen to, and to listen to those you genuinely believe are great [8].

So the two belong together rather than compete: learn from your pastor's preaching, and still seek God's own voice for yourself.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 4 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 1 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 33 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 20:19-21; Psalms 23:1; Matthew 7:22-23; Hebrews 6:12.
