items.question: How do I deal with betrayal in the church?
items.text:
Betrayal in ministry is painful, and it helps to know you are not alone in it — even Jesus was betrayed by one of His own twelve [5].

- **Expect it as part of leadership.** Betrayal is part of ministry and part of life; if Judas is anything to go by, one out of twelve people may be disloyal, and no leader is exempt [5]. Jesus was betrayed, and Paul was betrayed, so you should not be surprised when it comes to you [5].

- **See the danger clearly.** A disloyal associate operating freely is like allowing a devil to do what he wants in the church [1][2]. Jesus Himself called the betrayer a devil, so do not treat disloyalty as something trivial [1][2].

- **Be fierce and resolute.** All forms of disloyalty can end a church and a ministry, so you must not deal with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence [8]. Pastors who take a light-hearted attitude toward disloyalty live to regret it [1][2].

- **Bind it, shut it up, seal it.** The way God dealt with the devil — bound him, shut him up, and set a seal on him (Revelation 20:1-3) — is the pattern for dealing with the "Judases" in your life and ministry [7].

- **Teach preventively.** Regular teaching of the Word is a preventive method that immunizes people against deception, since it is only the deceived who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [6]. This is why leaders hold camps and congresses and meet constantly with their pastors and leaders [6].

- **Lean on loyal lay people.** Zealously committed lay workers inspire more loyalty in the ranks, and loyal lay people will report what is going on in the congregation [3].

- **Consider maturity, and give room to grow.** Some disloyalty is immaturity — Jesus overlooked what His disciples said, knowing they would come to understand, and after they abandoned Him He did not rebuke them but sent them out to preach [4]. One of the best ways to deal with mild disloyalty is to let the person go through the "school of hard knocks" by pioneering a church or serving as a senior minister, where he will mature and come to appreciate a leader's pressures [4].

- **Do not be intimidated, and do not moan.** Get ready for envy, jealousy, and betrayal as you rise, and survive them with determination and great faith [5]. Keep disloyalty to a minimum, survive the rebellion, and do not cry or moan about it — that is leadership [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 2 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 5 of *Church Growth*, chapters 4 and 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 54 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 12 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:7-9; 2 Chronicles 32:25; Psalms 41:9; Mark 14:27-31; John 6:70-71; Revelation 20:1-3.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
It's a good and brave question to ask, and the books speak to it directly.

- **Count the cost first.** Sit down and carefully consider what starting a church will involve, because it will not be easy, and not many people want to identify with a small thing — as Luke 14:28 says, a man intending to build a tower first sits down and counts the cost [1][2].
- **Don't be financially desperate.** Find a job and start the church as a lay person rather than depending on the new church for your survival; when people see you are not ministering for financial gain, they will be more interested in your new church [1][2].
- **Two or three is enough.** You do not need a crowd to begin — as Matthew 18:20 says, where two or three are gathered in His name, He is there in the midst of them [1][2]. One pastor went to Zürich knowing only one person, and today that church has several hundred people [1][2].
- **Don't be in a hurry.** No tree grows from a seed into a large tree overnight, and a hasty spirit will not succeed at starting a church; don't expect much within a year, and don't be surprised if you only have twenty people after two years [8].
- **Pray for and recruit pillars.** Ask God to give you helpers, then go out and recruit pillars, just as Jesus called individuals like Simon, Andrew, James and John to follow Him (Mark 1:16, 17; Mark 1:19, 20), and these later became pillars in the church (Galatians 2:9) [8].
- **Start honourably, without breaking another church.** The art of beginning a church is the art of witnessing, following-up and gathering sheep together, and you do not need to break up someone else's church to begin your own [1][2]. Be careful not to pressurize pillars in another person's church to leave, for you will reap what you sow (Galatians 6:7) [8].
- **Don't be discouraged by small or shifting numbers.** Don't be discouraged by fluctuating attendance or by members who come one week and not the next — that is how sheep behave, so take no notice of them [3][4].
- **You don't need the trappings.** You do not need a complimentary card, a briefcase, a constitution, a logo or a flag in the early stages; what matters is to have members and a regular congregation — just build the church and fill it with people, pray for them, preach the Word, visit the sheep and trust God [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

items.question: What does the Bible say about enjoying the money and blessings God gives you?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
The books have a good deal to say about this, and it's encouraging.

- **God takes pleasure in your prosperity.** When you serve the Lord, He actually enjoys giving you money and directing it to you; He has pleasure in the prosperity of His servant [6]. Serving God is key to your eventual prosperity, and He promises that His servants will spend their days in prosperity [6].

- **Eat your portion and spend on yourself.** It is an evil thing to have riches, wealth and honour and yet have no power to eat of them — that is called vanity and an evil disease (Ecclesiastes 6:1-2) [4]. So spend money on yourself, use some of the wealth you have earned, and invest in your surroundings; if you spend most of your time in your bedroom, make it the nicest bedroom in the world [4]. Failure to eat your portion will make you hate life and hate work [4].

- **Enjoy it with your spouse.** One of the ways to enjoy your work is to live happily with your spouse, for marital harmony is one of the rewards and blessings a person can have [4]. Have dinner together, make tea for each other, have fun, accept each other's friendship, and laugh together for a few moments "under the sun" [4]. Many millionaires live alone and estranged from their wives, their homes filled with empty rooms and unused swimming pools, with no shouts of joy or peals of laughter — and life is more than a pay package [4].

- **Remember that the blessing, not the money, is the real gift.** Money will not be poured out of Heaven; what is poured out from above is called a blessing, and money is one of the smallest and most insignificant blessings you could ever have [3]. The blessing of the Lord is what makes rich and adds no sorrow (Proverbs 10:22) [1].

- **Let your heart stay right, and keep honouring God.** When you have the right heart, wealth and riches cannot destroy you; it is the love of money, not money itself, that corrupts (1 Timothy 6:10) [2]. Abraham was very rich, yet he refused a large gift from the King of Sodom so that no one could say they had made him rich — he knew his prosperity came from one source (Genesis 14:22, 23) [2]. And when the blessings come, remember to pay your tithes and honour God first, for people forget the Lord in the day of their blessing [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 3 of *Name It Claim It Take It*, chapters 15 and 19 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*, chapter 9 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 6 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 14:22-23; Job 36:11-12; Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 23:5; Ecclesiastes 6:1-2; Ecclesiastes 9:9; Malachi 3:11; Matthew 4:8; 2 Corinthians 9:10; 1 Timothy 6:10.

items.question: How important is it to actually obey what Jesus says?
items.text:
Obedience is not a side issue in the life of faith — it is the very shape faith takes.

- **Believing and obeying are the same thing.** All through the Bible, believing is equated with obeying; to believe in the gospel is to pledge yourself to obey the commandments of God, and obeying the gospel is all that God expects from us [4].
- **Obedience is the sign of your love, and it draws His presence.** Jesus promised that He would manifest Himself to those who keep His commandments, and that He and the Father would come and make their abode with them; there is no manifestation toward those who do not obey [2].
- **It must come from the heart.** Teaching, preaching, giving, counselling, prayer, fasting — none of it benefits you if it is not done from the heart [1].
- **Don't weigh which commands are worth obeying.** Everyone silently assesses an instruction — "this is trivial, this is serious, this can wait" — and most of the time that assessment is wrong; that is why it is important to simply obey every single commandment [1].
- **Obedience is how you say thank you.** Paul's response to the mercy he received was to say thank you to Christ, and he did it by not being disobedient to the heavenly vision and by continuing faithfully in his call to the end, as Acts 26:19 and 26:22 record [7].
- **Say yes when He calls.** Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out, not knowing where he was going (Hebrews 11:8); saying yes is an important spiritual step of faith, and every calling flourishes on your faith [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 8 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*, chapters 2 and 66 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 10:12-13; Matthew 22:36-40; Mark 5:22-24; John 8:31; John 14:21-25; Acts 26:19; Acts 26:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9; Hebrews 11:8; 1 Peter 4:17.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy — a new life in Christ is the beginning of a great change, and it's good to want to start well.

- **Understand what has happened to you.** If you are born again, you have had a spiritual heart transplant, and you need to sit down and have it explained to you, the way doctors explain a surgery and its implications afterward [7]. Wisdom is the principal thing, and you gain understanding when you know principles [7].

- **Be taught the elementary principles of the faith.** Anyone who comes to Christ will have to be taught the elementary principles of the oracles of God, and the way you are taught those fundamentals permanently determines your spiritual make-up [2]. That is why your first teacher — the person who taught you the fundamentals of Christianity — is someone never to be forgotten [2].

- **Remember the one who led you to Christ.** Your greatest treasure is your salvation, so the person who helped you know the Lord is the most special person in your life, and you must not forget them [2]. It is presumptuous to assume salvation was your right; it comes through the toil and effort of dedicated Christians, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4:15, "I have begotten you through the gospel" [2].

- **Ask the questions that lead to salvation.** Questions like "What will happen to me when I die?", "Is Heaven real? Is hell real?", "Will I go to Heaven or hell?", and "Why did Jesus have to die on a cross?" are good questions to ask yourself, because they set your mind working on eternity [8].

- **Come to Him while you are young.** Everybody must come to Jesus Christ when they are young, and you must remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come [8]. It is often difficult to be saved after a certain age, because pride fills a man and makes him unyielding and unbelieving as he grows older [1].

- **Make haste.** Zacchaeus was told, "Make haste, and come down," and he made haste and received Him joyfully (Luke 19:5-6) [1]. Be faster at obeying God, faster at learning your songs, faster at waiting on God — perhaps your whole life will change if you introduce some speed into what you do [1].

- **Get active in ministry right away.** From the day he gave his life to Christ, one shepherd became very active in ministry — soul winning, following up converts, singing and playing instruments for the Lord — and he stayed fully involved while never giving up his schooling, completing his exams with distinction and later entering medical school [3][4][6]. The point he makes is that ministry is possible alongside other pursuits [3][4][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Determinants*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Forget*, chapter 4 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 6 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapter 3 of *Church Growth*, chapter 1 of *Seven Great Principles* and chapter 36 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 27:1-4; Genesis 27:19-20; Matthew 21:34-36; Luke 19:5-6; 1 Corinthians 4:15; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: How can I recognize when someone has gone from just being disloyal into open rebellion against God's servants?
items.text:
Here are the signs the books give for recognizing when disloyalty has moved into open rebellion.

- **They openly attack someone they once honoured.** Open rebellion is where a person openly attacks an authority figure he should rather honour, and it is the last stage in the pattern of behaviour called disloyalty [1]. They may openly attack someone they have previously hailed and honoured, or go out into the public and insult and accuse someone they have loved before [1].

- **Their behaviour turns bizarre and inappropriate.** Most people in the open rebellious stage exhibit bizarre and inappropriate behaviour, as though they have schizophrenia, with disorganized thoughts, speech and behaviour [1]. They may dishonour dignitaries and speak words that are inappropriate and bizarre [1].

- **They spread lies to degrade God's servants.** Openly rebellious people spread preposterous lies and wicked stories with the aim of demeaning, debasing and degrading God's servants, doing the exact opposite of good Christians who seek to honour them [1].

- **They defy and disobey God's servants.** Rebellion can be against the Lord and His servants, and many times when you are defying God's servants you are defying God Himself [2]. Disobeying God is seen as rebellion, and disobeying God's servant is also rebellion [2].

- **They appoint alternative leadership.** In their rebellion they appoint a captain, as Nehemiah 9:17 describes [2]. People who defy and insult their pastors are then forced to go to another ministry to submit to another man of God who does not even know them, and junior pastors have left a church in rebellion to seek appointments from other apostles elsewhere [2].

- **They turn into something grotesque.** Rebels you used to know as noble and upright servants of God turn into miserable monsters — grotesque, terrifying and abnormal [5]. Korah, an honourable elder of Israel, turned into a hidden reef, doubly dead, a cloud without water, a tree without fruit and a wandering star [5].

- **They repeat the pattern without provocation.** When disloyalty is part of a person's character, he often repeats this treacherous behaviour without provocation, as Jeroboam did — rebelling against King Solomon, then against Rehoboam, then against God [4]. This is what happens with people who move from church to church; they always find something wrong with the leadership [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Those who are mad*, chapters 6 and 8 of *Those Who Rebel* and chapter 2 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:1-3; Deuteronomy 31:27-30; Joshua 22:19; 1 Kings 11:26; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 139:21; Jude 11-13.

items.question: What is the difference between the true church and the false church?
items.text:
The books speak to this quite directly, and they draw the line in a few places.

The clearest mark is the message itself. The true church, the true bride of Jesus, is always inviting people to come to God and to Jesus — its constant word is "Come!" [1]. The false church says something entirely different: stay here, settle down, celebrate, prosper, secure and enrich yourself, make yourself happy [1]. One is calling people out of the dark ocean into the love of God; the other is telling them to relax and enjoy pleasant times with pleasant people [1].

A second mark is the fruit. Jesus said we would know them by their fruits (Matthew 7:20), and the books apply that to churches as well as to individuals: where people are genuinely being brought to the Lord and discipled, that fruit shows the thing is real, and where there is no such fruit, something is missing [4]. Real Christianity, they insist, is not just showing up on Sundays — it happens outside the church after Sundays, in prayer, worship, Bible reading and labouring for the Lord [4].

A third mark is the fear of God rather than the fear of people. The one thing that separates true ministry from false ministry is the singular ability to fear God rather than men [3]. A shepherd who fears the people — the rich, the poor, the associates, the politicians, even his own wife — has his sermons and decisions swayed, and loses his authority and blessing [3]. Jesus is the example here: He did not fear the Pharisees, His associates, or the rich, and He told the rich man to sell all and follow Him [3].

There is also the matter of doctrine and history. Many large and popular ministries preach doctrines that sound like the Gospel but are not the Gospel God sent us to preach, and the money-loving crowds lap it up [2]. Before you join a new church or ministry, the books urge you to study the doctrine, lifestyle, purpose and faith of the people concerned, and to delve into the historical background of that ministry — because many follow false religions without ever studying the history of that group [5]. Paul pointed Timothy to his own doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience, persecutions and afflictions (2 Timothy 3:10-11) precisely so Timothy could be sure of what he was following [5].

And there is the question of the light you follow. Jesus is the True Light (John 1:9), and just as a lighthouse directs a ship away from the rocks, following the wrong light will run your ship aground [8]. John the Baptist was not the light but came to bear witness to the light (John 1:6-8), and every preacher stands in that same place [8]. Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:24; Jeremiah 29:31; Matthew 7:20; John 1:4-9; John 5:41; John 8:12; 2 Corinthians 13:5; 2 Timothy 3:10-11.

items.question: Why is it so important for Christians to be part of a church assembly?
items.text:
Being part of the assembly matters more than most of us realize, and our books give many reasons why.

- **The assembly is where you are protected from isolation.** Wild animals survive by staying together, and a lion can only bring down a buffalo as big as itself by isolating it from the herd; in the same way, Satan is against the assembly because it keeps you from being isolated, and once you are in church you are protected by the presence of the others [2].

- **The assembly keeps you from drifting into a mocking, disloyal spirit.** People turn into mockers by separating themselves, and Scripture says of such people in Jude 1:18-19 that they separate themselves, not having the Spirit; so you should be concerned when people stop coming to meetings, because once separated from the assembly a person begins to think differently [1].

- **The assembly is where your needs are met.** The early believers had great grace upon them all and none among them lacked, because those who owned lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds (Acts 4:33-34); the church is a place where needs are met, and God supplies material, emotional, marital and family needs directly or indirectly through the assembly [1][4].

- **The assembly is where revelation and knowledge are imparted.** Paul taught that when we come together each one has a psalm, a doctrine, a tongue, a revelation or an interpretation, and all of it is to be done for edification (1 Corinthians 14:26); the assembly is a place where you are built up in knowledge, understanding, morals and faith [1][5].

- **The assembly brings healing.** When Jesus was teaching and Pharisees and teachers of the law had gathered from every town, the power of the Lord was present to heal them (Luke 5:17); healing is a mysterious ministry that takes place when we assemble, and the anointing for healing was present at the point when they were gathered [2][4].

- **The assembly brings the presence of God and drives out evil spirits.** Jesus said that where two or three are gathered in His name, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20), and in the synagogue a man with an unclean spirit cried out and was dealt with (Mark 1:2) [4].

- **The assembly is where praise, salvation and the filling of the Holy Spirit happen.** The believers continued daily with one accord in the temple, praising God, and the Lord added to the church daily those being saved (Acts 2:46-47); and when they had prayed together the place was shaken and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost and spoke the word of God with boldness (Acts 4:31) [4][8].

- **The assembly is where you grow and keep your fire burning.** A coal separated from the coal pot and the other burning charcoal dies out, and like that coal

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapters 18 and 19 of *Church Growth*.

items.question: Why should I be a soul winner?
items.text:
The books give many reasons, and they all come back to the same heartbeat. Here are the ones they press most:

- **Because it is the Lord's own command.** Soul winning is the great commission, the great mandate given to us by Jesus Christ, who said, "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations" [2].
- **Because it is the reason Jesus came.** He said the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost, so to be Christ-like is to be a soul winner [5].
- **Because people are perishing without Him.** People waste their lives away without Jesus, and there is salvation in no other name but Jesus Christ [1][4].
- **Because today is the day of salvation.** No one can guarantee tomorrow; everyone must have the opportunity for salvation today, and we cannot escape if we neglect so great salvation [1].
- **Because it gives you joy and purpose.** Soul winning releases the joy of the Lord and energizes Christians, and it shows you the reason for your own salvation [3].
- **Because it protects and promotes you.** Soul winning generates divine support and protection, and it earns you the right to kingdom promotion [3][7].
- **Because it prevents division.** When church members are engaged in fruitful soul winning, they have no time for the petty quarrels that bring splits [3].
- **Because there is a harvest waiting.** The fields are ripe now unto the harvest, and one day we will rejoice over the seeds we have sown [1][6].

If you want the shortest answer the books give: we do it because we love Him, and because the world He died for is still lost.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Tell Them*.

items.question: Why does God allow my enemies to stay instead of removing them?
items.book: WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous
items.text:
God's Word gives several reasons why He lets enemies remain rather than removing them at once.

- **To teach you how to fight.** God allowed undefeated nations to stay around Israel so the generations who had not known war could be taught war — He wants His people to grow up and learn how to fight and survive, which is why your enemies are not simply struck down when they show up [1].

- **To test your obedience.** Those nations were left "to test Israel by them, to find out if they would obey the commandments of the Lord" (Judges 3:1-4) — the test is whether you will keep walking in His ways [1].

- **To harden them for judgment.** God made Israel's enemies stubborn enough to keep fighting so He could claim them for destruction without mercy, as Joshua 11:20 says — the fight is not over because God wants them destroyed in the battle, and He is counting the months and years they have troubled you as the basis for acting [4].

- **To promote you.** Some of the greatest promotions come through enemies; God used even Judas more than the faithful disciples to bring about the cross, and there are things you will not accomplish without having enemies [5].

- **To work good in you.** God uses the afflictions of enemies to bring out good things in you — "It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes" (Psalm 119:71) — and when God wants to promote you, He sometimes sends an enemy [6].

- **To be an audience for your victory.** Your enemies will be there to see how God remembered you and helped you, as Psalm 23:5 says of the table prepared in the presence of your enemies [6].

- **To give you the blessing of overcoming.** Like Dan, described as small like an adder yet able to bring down a mighty horse (Genesis 49:17), you can step into the blessing of overcoming bigger, stronger, more powerful enemies [7].

So do not be discouraged. The prolonging of the conflict is not because you are too weak — you are stronger than your enemy, but God does not want it to end just yet. Keep watching; He will right all the wrongs in your life [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous*, chapters 7 and 15 of *TS2. Hope Secrets* and chapter 31 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 49:17; Joshua 11:20; Judges 2:21-3:4; Psalms 23:5; Psalms 119:71; John 12:24.

items.question: What does 'The Art of Shepherding' teach about visiting members?
items.text:
Our books speak to this, and here is what they teach about visiting the sheep.

- **Visit the sheep as part of your regular shepherding work.** Function as a shepherd by praying for the sheep, visiting the sheep, counselling them and interacting with them [5].
- **Be present when trouble strikes.** A shepherd must be there when the trouble is at its peak — found standing by the grave, in the hospital, at the operating theatre, by the bedside, or wherever the trouble has struck [6].
- **Let your visits flow from love, not from what you can get.** Bad shepherds visit the sheep to get money from them when they are rich, but good shepherds are there in times of trouble [6].
- **Notice when your sheep are in danger.** A good shepherd notices when his sheep are in distress, and even little things are picked up by him, whereas a hireling does not even see when the sheep are dying [6].
- **Keep watch over the very lives of the sheep.** It is the duty of the shepherd to watch out for the lives of the sheep, and it is only a good shepherd whose vigilance will save their lives [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 10, 27 and 32 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 16:23; 1 Samuel 17:20; 1 Samuel 17:34-35; 1 Samuel 17:38-40; John 10:12.

items.question: How can someone turn to God in a moment of complete desperation?
items.text:
When everything has fallen apart, God is not far off — He is near to the brokenhearted, and He is not condemning you for crying out what you feel.

- **Turn toward Him in your trouble, not away from it.** When things go from bad to worse, that is meant to turn you toward God; your problems are supposed to bring you to Him, as the prodigal "came to himself" and turned home (Luke 15:17) [2]. Even from the belly of the fish, Jonah cried out to the Lord in his affliction and said, "yet I will look again toward thy holy temple" (Jonah 2:1-4) [2].

- **Repent — turn around and go the opposite direction.** Repentance means to change your mind and humble yourself, to arise and go to the Father and say, "I have sinned" (Luke 15:18) [2]. God commands all men everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30), and when you turn from your wicked ways, He will forgive your sins [8].

- **Know that God is near and does not condemn you.** God comforts the depressed (2 Corinthians 7:6), and He is near to them that are of a broken heart, saving such as be of a contrite spirit (Psalm 34:18) [1]. He does not condemn the people in the Bible who were depressed for speaking out their feelings in their times of depression [1].

- **Don't push away the people who bring you joy and hope.** Everybody needs joy-givers and hope-givers, and Jesus is anointed for the brokenhearted and the depressed — He understands every weakness, hurt, and traumatic experience of your life [1].

- **Pray, even if it is short and desperate.** In a crisis there is no time to retreat, so pray a short and powerful prayer and believe that God has heard you, then act boldly as Jesus did at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:41-42) [6]. And when you can, spend long hours with Him too, as Jesus went out to a mountain and continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12) [6].

- **Let your time with God draw you close to Him.** Anyone you spend time talking to becomes close to you, so a Christian who spends time talking to God becomes close to Him, and when you pray, God gives you strength to overcome temptation [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Those who are mad*, chapters 5 and 43 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 5 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 6 of *100% Answered Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 34:18; Psalms 118:9; Proverbs 7:10; Isaiah 31:1; Jonah 2:1-4; Matthew 27:3; Matthew 27:5; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12; Luke 15:17-18 and 4 more.

- **Pray, even if it is short and desperate.** In a crisis there is no time to retreat, so pray a short and powerful prayer and believe that God has heard you, then act boldly as Jesus did at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:41-42).
And when you can, spend long hours with Him too, as Jesus went out to a mountain and continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12).

- **Let your time with God draw you close to Him.** Anyone you spend time talking to becomes close to you, so a Christian who spends time talking to God becomes close to Him, and when you pray, God gives you strength to overcome temptation.

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
Building a strong marriage is something you and your wife do together, on purpose — it doesn't just happen on its own [2]. Here are the ways the books lay out.

- **Make Christ the foundation and head of your home.** When God is the focus of both of you, your closeness to Him draws you closer to each other, and that is what produces a happy home; when only one of you is focused on God, or when you each follow your own dreams without Him, the home grows stale or drifts apart [2]. Jesus' picture of the man who dug deep and laid his foundation on rock, so the flood could not shake his house, is the picture of a home built on hearing and doing His sayings (Luke 6:47-48) [2].

- **Apply biblical principles and build your marriage around the church.** The Word of God is your manual for marriage, and the man who delights in the law of the Lord and meditates on it day and night is like a tree planted by rivers of water that bears fruit in season (Psalm 1:1-6); it is through wisdom that a house is built and by understanding that it is established (Proverbs 24:3) [2].

- **Develop family worship.** Hold regular devotions together, or at least each of you regularly and together once in a while, especially with the children; attend church services and be involved in church activities, sitting together in church; and train your children to know the importance of Sundays [2].

- **Think as a Christian spouse, not as two individuals.** Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves (Philippians 2:3) — reconcile the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, be willing to give up certain interests and preferences for its sake, and don't always insist on your own way but be ready to compromise [2][5].

- **Speak to each other, and speak life.** Speaking the truth in love makes you grow up in Christ (Ephesians 4:15), and it makes you grow closer to each other; speaking brings relief and healing, like a man full of matter who says "I will speak, that I may be refreshed" (Job 32:17-20); and since death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21), speak good things about your spouse, confess positive things about your marriage, and express your love verbally [4]. A clear sign of unhappiness is a couple who are silent at home but chat freely the moment a visitor arrives [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7, 9 and 60 of *Model Marriage*.

items.question: How can I tell if someone in my church is a false friend or a pretender?
items.text:
I'm glad you're asking this — it's a question every shepherd eventually has to face, and our books speak to it plainly.

- **Watch for people who are too quiet.** A person who says little in your presence but talks a great deal when away from you is showing you two different pictures — one near, one far — and that is a mark of a pretender [2][3]. Quiet people store up their thoughts within them, so you should develop a proper respect for what their silence may be hiding [2].

- **Watch for two temperaments.** Notice someone who is jovial and chatty with others but quiet and pensive around you; ask whether that is really two temperaments, or a person pretending to be something else in your presence [2].

- **Watch for a presentation that is too perfect.** A picture of righteousness, orderliness and holiness can be a façade for hidden things and dark secrets [2]. The Pharisees are the clearest example — white and beautiful on the outside, but full of hypocrisy and iniquity within, as Matthew 23:27-28 says [5].

- **Watch for feigned forgiveness.** Be careful with someone you would expect to be angry because he was wronged, yet who seems to have ignored the offence and become even more gracious than before; you must be sure that forgiveness is genuine [5].

- **Watch for absence in hard times.** It is in times of pressure that you see a person's true character — notice those who disappear when the church is going through difficulty [7]. Bishop Dag tells of a crisis in his church when he asked some pastoral trainees to accompany him to see government officials, wanting to show that the church had support from the community; they never turned up, and he felt deeply let down in a time of war [7].

- **Watch for a short history with you.** Someone who has served you only a short time has the potential to be a pretender, so a leader must surround himself with loyal people whose counsel he can trust [8]. Hushai the Archite is the classic impostor — he pretended to give good advice to the king, and because Absalom did not see through the pretence, it led to his downfall, as 2 Samuel 17:14 shows [8].

- **Judge by actions, not presentation.** Like a doctor who trusts symptoms to diagnose what is hidden inside a body, believe the signs you observe and look beyond the perfect picture being presented to you [2][3]. The Bible teaches us to prove all things and hold fast to that which is good, as 1 Thessalonians 5:20 says [3].

One caution from our books: since you cannot see into the hearts of men, be careful not to comment, and rely on your own heart and whether you are drawn to a person or not [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 2 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar*, chapter 8 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 18 of *The Art of Shepherding* and chapter 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 27:21-24; Genesis 38:13-19; Joshua 9:3-16; 2 Samuel 17:14; Jeremiah 29:31; Matthew 23:27-28; Luke 22:3-6; Luke 22:45-48; John 7:5; Acts 6:3 and 1 more.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
A Christian who wants to live simply and stop wasting money can hold to a few plain things our books teach.

- **Remember you will give an account.** God will one day ask you to account for what He put in your hands, and if you cannot account for it you will lose your position [1]. The steward in Luke 16:1-2 was called to give an account of his stewardship, and so will you [1].

- **Cut out waste deliberately.** Most poor nations waste half their resources, and that is why they stay poor; the same is true of a person who never learns to prevent wastage [6]. When you can stop the things that waste away your money, you will become rich [1].

- **Refuse an expensive lifestyle.** Cut your coat according to your size, and avoid grandiose and expensive things just because others are doing them [6]. Do not be deceived into following bad examples, because it will not end well [6].

- **Dislike loans and gifts.** Every admirer of gifts and loans is likely to fail in leadership, and many people do not pay back their loans [6].

- **Do things with your own hands.** Learn to do things yourself rather than sitting aloof as though you were an executive when you are not at that level [6].

- **Choose your company carefully.** The prodigal son did not waste his money alone; there were harlots to help him do so, and bad company will always be there to help you do bad things [3]. As 1 Corinthians 15:33 says, evil company corrupts good habits, so a born-again Christian should make friends with Christians [3].

- **Do not chase quick money.** Wise businessmen are wary of get-rich-quick schemes, and the Kingdom of Heaven is like a mustard seed that needs time to grow, so there are no short cuts [4].

- **Kill wrong desires while they are small.** If you have any strange lusts in you, deal with them now, or they will grow up and take over your life [5]. As Mark 4:19 says, the lusts of other things entering in choke the word and it becomes unfruitful [5].

- **Stay close to the house of the Lord.** When you come constantly to the house of the Lord you will see His beauty, and this will prevent you from living a wasteful life of sin [3].

- **Give yourself to something for God.** It is sad to see Christians waste their lives away doing nothing for the Lord, when we are all called to be fruitful [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapters 3 and 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 2 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent* and chapter 2 of *Many Are Called*.

items.question: What does the fear of man do to a person spiritually?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
The fear of man is not merely an emotion to manage — our books treat it as a spiritual force that does real damage. Here is what they say it does.

- **It opens you to demonic influence.** Fear is not just a thought or a mood; it is a demon, and the presence of any kind of fear is a sign of demonic activity in your life [2][4]. When Adam and Eve rebelled, they opened themselves to demons of fear, and fear became the commonest evil spirit that afflicts man [1].

- **It takes away your sound mind.** God has given us a spirit of love, power and a sound mind to replace the spirit of fear, so those with the spirit of fear do not have sound minds — fear makes people behave abnormally and can drive them along a queer road no one understands [2].

- **It destroys your love.** Someone who fears you does not love you, and fear manifests itself in suspicion and uncertainty; perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment, and he who fears is not made perfect in love (1 John 4:18) [6]. A fearful partner turns the home into a courtroom where the accused must constantly defend every move [6].

- **It makes you suspicious, accusative and disloyal.** Fearful men are suspicious men, accusative men, dangerous men, insecure and unable to take correction well, and they can become disloyal [3]. This is why Gideon removed all the fearful men from his army — they would have given him trouble later (Judges 7:3-4) [3].

- **It leads you into other evils.** Fear is a precursor to many evils: accusation, fault-finding, laziness, wickedness and poor performance [3]. People led by the fear of poverty do illegal things for money, and many marry out of the fear of never marrying, so that the marriage has an evil spirit in its foundation [4].

- **It makes you hide and withdraw.** Adam said he was afraid and hid himself (Genesis 3:9-10); the compulsion to hide must be replaced with the compulsion to be open, because being open shows that Satan has not corrupted something in your life [4].

- **It can bring on you the very thing you dread.** Job confessed that the thing he greatly feared had come upon him (Job 3:25) — fear often attacks the most blessed people, who have everything but happiness because they are scared of losing it [6].

The good news in our books is that fear can be overcome: go in the opposite direction to where fear is leading you, and do the opposite of your fears [6]. David prayed and the Lord delivered him from all his fears (Psalm 34:4) [4], and prayer is the spiritual antidote to fear — in everything, through prayer and supplication, we can make our requests known to God [

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 4 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 26 of *Now We Are At War* and chapter 9 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:9-10; Judges 7:3-4; Job 3:25; Psalms 34:4; 2 Timothy 1:7; 1 John 4:18.

items.question: Can I still serve God while I'm busy with my studies or other responsibilities?
items.book: How you can become a strong Christian
items.text:
Yes — the books speak to this directly, and the answer is a clear no, your studies or responsibilities do not have to keep you from serving God.

- **Your work or studies are a "care," not a curse.** Being a student is just another care of this world, and it must not be allowed to choke God's Word and work; the author, as a medical student, successfully combined his schoolwork with his pastoral work for years [2][7]. He even asked himself whether being a medical student meant he could not serve God anymore, and the answer was no [2][7].

- **Don't let the cares dominate you.** Paying bills, looking after family, and passing exams are legitimate, and there is nothing wrong with them — but God warns against becoming overburdened, because when these cares dominate your life they kill your fruitfulness [2]. The demands of your job, the pressures of academic work, or raising little children can make you unfaithful if you let them [3].

- **You can be fruitful in spite of them.** A new baby or a pregnancy should not stop you from bearing fruit — other Christians have made it, and so can you [2][7]. The author tells of carrying his seven-day-old son through cold weather, buses, and streets to keep a preaching appointment in Geneva; the baby did not die, and he says neither will yours if you continue to do the work of the Lord [2][7].

- **Don't be lazy about it.** The lazy Christian is full of amazing excuses, like the man in Proverbs 22:13 who says there is a lion in the street so he cannot leave his bed [2]. Anyone who wants to be successful must be prepared to work hard [2].

- **Let your love for God guide you.** When you have first love for God, you will not need long discussions about His will — your love will make you go out and do "mad things" for Jesus, bringing others to God and leading them to Christ [1]. The author says that as a student he did not need a vision, a dream, or a voice to know what to do; his love for God told him to start a fellowship, to preach in the halls of residence, to fast, and to pray for hours [1].

- **Watch the pull toward double-mindedness.** If you are trying to serve both a secular path and the ministry, that double-mindedness can leave you either loving the ministry and hating your work or the reverse, and it introduces a long period of confusion — "How long will you waver between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21) [4]. You cannot serve two masters (Luke 16:13) [4].

One more thing worth holding onto: it is not safe to assume there is more time, since we do not know the day or the hour, so the key is preparation and readiness [8

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*, chapter 10 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry* and chapter 6 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 16:15-17; 1 Kings 18:21; Proverbs 22:13; Proverbs 30:18-19; Mark 4:19; Luke 16:13; James 4:8.

items.question: How can a pastor grow an empty church?
items.text:
I'm glad you asked this — it's a burden many pastors carry, and our books have a good deal to say about it.

- **Go out and compel people to come in.** Church growth comes through a certain kind of evangelism — anagkazo — where you go out to the highways, gutters and bushes and drive people to God, rather than sitting in church and waiting for them to come [1]. Our little church games and programmes will not convince people in today's world; you must go out and compel them [1].

- **Let a burning vision drive you.** A shallow vision will not grow a church; the vision must eat you up and burn within your soul, becoming the invisible engine that carries you on the long, difficult road to growth [6]. That burning vision is what makes you humble enough to pray hard and to seek the wisdom and strategies you need [6].

- **Recognize the spiritual opposition.** The gates of hell are postured against the church, and demons attack the advancing church, so you must fight to achieve growth [2]. Sometimes the cause of barrenness is a real spiritual "salt" that needs God's healing hand — one pastor saw in a vision a demon sitting above his congregation, dealt with it, and the church then grew in leaps and bounds [3].

- **Deal with dryness in worship and prayer.** A church that is dry of the Spirit — a wilderness devoid of worship, prayer and the lifting up of hands — is barren, and introducing new worship songs or changing your worship leader can fight that barrenness [3].

- **Invest in the few who will bring the increase.** By the 80-20 principle, eighty percent of your growth comes from twenty percent of the people, so spend more time with the leaders, teachers and pastors who make up that twenty percent rather than with the rich and influential [5].

- **Put your lay people to work.** Lay people can do far more than give money — doctors, teachers, bankers, lawyers and others can win souls and even pastor churches, and helping them do so helps your church grow [8].

- **Be honest about your numbers.** Don't say "the whole outside was full" or "thousands were here" when only a few hundred came; have real numbers [5].

One more thing worth naming: a pastor who is a "salted land" cannot bring forth, and there are those who hold back — who have the finances and anointing to plant churches but give their strength to other things — and that restraint is itself a cause of barrenness [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3 and 27 of *Church Growth*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 11 of *Church Planting* and chapter 13 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 63:1; Proverbs 29:18; Proverbs 30:16; Isaiah 41:18; Jeremiah 17:6; Jeremiah 30:19; Acts 16:5.

judged.sentence: - **Go out and compel people to come in.** Church growth comes through a certain kind of evangelism — anagkazo — where you go out to the highways, gutters and bushes and drive people to God, rather than sitting in church and waiting for them to come.
Our little church games and programmes will not convince people in today's world; you must go out and compel them.

- **Let a burning vision drive you.** A shallow vision will not grow a church; the vision must eat you up and burn within your soul, becoming the invisible engine that carries you on the long, difficult road to growth.
That burning vision is what makes you humble enough to pray hard and to seek the wisdom and strategies you need.
- **Recognize the spiritual opposition.** The gates of hell are postured against the church, and demons attack the advancing church, so you must fight to achieve growth.

Sometimes the cause of barrenness is a real spiritual "salt" that needs God's healing hand — one pastor saw in a vision a demon sitting above his congregation, dealt with it, and the church then grew in leaps and bounds.

- **Deal with dryness in worship and prayer.** A church that is dry of the Spirit — a wilderness devoid of worship, prayer and the lifting up of hands — is barren, and introducing new worship songs or changing your worship leader can fight that barrenness.

- **Invest in the few who will bring the increase.** By the 80-20 principle, eighty percent of your growth comes from twenty percent of the people, so spend more time with the leaders, teachers and pastors who make up that twenty percent rather than with the rich and influential.

- **Put your lay people to work.** Lay people can do far more than give money — doctors, teachers, bankers, lawyers and others can win souls and even pastor churches, and helping them do so helps your church grow.
- **Be honest about your numbers.** Don't say "the whole outside was full" or "thousands were here" when only a few hundred came; have real numbers.

One more thing worth naming: a pastor who is a "salted land" cannot bring forth, and there are those who hold back — who have the finances and anointing to plant churches but give their strength to other things — and that restraint is itself a cause of barrenness.

items.question: How can I learn to work with different kinds of people to accomplish what God has called me to do?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
Learning to work with all kinds of people is a skill you develop, and it grows your calling. Here are the ways our books point to:

- **See it as the measure of your calling.** Nehemiah worked with forty-one different kinds of people, and the number of different groups you can work with reveals the magnitude of your calling [1]. Jesus died for all people, all kindred, all nations, all tribes and all tongues, so assess yourself by how many different groups you can work with [1].

- **Start with the people already around you.** Develop the art of working with the church members you preach to every Sunday, combining being soft and understanding with being hard and demanding [2]. Also learn to work with lay people you do not pay, because many good people want to volunteer, and they feel happy when given a little task [2].

- **Learn to work with those unlike you.** Work with unbelievers whose expertise you need, since some people from other religions are better suited for certain jobs [2]. Work with people older than you, with carefulness and respect [2]. And relate with all kinds of people, including those who are not your "type," because there are more people different from you than like you [4].

- **Handle the hard combinations.** Work with people who do not like each other but who need to work together; Paul had this problem with Euodias and Syntyche and urged them to be of the same mind in the Lord (Philippians 4:2) [2]. Work with technical people without letting their technicalities destroy the mission, by knowing a little about everything and asking many questions [2].

- **Become another of the same kind.** Becoming an *allos* makes you dependent and sheep-like rather than independent and solitary, gives you access to methods and formulae that have worked for your kind, makes you a member of a particular group, and is how you find your way in the ministry [3].

- **Lean on others to overcome your limits.** Your limitations in ministry are overcome by recognizing the contribution of others, humbling yourself to learn from pastors with bigger and smaller churches, because every joint supplies something until you become what God has called you to be (Ephesians 4:16) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 22 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 14 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*, chapter 100 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 6 of *Many Are Called*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 10:28; 1 Corinthians 9:22-23; Ephesians 4:16; Philippians 4:2.

items.question: Can my friends keep me from staying close to God?
items.text:
Yes, they can — and Scripture takes that seriously. The psalm says plainly, "They that are far from thee shall perish," and then adds, "it is good for me to draw near to God" [3]. That is why closeness is described as a test of survival, not a small matter [3].

But notice where the real danger lies. Distance from God is not measured in miles. Someone can sit right next to a man of God and still be spiritually far off, while someone thousands of miles away draws nearer than the person in the same room [1]. Jesus said a prophet is not honored in his own country and house (Matthew 13:57), and He told one man, "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God" (Mark 12:34) — both showing that nearness is a matter of the spirit, not of physical proximity [1]. So a friend's influence over you is not decided by how often you are together, but by whether you open yourself up to what they carry. You are spiritually far from evil things unless you give place to the devil [1].

The safeguard is not mainly managing your friends; it is drawing near to God yourself. James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [7]. That nearness grows through a regular daily quiet time — a personal, one-to-one relationship with the Lord, which public meetings and church attendance by themselves cannot produce [7]. It is up to you to draw near to Him daily, not to wait for Him to come to you [7].

And be careful not to make a rule out of this. God is not a book, and the Bible is not God; it takes a personal, intimate relationship with Him to stay close [6]. Jesus warned, "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God" (Matthew 22:29) — error comes from knowing the Scripture without the power, or the power without the Scripture [6]. So let your closeness to Him, not merely a set of principles about friendship, be what steers you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 16 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 6 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous*, chapter 16 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 65:4; Psalms 73:27-28; Matthew 13:57; Matthew 22:29; Matthew 26:40-41; Matthew 26:45; Mark 12:34; James 4:8.

items.question: Why do people who speak against God seem to prosper?
items.text:
It's a hard thing to watch, and Scripture itself takes it seriously. Here is what our books say about it.

- **Their prosperity is permitted for a set time.** Daniel 11:35-36 says such people "shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done" — they flourish because it is determined that they should, and they are allowed to carry on for a season [1]. Revelation 13:4-7 shows the beast given a mouth of blasphemy and power to continue forty-two months, and at the end of those months the blasphemies were no longer allowed [7].

- **Apparent success is not proof of God's pleasure.** Everything can seem alright with people in what some call the permissive will of God — their ministries flourish and favour seems to be on all they do — but abundance and apparent success do not mean God is pleased with them [5]. Money and abundance have never been a sign that God is pleased with you; the devil also gives money to those who serve him, and Satan offered Jesus the whole world if He would bow down [5].

- **God's judgment is not always swift, but it is fitting.** Miriam criticized Moses and was struck with leprosy almost immediately — God's earth-bound judgment was swift, direct and severe [2]. Yet many criticize today and seem to get away scot-free for years, even prospering as their mouths are filled with wicked criticisms of God's anointed [2]. God allows people to stray into His imperfect will and then receive a sound and fitting thrashing for their rebelliousness; in the end all men receive the appropriate, well-tailored judgments of God [5].

- **Do not be put off by it.** Do not be put off by blasphemies and injurious speech levelled against God's man of faith and power [7]. Since great words of blasphemy and insults were spoken against our Lord Jesus Christ, why would you want to escape your fair share of them? [1] Paul was in prison and died at the hands of cruel and unjust men, under Nero, one of the most depraved emperors of all time; many did not know who Paul was then, but today Paul is more famous and more known than Nero [7].

- **The more you prosper, the more you will be spoken against.** The more you exercise faith, the more you will prosper, and the more you are blessed, the more people will speak against you; ignore their hatred, keep on, and make sure you please God with your faith [3].

- **Look for God's presence, not money.** When you come into contact with a minister, look to see if the presence of God is with him, and watch whether the voice of God and the word of the Lord are present — God's presence and the voice of the Holy Spirit are what you must look for, not the presence of

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Predestination*, chapter 7 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 5 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 1 of *The Art of Hearing* and chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 18:19; Numbers 12:1-15; Daniel 11:35-36; Hebrews 11:6; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good desire — to keep meeting God in the morning, and to keep it fresh. Our books speak to this.

- **Feed your spirit on the Word every morning.** A daily Quiet Time of Bible study and prayer is the most consistent way to feed your spirit, and your spirit does not grow unless it is fed on the Word of God [1]. The Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes, so a daily quiet time drives away weariness and dejection [7].

- **Come to Him early, alone, like Moses.** Moses went up the mountain early in the morning to meet the Lord, taking two tables of stone to write down what God would give him; you need that kind of Quiet Time — early, alone with the Lord [1]. Jesus Himself rose a great while before day and went to a solitary place to pray [4].

- **Take in the Word by hearing as well as reading.** Listening to preaching and watching church services is another way to feed your spirit, since faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17) [1].

- **Pray in tongues and build yourself up.** Every Christian should develop the art of spending hours praying in the spirit; the Bible says you build yourself up in the faith when you pray in the Holy Ghost [1].

- **Let it become a habit, not a mood.** A habit is an act repeated easily without thinking or planning, and good habits are difficult to form but easy to live with [3]. Daniel knelt and prayed three times a day "as he did aforetime" — the sameness was the strength [3].

- **Guard the time from other things.** Television takes up the time that would have been used reading, praying, having a quiet time, and talking with God [5].

- **Expect the relationship to grow.** You naturally develop a relationship with anyone you talk to often; God has spoken to us in His Word, and as you talk to Him and He talks back, you come to know Him and He knows you [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*, chapters 1 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*, chapter 44 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 9 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:1-3; Isaiah 55:10; Daniel 6:10; Matthew 26:40-41; Mark 1:34-36; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; 1 Peter 2:2; Jude 20.

items.question: How can I escape the curse on this earth and start living in God's blessings instead?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and they give you real handles to take hold of. Here is how they describe escaping the curse and stepping into blessing.

- **Let wisdom be your master key.** Wisdom is the master key for escaping the full effects of curses, and God's wisdom from above is the key to overcoming the curse on this earth — anything in the Word of God is that wisdom, and following any aspect of it lifts you above the curse [1]. The wisdom of God is not the wisdom of this world, as 1 Corinthians 2:6-7 says [1].

- **Seek first the kingdom of God.** When you seek the kingdom of God you set aside frustrating earthly ambitions, and the supernatural power of God is released to make you prosper, as Matthew 6:33 says [1]. When you work for God you avoid the curse that is in the ground, because you are not tilling the ground for bread but working in His vineyard, and those who serve Him are promised to spend their days in prosperity, as Job 36:11 says [1].

- **Be led by the Holy Spirit.** The master key to breaking away from the curse, the burden and the yoke is the anointing — the Holy Spirit — and the master key to exiting the cursed path is to follow His direction [2]. As Romans 8:14 says, as many as are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God, so being led by Him lifts you out of an ordinary human existence into a higher life [1][2]. The author tells how, when he finished medical school, the Holy Spirit directed him to give himself wholly to the ministry, and that direction caused him to rise above most of his colleagues; on another occasion the Spirit led him away from debt into a realm of unusual prosperity [2].

- **Hearken to the voice of God.** Israel was to be set high above all nations by hearkening diligently to the voice of the Lord, as Deuteronomy 28:1 says, and the promise is that all these blessings shall come on you and overtake you if you hearken to His voice [2][5]. Blessed is the man that hears Him, watching daily at His gates, as Proverbs 8:34 says, and blessed are all they that put their trust in Him, as Psalm 2:12 says [5].

- **Serve God and accept His call to be near Him.** To serve the Lord is to be blessed — He blesses your bread and your water and takes sickness away from your midst, as Exodus 23:25-26 says [5]. Blessed is the man whom God chooses and causes to approach Him, as Psalm 65:4 says; being chosen by God is itself a blessing [5].

- **Seek out the major blessings and induce them.** Being a blessed person is more important than working hard or going to school, and a blessing can

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 23, 24 and 30 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

items.question: How can a young leader make up for not having much experience?
items.text:
It's a real weight to feel the gap between your years and what the work demands — but the books speak to exactly this.

- **Study history.** A young leader's best substitute for personal experience is the experience of others, so study church history and secular history; as Ecclesiastes 1:9–10 says, there is no new thing under the sun, and what has been done will be done again [1]. History is the greatest source of knowledge and wisdom, second only to the Scriptures, and God even commanded His leaders to teach history so His people would not forget and repeat old mistakes [1].

- **Read widely.** Confidence grows through knowledge, and knowledge comes by reading — Paul told Timothy to give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine (1 Timothy 4:13) [2].

- **Learn from older, experienced fathers.** Deliberately draw on those who have walked further than you, and surround yourself with wise counsellors [2].

- **Pray for wisdom.** Ask God for it rather than assuming you must manufacture it yourself [2].

- **Let experience itself teach you.** Some things can only be learned by going through them; even Jesus learned obedience through the things He suffered (Hebrews 5:8), so allow the experiences God gives you to shape your mind [6].

- **Learn the difference between the ideal and the real.** Experience is what teaches you that the ideal is like the stars — it shows where you want to go — while the real shows where you actually are; church growth principles may be applied and the church still not grow, and that gap is something maturity teaches you [5].

And take heart about your youth itself: Paul told Timothy, "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity" (1 Timothy 4:12) [2]. Young people are especially useful to God — Jesus Himself began His ministry young, and Timothy was young yet greatly used — and your zeal, your faith, and the years ahead of you are real advantages, not liabilities [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 35, 40 and 124 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 35 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 1:9-10; 1 Timothy 4:12-13; Hebrews 5:8.

items.question: Can I get to heaven after I die if I know the right people?
items.book: How to be Born again & Avoid Hell
items.text:
No — the books are clear that no connection or contact can move you from hell to heaven once you have died. There is a great gulf fixed between the two, so that no one can cross over from one side to the other, as Luke 16:26 says [1][2]. If you want to cross, you must cross now, because you cannot transfer when you die [1][2].

This will be hard for anyone used to getting things done through "whom you know." The books tell of a prestigious school in Ghana that was meant for two hundred and fifty children but grew to hold one thousand five hundred, and after the qualified entrants were admitted, a new student arrived every single day — everyone knew these were children connected to the rich and powerful [1][2]. The point is that heaven and hell will not work that way: no one will be transferred from hell to heaven because of whom they know, and salvation comes through the blood of Jesus, not through connections [1][2].

So the real question is not who you know, but whether you are born again. Jesus said, "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3) [4]. He is the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him (John 14:6) [4]. You must receive Christ as your personal Saviour — there is no other option [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 20 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell* and chapter 16 of *People Who Went to Hell*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:13-14; Luke 16:25-26; John 3:3; John 14:6; Romans 10:3.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
You're asking a question the books take seriously, and they answer it in several ways.

- **Respect your desires instead of denying them.** Your sexuality is something to be respected, and a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [4]. Young people sense strong sexual urges that constantly remind them of their lack of holiness, and that feeling removes their confidence in the things of God [5].

- **Be filled with the knowledge of God's will for your sexual life.** The will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality, as 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 says, so make sexual purity one of your clearest and most energetic goals [3]. Stay away from anyone who would want such a relationship with you [3].

- **Find your own way of keeping yourself from fornication.** Everyone has a different way by which he keeps himself from it, and you must find out what God's will is for your own journey of staying away [3]. It may be His will for you never to read certain books or watch certain films, never to have certain friends, never to work with women or have female secretaries, or to travel everywhere with your wife [3].

- **Avoid untimely relationships.** Very young people should not enter into relationships for courtship, because to everything there is a season, as Ecclesiastes 3:1 says [6]. Why enter a relationship when you are still in school and do not even have a job in sight [6]?

- **Only enter relationships that lead to marriage.** The only intimate relationship between men and women that God approves of is marriage, and a Christian man and woman must move towards God's plan, which is marriage [6].

- **Turn away from riotous living.** Riotous living has to do with having many girlfriends or boyfriends, and fooling around with the opposite sex is what destroyed the young man in the story of the prodigal son [7]. One day a young man who enjoyed sleeping with many different girls was told he was creating a situation in which he would be unable as a married man to live with one girl, because when you develop a taste for a different girl every other day it becomes difficult to live happily ever after with one woman [7].

- **Do not join yourself to the world.** In the story of the prodigal son, the young man joined himself to a citizen of that country, but that did not help him — the citizens made things worse for him and made him grovel with pigs [7].

- **Be visible, not hidden.** Do not sit at the back or hide among the crowd; make sure your pastor knows your name, sit in the front in church and in class, and be seen, because people who stand afar off are often practicing some kind of evil and do not want to be detected [7].

items.question: Why do people leave the church over small offenses?
items.text:
That's a heavy thing to carry, and I'm sorry you're feeling the weight of it.

Our books point to a few reasons. One is that unresolved hurt does the leaving, not the offense itself. A man once came to Bishop Dag insisting the Spirit had led him to a new church, but when pressed he admitted there had been "a slight problem" in his old one; the bishop saw that his unhealed hurts had cut him off from his church, and named this as one of the commonest reasons people backslide and leave [7]. The same book warns that a Christian who is not deep will fall away at the next shaking and crisis, and that only a shallow Christian would leave over a leader's scandalous sin — asking what that man's sins have to do with your own salvation [4][8].

Another reason is that some people are simply contentious. There are those who are always causing offences and quarrels, delighting to magnify frivolous and vexatious issues until they become a pivot for divisions, and Scripture tells us to mark such people and avoid them (Romans 16:17) [1].

And sometimes the leaving is selfishness. A pastor Bishop Dag had blessed turned against him after departing, spreading false stories and damaging the church; the book asks how a person can eat up all the good pasture and then tread down the rest of it, or drink the clear waters and then foul them, so that no one else can benefit (Ezekiel 34:18) [2][3]. It even tells of a man who was lifted from being an impoverished illegal immigrant to a prosperous pastor, yet later spoke to the one who had raised him with confidence and disrespect, because he could not remember his starting point [6].

If you are the one being left, remember that you are not the only child that man of God will ever nurture; there will be others [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 2 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 7 of *Opportunities*, chapter 2 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 4 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 3 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:3; Numbers 16:8-9; Ezekiel 34:18; Romans 16:17; Galatians 2:18.

items.question: What does it mean that Jesus is a warrior king and we fight alongside him?
items.text:
What a good question to sit with, pastor — and our books have a great deal to say about it.

Jesus is the commander of heaven's armies, and He makes war in righteousness; when John saw heaven opened, the rider on the white horse was called Faithful and True, clothed in a vesture dipped in blood, and the armies of heaven followed Him on white horses [1][2]. So this is not a figure of speech — He truly leads, and He wages war the right way, in His way and His wisdom [2].

And He is not only a commander but a lamb who makes war: when the ten kings united against Him, the Lamb overcame them, for He is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with Him are called, chosen and faithful [2]. If you want to be like Jesus, you must learn to fight [2].

That is why He teaches our hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by our arms (Psalm 18:34) [2]. We are instructed to fight the good fight of faith and lay hold on eternal life (1 Timothy 6:12), and Timothy — one of the first pastors in church history — was charged to war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) [2]. Paul even counted his own ministry as warfare, asking, "Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges?" [2][4].

But know who the fight is really against: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places (Ephesians 6:10-12) [7]. The dragon makes war against those who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ (Revelation 12:17), so if you keep His commandments, expect the dragon to take you on [7].

And expect the atmosphere of it to be rough. Every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, garments rolled in blood, and burning of fuel and fire (Isaiah 9:5) — danger, confusion, stress, tension, sorrow and shock [8]. Jesus Himself lived in that atmosphere: attacked by a spirit of murder before He could grow up, attacked in the wilderness while He fasted, attacked through the Pharisees, and finally through Judas Iscariot [8]. If we do not get used to the battle atmosphere, we will never function properly [8].

One more thing worth holding onto: good people have to fight too. David was a good man, yet Saul spoke to Jonathan and to all his servants that they should kill David [6]. So do not be surprised when the war comes to you — be prepared to fight and win, because our Saviour is leading His armies into victory [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in *Now We Are At War*, chapters 1, 4 and 7 of *A Good General* and chapter 5 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 22:31; Psalms 18:34; Isaiah 9:5; Ephesians 6:10-12; 1 Timothy 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:12; Revelation 12:17; Revelation 17:12-14; Revelation 19:11-16.

items.question: What does Loyalty and Disloyalty say about the stages of disloyalty?
items.text:
Disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — it's a process, and most people don't even realize they're moving through it [1]. Here are the stages the book lays out:

- **An independent spirit.** It starts subtly: someone becomes autonomous within the group, no longer controlled by its rules, doing what they want despite contrary instructions — like a person told the church is fasting Friday who decides to fast Wednesday instead [1]. Pastors are warned to watch for deacons and leaders who attend only the meetings they deem important and obey only the instructions they think matter [1].

- **Offence.** Jesus said many would be offended and then betray and hate one another (Matthew 24:10), so offence opens the door to treachery [3]. Leaders are told to look around at those wounded by some event; if they haven't genuinely overcome their hurts, they are potential separatists [3]. Absalom was grievously hurt by his sister's rape and by David's failure to act, and hurts and offences usher people down the road of disloyalty [3].

- **Passivity.** After being offended, people become passive — uninvolved, unconcerned, sitting and watching [3]. Members who skip prayer meetings and smaller group activities fit this picture, and they may say, "I don't want any more trouble in this church. Let me just keep to myself" [3]. Absalom said nothing for two whole years (2 Samuel 13:22) — that is passivity [3][6].

- **The critical stage.** A disloyal person doesn't stay passive forever; he moves to noticing and magnifying faults — finding fault with the preaching, the order of service, the building [6]. Miriam, who had followed Moses out of Egypt, began to see his faults and spoke about his marital problems (Numbers 12:1) [5][6].

- **The political stage.** He tries to involve others in his ideas, gathering a following and convincing people he has identified a real problem [5]. His favourite phrases are "a lot of people are saying," "everybody is saying," and "many people are saying" [7]. Absalom sat at the city gate, sympathizing with each visitor's complaint (2 Samuel 15:3) [5]. At this stage the person is dangerous to the unity and stability of the church, and the author's opinion is that you have more than enough grounds to get rid of him [7].

- **Deception.** People who rebel are grossly deceived; if they weren't, they wouldn't do what they do, and most who rebel end up in destruction [7].

- **Open rebellion.** The deceived insurrectionist fights openly against authority, having gained confidence and support over months and years [4]. Lucifer did this (Revelation 12:7), Absalom fought his father (2 Samuel 16:1),

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.
