items.question: How can I make my faith stronger?
items.book: Name It Claim It Take It
items.text:
The books give a clear answer to this, and it comes down to a few simple practices.

- **Hear the Word, again and again.** Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17), so the principal way to improve your faith is by hearing [1]. Keep listening to preaching and teaching, listen to the messages you love over and over, old ones and new ones, and read the books God has placed in your hands [4]. Listen while you walk and while you work; your faith grows without you even realizing it [3][4].

- **Use the faith you already have.** Faith also grows when you use it, because we gain by using what we have (Luke 19:15) [4]. As you step out and act on what you believe, you will find you can do things you could not do before, and things that were impossible become easy [4].

- **Feed your hope.** It is only the hopeful who have strong faith; Abraham was strong in faith because he was hopeful, not staggering at the promise of God through unbelief (Romans 4:18-20) [8]. Expectation of good in the future makes a person stronger in believing the promises of God [8].

- **Make God your strength and trust His mercy.** When you trust in other things you become weaker, but the one who makes God his strength is like a green olive tree in the house of God (Psalm 52:6-8) [5]. Strengthen yourself in God rather than in the world, for the world can never be a source of strength for the believer [5].

- **Strengthen yourself so you can stand against the wicked one.** The young men John wrote to were strong because the word of God abided in them, and so they overcame the wicked one (1 John 2:14) [6]. The devil is a seasoned warrior, so rise up and become stronger [6].

Keep at it, pastor — your faith is growing even when you do not feel it, and as it grows you will obey greater instructions and accomplish greater things for God [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Name It Claim It Take It*, chapters 48 and 68 of *Faith Secrets*, chapter 6 of *The Determinants*, chapter 1 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 1 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Chronicles 20:11-25; Psalms 52:6-8; Ecclesiastes 9:11; Amos 4:12; Luke 19:15; Luke 22:32; John 15:16; Romans 4:18-20; Romans 10:17; 2 Thessalonians 1:3 and 6 more.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
The books have a good deal to say about this, and it comes down to a handful of habits worth building into your life.

- **Work on the people themselves.** Leadership is not a title or a fancy position; to lead is to work on people until they become better human beings, the way Jesus transformed his disciples over three years, so that people took knowledge of Peter and John that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13) [1].

- **Reproduce yourself in others.** A good leader makes himself no longer essential, preparing the people he leads for the day he will not be around, as Jesus did with his disciples when he spoke of the time when he would go away (John 16:4-5) [3].

- **Lead people somewhere.** Be yourself rather than a pretender, believe totally in the future your leadership is creating, and go yourself where you are trying to get people to follow — you cannot get people to pray if you do not pray yourself [8].

- **Value every person.** Every person has a value, and valuable people are sometimes unassuming, sent into our lives in disguise; people are drawn to places where they are valued, and everyone who feels undervalued will move away [7].

- **Be at peace with those around you.** A leader does not bring more confusion but peace, following peace with all men (Hebrews 12:14); accept people as they are rather than trying to change everyone, and do not fight others because of their success [2].

- **Make peace between people.** Anyone who is a leader will need to learn the art of peace-making, since human beings have so many conflicts between each other [2].

- **Be an encourager, and mind the small courtesies.** Notice when somebody has made an effort and appreciate it even if you did not like it, say thank you for everything, and smile, because people gravitate around smiling and friendly people [6].

- **Listen, and keep the conversation off yourself.** Learn the art of listening rather than talking, and let conversation centre on others and what they are doing rather than on yourself and what you are [6].

- **Do not be partial.** People notice partiality in leaders quickly, and the wisdom from above is without partiality (James 3:17) [6].

- **Study leadership and decide to be good at it.** Good things do not drop on you like ripe mangoes from a tree; if you are called to the ministry you are called to leadership, so decide to be a good minister (1 Timothy 4:6) [4].

- **Lean on wisdom.** By wisdom kings reign (Proverbs 8:15-16), and wisdom is the master key to the leadership skills you need, because human beings are difficult to lead and to control [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 20, 23, 79, 86, 121 and 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 4 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; Proverbs 8:15-16; Proverbs 8:20; Matthew 10:17; Matthew 20:16; Mark 1:17; John 16:4-5; John 16:16 and 7 more.

items.question: How do we know the Bible is really God's Word and not just written by men?
items.text:
That's a question worth sitting with, and our books have a good deal to say about it.

- **The Bible's own claim is that God spoke through men.** The Scriptures say that prophecy never came by the will of man, but that holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:20, 21), and that all Scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Timothy 3:16) [2][3]. So the Bible presents itself not as human speculation but as God's Word written through mortal hands [2].

items.question: What does the Bible say will happen to people who gossip and slander others in the church?
items.text:
Here is what our books say about those who gossip and slander in the church.

- **They come under a curse.** The words and actions of a slanderer are so painful that he is due a curse, and all who spread stories to harm someone should know that curses will abound in their direction [1]. Slanderers are cursed people because they have blasphemed, and the end of all blasphemers and disloyal people will be fire, brimstone, cursing, vexation and desolation of long continuance [5].

- **They will not endure on the earth.** Slanderers are destined to have their stay on earth cut short, and evil will hunt them; as Psalm 140:11 says, "May a slanderer not endure on the earth; may evil hunt a violent person violently" [1].

- **They will not be allowed to remain in the church.** Psalm 15 describes who may dwell in God's tent and settle on His holy hill — the one who walks with integrity and does not slander with his tongue — so once you have slandered the brethren, you can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell amongst us [1]. Do not allow slanderers on your leadership team or in your board meetings, for he who slanders others to you will slander you to others; it is just a matter of time [1].

- **They are dangerous and will turn on you.** Anyone who goes around slandering other ministers is a dangerous person; snakes are not discriminating when they begin to bite, and after spreading venom about someone else, they will turn on you [2]. A person who poisons your mind about others is a devil — the word slanderer in the New Testament is translated from the Greek word diabolos, which means devil [8].

- **They bring weakness, confusion and division.** Slander, gossip and faultfinding are all forms of accusation, and these things weaken, paralyse and confuse the church, both within and without [3]. A slanderer separates close friends, as Proverbs 16:28 says, and wherever a slanderer has lived and operated there is strife, division and confusion; through slanderers many loyal church members fall away and are separated from their shepherd [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*, chapters 1 and 5 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty* and chapter 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 140:11; Proverbs 16:28; Micah 7:8; Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 3:11; Revelation 12:10; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How can I receive a share of the Holy Spirit's anointing like the seventy elders did with Moses?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and they point to a few clear ways.

- **Join yourself to someone who carries the anointing.** If you participate in someone's ministry and commit to it, you can merge into the anointing that person carries; by involving yourself and joining yourself with anointed people, you become anointed too [1]. Elisha is the picture of this — he bonded and merged himself with Elijah so completely that when Elijah tried to send him away, he refused to separate [1].

- **Respect and carefully handle the anointed man.** You must deal with God but also handle the man who is anointed, because he is carrying the anointing you want transferred to you; many who quarrel with their spiritual fathers and mentors never receive the anointing they desire, praying to God all right but fighting the fathers and mentors God gives them [2].

- **Direct your prayers to God, not to the anointed.** You cannot pray to or worship an anointed person — he is only carrying a gift he did not engineer — and your prayers must be directed to God, since a man can receive nothing except it be given him from heaven (John 3:27) [2].

- **Follow the Lord faithfully for several years.** Everyone who received the anointing in the upper room had followed the Lord faithfully for several years; the qualification for an apostle was to have been around at least three years, so do not expect the most important treasures of God's kingdom after serving for a few minutes [7].

- **Be available for everything God has for you.** Those who received the anointing were the ones who had actually seen the risen Lord and met with Him over those forty days [7].

- **Wait on God.** Waiting is an important step to becoming anointed; as you wait on the Lord you gain new strength and mount up with wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:31), and few Christians have the time to wait, leaving out one of the most powerful keys [8].

- **Pursue love and unity.** You will have to move away from strife, confusion and bitterness, and your team must be of one mind and one heart, because God does not anoint a confused quarrelling mob — the apostles waited until they were all in one accord before the anointing came (Acts 2:1) [8].

One caution runs through all of it: God is the initiator. It was God who took the anointing on Moses and put it on the seventy elders — not Moses, and not the elders themselves — and you cannot engineer the anointing or shout it into existence; wearing an anointed person's clothes, serving him, giving him offerings and having hands laid on you will not guarantee that you catch it [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*, chapter 10 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 11:16-17; Numbers 11:24-25; Numbers 16:1-4; Isaiah 40:31; John 3:27; Acts 1:4; Acts 1:8; Acts 1:21-23; Acts 2:1; Acts 2:4 and 1 more.

items.question: Why did the people on Malta first think Paul was a murderer and then change their minds to think he was a god?
items.text:
The people of Malta first judged Paul by what they saw happen to him, and then changed their minds when the outcome was different from what they expected. When a viper fastened on his hand, they said among themselves that he must be a murderer whom vengeance would not let live, though he had escaped the sea [1][2][3]. But after they had watched a long while and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god [1][2][3][4].

The book draws a lesson from this about honour: those first thoughts were dishonourable, and negative thoughts about a person are a clear sign of the absence of honour [1]. When Paul did not die, they began to think highly of him, and after he prayed and laid hands on Publius' father and healed him, and many others on the island were healed, good thoughts about Paul abounded — they saw him as a man of God, a man sent from God, and did not question his background any more [1][4]. From then on the people of Malta honoured Paul, and he was honoured on that island into the twenty-first century [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 8 of *Those Who Honour You*, chapter 11 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church* and chapter 53 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

Scriptures referenced: Malachi 1:6-8; Acts 27:41-28:10.

items.question: Does sleeping too much really lead to poverty?
items.text:
Yes, our books say plainly that it does. Too much sleep and too much rest bring poverty, and the Scripture they lean on is Proverbs: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man" [1][3][5]. The picture is of poverty arriving like a traveller you cannot send away, and want coming like an armed man you cannot easily dismiss [1].

It is not only about money. A field left untended because its owner slept too long grows over with thorns and nettles, and the vineyard stops bearing the fruit it should [1][2]. The same is said of a church: a field overgrown and its walls broken down is a church attacked by poverty and scarcity, and the cause is named as laziness — too much sleep, too much rest, too much vacation and holiday [2]. Jesus called such a servant wicked and lazy for not using what he was given [2].

The books also say this is a matter of understanding, not just effort. When Jonah slept in the ship, it was as though he did not grasp that everyone's life was in danger while they cried out to God [1]. And a little sleep at the wrong moment can change a whole life — a little sleep when you should have been studying can mean becoming a clerk instead of a lawyer, or a nurse rather than a doctor [5].

One caution the books themselves give: sleep is necessary and good for the body, for rest, relaxation and productivity, and it is possible to sleep too little as well [1]. The warning is against sleep that is inappropriate — sleeping when you should be praying or studying, and sleeping far too long [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 9 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 85 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 12 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 6:9-11; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:30-34; Romans 13:11-14; 1 Timothy 5:23; James 3:5-6.

items.question: How can wisdom help me when I'm facing a situation that seems impossible?
items.text:
Wisdom is exactly what you need when a situation looks like there's no way out — the books speak to this again and again, and here is how it helps.

- **Wisdom is the application of God's word to impossible situations.** An impossible situation is one where you cannot see any way out, and wisdom is what gives you the grace to overcome where others would have drowned [1].

- **Wisdom can deliver you when strength cannot.** A little city with few men in it was besieged by a great king, and everyone was doomed — until a poor wise man in the city delivered it by his wisdom, not by military skill or strength (Ecclesiastes 9:14-15) [1][3]. Many lives are like that desperate city, and wisdom is the way forward [3].

- **Wisdom is profitable to direct.** The Bible teaches that wisdom is profitable to direct (Ecclesiastes 10:10), so God will direct you out of every difficult situation [3].

- **Wisdom is the principal thing — so get it.** Scripture says to exalt and embrace wisdom, and it will promote you and bring you to honour (Proverbs 4:7-8) [2][3].

- **You get wisdom by praying for it.** If any of you lacks wisdom, ask God, who gives liberally to all and does not upbraid, and it shall be given (James 1:5) [3][6]. The most important prayer for a leader is the prayer for wisdom [6].

- **You get wisdom by studying the Word.** In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and the closer you get to God, the more wisdom you will have [3]. Reading the books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes every day and asking God for wisdom for the affairs of this life is one of the ways wisdom comes [6].

- **In a crisis, let the wisdom from above guide every decision.** James 3:17 describes that wisdom as first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality and without hypocrisy — so do what is pure, what is peaceful, and what is gentle, and you will come out of your crisis [8].

Medical knowledge is God-given wisdom, and the curse associated with childbearing has been overcome by the use of medical science [2].

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 47:9; Proverbs 4:7-8; Ecclesiastes 9:14-16; Ecclesiastes 10:10; 1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 2:3; James 1:5; James 3:17; Wisdom of Solomon 1:1-77.

items.question: How do I understand when Jesus says we must hate our father and mother to be His disciple?
items.text:
That is one of the hardest sayings of Jesus, and it is worth sitting with rather than rushing past. Here is what our books draw out of it.

- **It is a real word from Jesus, not a figure to explain away.** Jesus plainly said that unless a man hates his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be His disciple [1][3]. These absolute statements are not to be softened or ignored; they carry a power the church is often missing today [4].

- **It sits alongside the command to love.** The Word teaches us to honour our fathers and mothers, to love our wives, and to love our neighbour as ourselves — and yet Jesus speaks of hatred for father, mother, wife, and even one's own life [1]. The books do not resolve the tension; they hold both, saying there is a time and a place where hating even your own father and mother is required to please God [1].

- **It is a matter of first love, not cruelty.** The Bible teaches us to love our wives, but it teaches us to love God first [5]. Many people fail to fulfil God's will because they try to please their wives, and Jesus' word about hating family is set right beside the parable of the man who refused the dinner because he had married a wife (Luke 14:20) [5].

- **It is a higher teaching, often reserved for those called further.** Jesus said things to His disciples in private that He did not say in public, and this teaching about marriage is applicable to people called at a higher level who may have to hate their wives to fulfil their divine calling [2]. If you do not travel with the anointed, you will only hear congregational sermons [2].

- **It is the standard for every disciple, not lowered for anyone.** Jesus did not make things easy for anyone, did not lower the bar, and gave no one special treatment — He was inviting us to the greatest privilege ever given to mankind [3]. If hating these things qualifies you as a disciple, how much more does it apply to a Christian leader [5].

- **It is a call to sacrifice for a great cause.** Under Jesus' leadership many people gave up their lives for a great cause, and a leader is someone who can convince people to make sacrifices toward one [8]. The key to being that kind of leader is to have made great sacrifices yourself, because people are convinced when they see you practise what you preach [8].

items.question: Why doesn't God answer some of my prayers?
items.text:
This is one of the most honest questions a praying person can ask, and our books take it seriously rather than brushing it aside.

Sometimes the answer is that God is not presently at work in the thing you are asking for. Jesus prayed for only one sick man at the pool of Bethesda though hundreds needed healing, and He explained it by saying He only did what He saw the Father doing [1][2]. The counsel is to be led by the Spirit and pray for what you see the Father doing, rather than rushing into complex situations with prayers God will not answer [1]. It may be legally right to do something, but it is very difficult to succeed in it if God is not presently involved with it [1][2].

Sometimes the answer is sin. Our prayers are not answered because our iniquities have separated us from God, and our sins have hidden His face from us, as Isaiah 59:1-2 says [5]. God is affected by the sins of our hands, our tongues and our mouths [5].

Sometimes the answer is disobedience or barrenness. God answers the prayers of people who obey Him, and if you are living a life of disobedience He will not honour your prayers [7]. Answered prayer is also directly connected to the fruit a person bears, as John 15:16 shows, and if you sit in spiritual barrenness just wanting God to answer prayers, you may wait forever [7].

Sometimes the answer is that the request itself is impossible for Him to grant. God will have to say no when you ask Him for things which are impossible for Him to do [1][2].

And sometimes it simply remains a mystery. God seems to want us to keep coming back to Him with the same things, as 1 Thessalonians 5:17 says to pray without ceasing, yet He also calls some prayers vain repetitions, as Matthew 6:7-8 says [8]. Which prayers to keep praying and which are repetitious to God is not easy to solve or answer [8]. But these mysteries must not keep us away from prayer; we must keep praying, and we will become experienced as we walk with Him and learn what to say and when to say it [8].

One more thing worth holding onto: God does want to answer one hundred percent of our prayers, and that must be our aim [3]. He is alive and He can hear — He is not a stone or a piece of wood [4][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 8 and 9 of *How to Pray*, chapters 1 and 5 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapter 110 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 3:29; 1 Kings 18:27; Psalms 91:15; Psalms 119:133; Isaiah 59:1-2; Matthew 6:7-8; Matthew 21:22; John 5:1-8; John 5:19; John 14:13-14 and 6 more.

items.question: How can I receive an impartation of understanding from the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the counsel is wonderfully practical.

- **Pray for the Holy Spirit, and keep praying.** Jesus told us to ask for the Holy Spirit, and Luke 11:13 promises He will be given to those who ask [2]. You never reach a point where you have enough of Him; there are always further measures and gifts to be added to what you already carry [2]. The most anointed people are often the ones still praying for the Holy Spirit [2].

- **Listen to the anointed with faith, again and again.** The Spirit is received by the hearing of faith, as Paul asks in Galatians 3:2 [4]. When Peter preached at Cornelius' house, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word (Acts 10:44) [1][4]. So don't treat your time listening to anointed teachers lightly — expect not only insight but an impartation of the Spirit that gathered it [3]. Listen more than once, even to what you don't yet understand; soak in a series of messages until you are saturated [4].

- **Watch for the sudden illumination of understanding.** Since the spirit of understanding is part of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11:1), a sudden great illumination of understanding, knowledge or revelation should alert you that an impartation has occurred [1]. The Holy Spirit is not limited to fixed Sundays and Wednesdays — once your heart is open to the anointed, expect an impartation on any day and at any time [1].

- **Open your heart as a tablet.** When you present your heart that way, you receive not only insight but the impartation that enables the insight to produce [3]. One man listened to Kenneth Hagin for ten years before he received the anointing to teach; one night while praying he played a tape all night, and at about 2.00am something jumped out of the tape and entered his belly, and he heard a voice say, "From today you can teach" [4]. He had received the Spirit by the hearing of faith [4].

- **Come with a cleansed heart.** Confess your sins and ask God to forgive you, for the blood always comes before the oil — the priests were anointed with blood and then with oil (Leviticus 14:14-15), and it is only after being cleansed by the blood of Jesus that you can receive the Holy Spirit [6].

- **Gather with others to pray.** When the believers had prayed, the place was shaken and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost (Acts 4:31) [2].

Keep asking, keep listening, keep your heart soft — and expect Him to answer.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*, chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing*, chapter 8 of *Catch The Anointing*, chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 5 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 14:14-15; Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 34:16; Ezekiel 2:2; Luke 11:13; Acts 10:44; Galatians 3:2; Galatians 3:5; 1 Timothy 5:22.

items.question: What happens if I don't forgive someone?
items.text:
This is a heavy thing to carry, and I'm glad you're asking it honestly. The books speak very directly to what unforgiveness does.

If you will not forgive, God will not forgive you. Jesus said it plainly: "if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses," so the Father will deal with you the same way [2]. Mark 11:25 says that when you stand praying you must forgive, so that your Father in heaven may forgive your trespasses [1]. The book puts it starkly: God will forgive murder, lying, adultery and witchcraft, but He will not forgive a grudge — that is the point at which His forgiveness stops [1].

Your prayers go unanswered, and the tormentors get access to your life. The Bible says the servant who would not forgive was handed over to the tormentors, and many Christians do not know why they are tormented — it could be unforgiveness [1]. Powerful men of God may lay hands on you, but the tormentors remain because of unforgiveness [2]. They can reach you with sickness, disease, poverty and marital disharmony, and that may explain a lack of breakthroughs [2].

It can also cost you your inheritance and isolate you. Jacob gave Joseph one portion above his brethren, and the book says you will not enjoy the inheritance God has for you if you do not learn to forgive [4]. Forgiveness keeps you from being isolated and separated; people who are hurt withdraw and live alone, and it takes a lot of forgiveness to build a large family [4].

And it leaves you with no room for God to act on your behalf. God has a repayment plan for those who harm you — "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19) — but your unforgiveness, bitterness and personal revenge are the very thing blocking His vengeance [6]. Your duty is to forgive; God's duty is to repay [6].

There is one more thing the book says, and it is meant as a warning, not a verdict: an unforgiving nature may indicate that you are not a "new man," or that you are a pretending Christian [1]. But it ends with hope — pray for the grace to forgive, pray for a loving, forgiving and sweet spirit, for God has determined to help you walk in His love [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5, 7 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 46:26-27; Genesis 48:20-22; Deuteronomy 7:9-10; Psalms 130:4; Jeremiah 17:9; Matthew 18:32-35; Mark 11:25; Romans 12:19-20.

items.question: What is blasphemy?
items.text:
Blasphemy, in the plainest terms our books give, is speaking reproachfully about God and His work — an irreverent way of speaking about God or sacred things, showing contempt for Him [1][4]. It is a bitter denunciation and complaint uttered by a godless man, and it includes speaking impiously about God, His church, and His servants [1].

It also means attacking the good reputation of God, His church, and His servants with malicious and injurious words — defaming and speaking damaging words against God's ministers, railing at and insulting them, even speaking or writing extremely evil words against them [1]. In short, it is vilification, slander, and injurious speech spoken against another's good name [3].

Our books go further and say that disloyalty itself is equated with blasphemy. When the children of Israel came into the land God had promised them, they turned to the hills and trees and offered sacrifices to other gods, and the Lord called this blasphemy — He equated their disloyalty to blasphemy [2]. So blasphemy is irreverent behaviour toward anything held sacred, and disloyalty is irreverent behaviour against a sacred thing [2].

One thing worth naming plainly: blasphemy is not only speaking irreverently against God, but also speaking irreverently about sacred things, and ministers of the gospel are in a certain sense sacred because they have been set apart to minister the holy things of the Lord [4]. That is why Jesus, when the scribes said He cast out devils by the prince of the devils, taught on blasphemy — they were ascribing the work of the Holy Spirit to the devil [4]. And He said that blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall never be forgiven, neither in this world nor in the world to come [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Make Shipwreck*, chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty*, chapter 16 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 6 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*.

Scriptures referenced: Ezekiel 20:27-28; Matthew 12:31-32; Mark 3:22; Mark 3:28-30; Luke 12:10; Acts 18:6; 1 Timothy 1:12-13; 1 Timothy 1:19-20; 2 Timothy 3:2; 2 Peter 2:12 and 2 more.

items.question: How does the blood of Jesus cleanse me from my sins?
items.text:
The books speak to this often, and always with wonder at what the blood of Jesus alone can do.

- **Nothing else can wash the stain away.** A woman once told Bishop Dag Heward-Mills that she could wash out palm oil, dirt, chocolate, tea, coffee, stew, soup and toothpaste with soap, but she could not wash out a coconut stain — nothing could. Every time he thinks of that coconut stain he thinks of the stain of sin, and asks what can wash away our lies, our stealing, our fornication and our murders; nothing but the blood of Jesus can [1][2].

- **It cleanses us from all sin as we walk in the light.** As 1 John 1:7 says, if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanseth us from all sin [3][4][7]. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9) [7].

- **It washes us in His own blood.** As Revelation 1:5 says, unto Him who loved us and washed us from our sins in His own blood [3].

- **It removes the filth and gives us a change of raiment.** As Zechariah 3:3-4 records, Joshua stood clothed in filthy garments, and the angel said, "Take away the filthy garments from him... Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment" [3].

- **It carries the poison away.** Just as human blood carries away unwanted poisonous chemicals like urea and disposes of them through the kidney, the blood of Jesus carries away our sin and filthiness — it is a sin-removing liquid flowing from Calvary's cross to the whole world [5][7].

- **It goes beyond forgiveness to cleansing.** Bishop Dag tells of a young man chased by a crowd who suspected he was an armed robber; he fell into a huge watery septic tank, could not swim in that swirling stew of faeces, and was pulled out by a rod and saved from death. The crowd forgave him, but when he got home someone said, "You better go and have a bath. Your life has been saved but you still smell bad!" — and he was ushered away for a thorough disinfecting bath. That is how salvation is: you are forgiven, but there is a need for your cleansing [4][6][8].

- **It sanctifies and sets you apart.** As Hebrews 13:12-13 says, Jesus suffered without the gate that He might sanctify the people with His own blood [5][6][7]. Sanctification takes you even further than forgiveness and cleansing; it means you have been set

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12, 13, 14, 16 and 46 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 3, 5 and 6 of *Blood Power*.

items.question: Does God want me to fight spiritual battles, and how do I do that?
items.text:
Yes — the books are clear that God does want you to fight, and that He is the one who raises up warriors. Here is how they describe it.

- **Accept that building and fighting go together.** You will have to build for God and fight many battles at the same time; it is part of the call, especially in these last days, and you will face battles outside and within, from enemies who look like enemies and from those who look like friends [1]. Anyone who attempts to build the church of God must be ready for a fight, because the gates of hell are postured against the building of the church, and it is only when Jesus spoke of building the church that He mentioned the gates of hell (Matthew 16:18) [8].

- **Know your real enemy.** Your principal enemy is Satan, not other human beings; he is the leader of the demonic forces and a powerful being who fell from a glorious estate [5]. So the fight is not against people but against spiritual forces that have captured the souls of millions [5].

- **Fight the good fights.** Scripture says, "Fight the good fight of faith" (1 Timothy 6:12), and the books list good fights to be ready for: to be a strong Christian, since it takes great effort to become strong in the Lord (Ephesians 6:10) [2]; to be led by the Holy Spirit and to be in the will of God, since many voices and demons vie for your attention [2]; to be spiritual and not carnal, for to be carnally minded is death, but to be spiritually minded is life and peace (Romans 8:6) [2]; and to walk in love and bear the fruit of the Spirit, since it is more natural to be angry and bitter (Galatians 5:22-23) [2].

- **Put on the whole armour.** You are told to put on the whole armour of God so that you can stand against the wiles of the devil (Ephesians 6:11), and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds (2 Corinthians 10:4) [6]. Ministers who lack this armour are doomed to destruction, so do not take it lightly [6].

- **Fight in God's way and wisdom.** There is a godly way to make war and a wise way to wage war; God judges and makes war in righteousness (Revelation 19:11), and He wants you to wage war in His way [3]. Anyone who thinks we are not at war lacks understanding — Satan would like you to believe you are living in peace with nothing to worry about, but God's Word is clear that we are at war [3].

- **Let God use you as His weapon.** God wants you to be His battle-axe and weapon of war, to break

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapters 1, 3 and 60 of *A Good General*, chapter 4 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry* and chapter 7 of *Attempt Great Things for God*.

- **Fight the good fights.** Scripture says, "Fight the good fight of faith" (1 Timothy 6:12), and the books list good fights to be ready for: to be a strong Christian, since it takes great effort to become strong in the Lord (Ephesians 6:10); to be led by the Holy Spirit and to be in the will of God, since many voices and demons vie for your attention; to be spiritual and not carnal, for to be carnally minded is death, but to be spiritually minded is life and peace (Romans 8:6); and to walk in love and bear the fruit of the Spirit, since it is more natural to be angry and bitter (Galatians 5:22-23).

- **Put on the whole armour.** You are told to put on the whole armour of God so that you can stand against the wiles of the devil (Ephesians 6:11), and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds (2 Corinthians 10:4).
Ministers who lack this armour are doomed to destruction, so do not take it lightly.

- **Fight in God's way and wisdom.** There is a godly way to make war and a wise way to wage war; God judges and makes war in righteousness (Revelation 19:11), and He wants you to wage war in His way.
Anyone who thinks we are not at war lacks understanding — Satan would like you to believe you are living in peace with nothing to worry about, but God's Word is clear that we are at war.

items.question: Do pastors and church workers have the right to be paid and take time off?
items.book: Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)
items.text:
Yes, the books speak to this clearly, and they treat both pay and rest as genuine rights of those who work in ministry.

- **The right to be supported by the gospel.** Those who preach the gospel should live off the gospel, as 1 Corinthians 9:14 says, and the husbandman who labours must be first to partake of the fruits, as 2 Timothy 2:6 says [5]. A soldier does not pay his own expenses, a farmer eats from the crop he harvests, and a shepherd drinks the milk of his flock [1]. God sees His priests as hard-working people who deserve to be rewarded, and their work is not merely honest work but God's work [1].

- **The right to eat and drink as you work.** It is important to eat and drink as you work, because people who do not grow weary and give up; there is no reason a full-time minister should fast every day simply because of where he works [1].

- **The right to rest and take breaks.** Rest is part of God's plan for His cherished ministers, and vacations, days off and times of rest are their right; a worker should not feel bad about taking a day off [1]. Full-time workers should have rest and leave periods, with the kinds of leave determined by the administrators and bishops of each church [2]. In one church Mondays are the resting day, a little time of leisure and family respite [1], and Mondays can be taken as a day of rest and a day off for full-time workers [2].

- **A caution against refusing your privileges.** A leader must know when it is time to take his place and enjoy his benefits; refusing your privileges and blessings when it is your turn to have them is called an error that proceeds from a ruler [5].

- **A caution against idleness.** At the same time, work in the church should be project-oriented, with staff expected to meet targets rather than idle in church offices, and those who do not accomplish their projects may be demoted, laid off or dismissed [2]. Some pastors become idle and lazy as they wait for Sunday to deliver their next sermon [6].

- **Working hours differ from other professions.** Pastors are not bankers, accountants or pharmacists but shepherds who look after sheep, so their working hours are different; a pastor is most active in the evenings when the sheep become available, and works late into the night [6]. A shepherd's working hours should be the weekends, especially Sundays, and some evenings, which means giving up some leisure and rest as a sacrifice for the kingdom [7]. Ministry work consumes a large amount of time, and you cannot claim to be doing the work of the ministry until it actually consumes a reasonable amount of time in your week [7].

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22-23; Ecclesiastes 10:7; 1 Corinthians 9:4; 1 Corinthians 9:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 4:15; 2 Timothy 2:6.

items.question: How do I heal from the hurts and offenses I've experienced in life and ministry?
items.text:
I'm sorry for the wounds you've carried — and I'm glad you're asking how to heal rather than how to hide them.

- **Expect the wounds; they are part of this life.** Jesus said offences must come, and He told us these things so that we would not be offended [2][8]. If you are in ministry, expect to be hurt and wounded by fellow pastors; if you are married, expect to be wounded by your spouse [2]. The wounds pastors carry most often come from ungrateful and disloyal people [7].

- **Refuse to let the wound go unhealed.** Bitterness is an advanced, deep-seated form of offense, and many who walk out of a church are offended Christians whose wounds never healed [1]. A pastor once told of a diabetic toe that would not heal until the wound spread and the whole leg was nearly amputated; the Spirit used that to show how Christians who never recover from their hurts separate themselves from other believers and end up isolated from the body of Christ [1][3]. So confess your faults to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed, as James 5:16 says [2].

- **Let healing be your aim, not merely relief.** Your broken heart must be healed, for the Lord was anointed to heal the brokenhearted (Luke 4:18-19), and you will not bear fruit until you endure offences well and come out perfectly healed — healed means no longer bitter [2]. Come out of the test with patience, that is, cheerful, hopeful endurance, as James 1:4 describes [2].

- **Forgive quickly, and don't let the wound become your identity.** Jesus was wounded many times but He forgave, and that is the example we follow [7]. Derek Prince, in the last interview of his life, said he regretted not forgiving the people who hurt him as quickly as he should have [7].

- **Press on toward wholeness, and let the scars serve others.** If your life has been damaged by abuse, press on toward healing and wholeness, and hold to Romans 8:28, that all things work together for good to those who love the Lord [4]. Your wounds will become scars lined with gold, and those scars become the basis of your healing ministry — without scars you will never have authority [4]. You have a choice: let the abuse destroy you, or arise into the next phase of your ministry [4].

- **Remember Joseph, who was wounded and healed.** Joseph was betrayed by his brothers, made a slave, imprisoned, deceived by a woman, and forgotten by the butler; yet God healed him and gave him a double portion, and his bow abode in strength (Genesis 49:22-26) [5]. Even the beast in Revelation 13 was wounded and healed, and it was that healing that impressed the world —

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 17 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*, chapter 3 of *Backsliding*, chapters 9 and 18 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 49:22-26; Leviticus 21:18-23; Matthew 18:6-7; Luke 4:18-19; John 16:1; Romans 8:28; James 1:4; James 5:16; Revelation 13:1-5.

items.question: How should an assistant minister behave during counselling sessions with the senior pastor?
items.text:
During counselling sessions, your role is to support and strengthen what your senior pastor is saying, not to compete with it.

- **Do not contradict or redirect.** You must not contribute any counsel that is contrary to what is being said, and you must not try to develop a completely new train of thought, which would only confuse the person receiving counsel [1][2].
- **Emphasize what your pastor says.** Simply help your senior to say what he is saying better and emphasize what he has already said, rather than trying to impress anyone with high-sounding wisdom [1][2].
- **Do not stay silent.** Remaining quiet will make you look like a spectator and will make the counsellee feel awkward [1][2].
- **Use simple, powerful phrases at intervals.** For example: "Do you understand what pastor is saying?", "Do you understand that pastor is only trying to help you?", "Pastor is only saying this because he loves you," and "I wish I had had someone to speak to me in this way when I was in a similar situation" [1][2]. Interjecting comments like these lends greater impact to his words [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 3 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:16; Matthew 10:40; John 3:30.

items.question: What should I do if I'm bitter about being moved away from a pastor who helped me?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this — being moved away from someone who helped you can leave a real ache, and bitterness is a heavy thing to hold.

The books speak to this in a few ways. Bitterness is described as an advanced, deep-seated form of offense, and the warning from Hebrews 12:15 is that a root of bitterness can spring up, trouble you, and defile many [2][3]. So the first counsel is simply not to let bitterness move you away from God [2].

They also say you are the key to your own recovery — whether and how soon you heal depends on you, and God's grace is available for your emotional healing [7]. Part of that healing is forgiveness: choose to forgive, let go, release the grudge, and pray sincerely for the other person's well-being, because you will not get healed if you do not genuinely forgive, and God will not forgive you if you don't forgive [7]. It helps to talk your pain through with spiritually mature counsellors, pastors, or godly friends, though after a while you must consciously stop talking about it so you don't wear them out or stall your own progress [7].

There is also a word here about the transfer itself. One book says people who struggle with being transferred from place to place are often agitated by a spirit of rebellion, and that pride is what makes a person offended with a transfer [5]. It also says a pastor must not be angry when rebuked, but receive correction like a humble, open child [5]. I'll be honest that this is a hard word, and it may or may not fit your situation — only you and God know what's actually in your heart.

And one more thing worth sitting with: a pastor who had two gifted associates watched them grow bitter over being transferred away from him, and both eventually left and seemed to wither, while the senior pastor's ministry kept growing [1]. The lesson drawn there is not to be afraid of acknowledging that God used a man to change your life [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Forget*, chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 10 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 14:31-32; 1 Chronicles 12:33; Psalms 103:8; Psalms 147:3; Proverbs 9:8; Mark 11:24-25; John 12:44; Hebrews 12:15; James 5:16.

items.question: How does prayer make me stronger?
items.text:
Prayer is one of the great ways God builds strength into you, and the books describe several sides of it.

- **Prayer strengthens your inner man.** Paul prayed that the Ephesians would be "strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man" (Ephesians 3:16), and he prayed the same kind of strengthening for the Colossians (Colossians 1:9-12) [1][8]. You become spiritual by giving yourself to the word of God and to prayer, so that your spirit grows and dominates your life [8].

- **Prayer strengthens your soul.** The psalmist says that in the day he cried out, God answered him and strengthened him with strength in his soul (Psalm 138:3) [1][2]. Your soul is your emotions, will and intellect, and prayer gives you emotional strength so your feelings don't drag you in the wrong direction [2].

- **Prayer strengthens you for ministry.** Strength is needed to make it in ministry, which is why the Lord strengthened Paul when He put him into service (1 Timothy 1:12) [2]. Many people are willing and interested in serving the Lord, but willingness is different from having the strength to do His will — and that strength comes through prayer [3].

- **Prayer strengthens you against the enemy's attacks.** Paul said the Lord stood with him and strengthened him, and he was delivered out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:17) [2]. In every spiritual war, Satan is after your prayer life, because your prayer life is the source of your strength [4].

- **Prayer strengthens you against temptation.** Jesus told His disciples to watch and pray so they would not enter into temptation, because the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41) [3]. When you pray, God gives you strength to overcome temptations and to do His will [5].

- **Praying in tongues builds you up.** "He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4) — every time you pray in tongues, you become strong [1].

- **Prayer replaces fear with power.** Fear makes you weak, and the spirit of fear is the spirit of weakness; pray for the Spirit of power, love and a sound mind, for God has not given us the spirit of fear (2 Timothy 1:6-7) [1].

- **Strength can come through angels in prayer.** When Jesus knelt and prayed in the garden, an angel appeared to Him from heaven, strengthening Him (Luke 22:41-43) [1].

One more thing worth holding onto: prayer is also what keeps you close to God, and closeness is where that strength flows. A Christian who spends less time praying is unknowingly moving away from God, while the one who spends time talking to Him becomes

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12 and 14 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities*, chapter 2 of *Prayer Changes Things*, chapter 5 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 6 of *Enlargement Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 16:4-6; Psalms 138:3; Proverbs 7:10; Matthew 26:41; Luke 22:41-43; 1 Corinthians 14:4; Ephesians 3:14-19; Colossians 1:9-12; 1 Timothy 1:12; 2 Timothy 1:6-7 and 1 more.

items.question: Can someone who gossips or slanders others still be a member of our church?
items.text:
This is a hard question, and I want to answer it gently but honestly from what our books say.

The short answer is no — a slanderer cannot be allowed to remain among you. Psalm 15 asks who may dwell in God's tent and settle on His holy hill, and the answer includes the one who "does not slander with his tongue" [1]. Once someone has slandered the brethren, they can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell among you [1]. The counsel is plain: drive away slanderers, let them go, and do not feel sorry for them — you are better off without a slanderer [1]. A slanderer is described as a living, moving, active human devil in your midst [5], and such people are to be driven away from the church [4].

This applies to leaders too, not only members. Do not allow slanderers on your leadership team or in your board meetings, because he who slanders others to you will slander you to others — it is only a matter of time [1]. And be careful about receiving newcomers who arrive full of stories and rumours against their former church or their last employer [1].

There is a reason the books speak so sternly. Slander damages people irrevocably, and it is almost impossible to change minds once the stories are out [1]. A slanderer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28) and separates the sheep from their shepherd, so that loyal members fall away [3]. Slander can even endanger a life — one account tells of a man driving his mother-in-law to the hospital when she died in the car; a rumour spread through the village that he had killed a woman and was secretly going to bury her, and the crowd beat him to death over a false story [3].

So guard the flock. Wolves do not care whether young Christians are confused or thrown off the narrow way by all the accusations and stories flying about [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*, chapter 11 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 2 of *Those Who are Wolves*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 31:12-13; Psalms 54:5; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 140:11; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 16:28; Micah 7:8; Philippians 2:14 and 1 more.

items.question: How can I encourage others who are going through hard times?
items.text:
The books speak to this in several ways, and they all begin with what you yourself have walked through.

- **Let your own troubles become your message.** Paul said he received a message from the Lord through the tribulations he experienced — a message of comfort for people in trouble — and the only way he could speak to them was to share what he learned in his own trouble [1]. The whole world lies in wickedness and trouble is everywhere, and you will never have a message for this world unless you experience some of its troubles yourself [1]. Even the comfort God gives you in your affliction is given so that you can comfort others with the same comfort, as 2 Corinthians 1:3-5 says [1].

- **Remember what it felt like, and reach out from that memory.** God warns us in His Word to remember how we felt in hardship and to help others in a similar situation — if you came from poverty, He expects you to reach out to the poor because you know what it feels like [5]. Wicked people simply cannot remember what it was like to be on the other side [5].

- **Mourn with those who mourn.** Times of sorrow are some of the most remembered times in people's lives, and if you are by someone's side in that period they will never forget you [8]. The writer tells of people joining his church simply because he stood with them when their parents died [8].

- **Go the extra mile to help.** Whenever you help someone in need, he remembers you; people see when you make the extra effort and it touches their hearts, and when you later ask them to rally around a cause they will be there because they remember [8]. If you do not sow a seed of help in someone's life, no one will help you in the future [8].

items.question: Why is loyalty so important in ministry, especially during hard times?
items.text:
Loyalty matters in ministry because it is the very thing God looks for in a servant, and it is most clearly seen when times are hard.

- **It is the main qualification for ministry.** The Bible says plainly that "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2), and that faithfulness—not gifting, friendliness, or eloquence—is the cardinal requirement for leadership [3][6]. Loyalty, dependability, and constancy are requirements for ministry the way brakes and headlights are requirements for a car; you cannot do without them [6].

- **It is most appreciated in hard times.** In the good times everybody seems loyal, but those who stick with you through difficult times are different from those who come in when everything is working well [1][2]. Jesus told His disciples they would receive a special kingdom because they had continued with Him in His temptations (Luke 22:28-29), and their names are written on the foundations of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14) [1][2].

- **It leads to life, righteousness, and honour.** Proverbs 21:21 says that one who pursues righteousness and loyalty finds life, righteousness, and honour [4]. Churches die when they are not faithful and loyal to the Great Commission, but faithfulness to your call extends your life so you can fulfil your ministry [4].

- **It is the master key to expansion.** Matthew 25:21 promises that the faithful servant is made ruler over many things [5]. Almost all large churches are led by pastors who have remained faithful to the same church for a long time, and the blessing of largeness is reserved for faithful and loyal people [5]. One man can only do so much; to build a great church you need loyal assistants, and without loyalty every network of churches constantly disintegrates [7].

- **It brings the joy and favour of God.** The second blessing of faithfulness is entering the joy of the Lord, which means experiencing the favour of God, so that your enemies will not flourish [5].

- **It requires wisdom to sustain.** Solomon reigned peacefully over a vast region because all the people under his leadership were loyal to him, with no rebellion or breakaway kingdoms [8]. The key to a loyal, worldwide ministry is the wisdom of God, not merely prayer and fasting [8].

One day we all hope to hear those words, "Well done, good and faithful servant" [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 6 and 7 of *Why Loyalty?*, chapters 1 and 12 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 2 of *Pillars of Loyalty* and chapter 6 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 21:21; Ecclesiastes 12:12; Matthew 16:18; Matthew 25:21; Luke 22:28-29; 1 Corinthians 4:2; Revelation 21:14.

items.question: How does the Holy Spirit teach us today?
items.text:
The Holy Spirit is first and foremost a teacher, and He makes Himself visible to us most often by teaching us all things [3]. Here are the ways our books describe Him teaching us today.

- **He speaks to you directly.** The anointing you have received teaches you of all things, so you may hear His voice yourself as an impression, a perception, or a conviction — sometimes vague, sometimes clear and explicit [1].
- **He teaches you through anointed teachers.** God gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, and the Holy Spirit speaks to you through people anointed to teach the Word; do not miss that voice [1].
- **He guides you into truth.** The Spirit of truth guides you into all truth, and since God is where truth is, being guided toward truth is being guided toward Jesus — so go toward truth no matter how hard it is [1].
- **He points you to books.** The Holy Spirit leads you to books you must read, so expect it and look out for it [1].
- **He reminds you of things.** The Comforter brings all things to your remembrance, whatsoever Jesus has said (John 14:26); He uses the past to guide you today so you do not go round in circles [1][4].
- **He predicts the future.** The Spirit of truth will show you things to come (John 16:13), and He is concerned with what is going to come [1][6].
- **He glorifies Christ.** He receives of what is Christ's and shows it to you (John 16:14), so if you love Jesus you will love the Spirit [1].
- **He teaches through revelation.** He gives the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him (Ephesians 1:17) — sudden bursts of revelation that are exciting and exhilarating [1].
- **He gives you knowledge.** God has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness through the knowledge of Him (2 Peter 1:3), and the knowledge the Spirit gives about God leads you into everything that pertains to this life [4].
- **He speaks to your spirit, soul, or body.** He has a voice and may speak to any of the three; when He speaks to your spirit you do not hear an audible voice — this is what people call the inner witness [6].

If you want a permanent blessing, you need the Holy Spirit as a teacher, and you will not go far with God until you ask Him to teach you [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *The Love of the Spirit*, chapter 7 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit* and chapter 10 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 9:20; Luke 11:29; John 6:45; John 8:32; John 14:26; John 16:12-14; Ephesians 1:17; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Peter 1:3 and 2 more.

items.question: How should I respond to people who try to turn me against my church leaders?
items.text:
It's a painful thing when people work to turn you against the leaders God has placed over you, and the books speak to it plainly.

**Recognize the strategy for what it is.** It is a clever strategy to discredit a book or a leader to ignorant followers so that they never find out the truth for themselves [2]. Absalom thrived on the ignorance and naivety of the people, and dangerous sons campaign against fathers, trying to make you turn against your own father [2].

**Watch the pattern of those who do this.** Watch out for those who constantly have problems with parents, leadership and authorities, who cannot stand to be guided or counselled, and who react angrily to correction [1]. People influenced by Satan share this characteristic: they have conflicts with those above them and try to ascend out of their place and challenge divinely ordained authorities [1].

**Understand what is being stolen.** Dangerous sons want what does not belong to them, and the most valuable thing a leader possesses is the heart of his followers [2]. Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel, as 2 Samuel 15:6 says, and when David heard that the hearts of the men of Israel were after Absalom, he knew he had to flee [2].

**Expect that not everyone will believe the stories.** When conflicts and crises come, the hearts of the people respond in three ways — some are confused, others believe the stories, and others do not believe any bad thing about the leader [6]. Those who love you will never believe bad things about you [6].

**Do not be offended when your leader is under fire.** Jesus said, "Tonight, you will be offended because of me" (Matthew 26:31), and it is normal and expected for God's servants to go through fiery trials and temptations [6].

**Reject rebels rather than admire them.** Rebellion is always evil, no matter who does it, and if you find anyone rebelling you must not have anything to do with the person — if you admire a rebellious person, you are in great danger of becoming a rebel yourself [8]. The psalmist says, "Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and abhor those who are in rebellion against you?" (Psalm 139:21) [8].

**Be careful with your own words toward those who hurt you.** You must be careful of issuing random curses on people who hurt you, and you must realise that you sometimes also hurt others without knowing what you are doing [7]. Paul said, "Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not" (Romans 12:14) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended*, chapter 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 8 of *Those Who Rebel*.

Scriptures referenced: Joshua 22:19; 2 Samuel 15:6; 2 Samuel 15:13; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 109:17-20; Psalms 139:21; Matthew 26:31; Luke 15:17; Romans 12:14.

items.question: According to Church Growth, why do some churches stop growing?
items.text:
Some churches stop growing because they fail to share the burden of ministry. A church can grow to a point and then come to a standstill, and the reason given is that the burden is not shared [3]. The burden of the ministry cannot be carried by one person; it is simply impossible [3]. When people hold back from sharing it—sometimes because they want all the glory, or because they fear rebellion or being outshone—the work cannot expand, since you cannot expand without trusting people [3].

There is also the matter of vision. A shallow or superficial vision for a large church will not make a church grow; in the absence of a burning vision for a large church, real church growth never comes [2]. Without that burning vision, a pastor will not spend the time seeking the wisdom that brings growth, will grow irritated with the strategies taught by church growth pastors, and will not listen to the messages that bring growth—even criticizing the very thing he needs most [8].

And churches that do not grow are often isolated. Silently living in isolation will not help anybody, and it will certainly not help someone who wants his church to grow [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 4 and 21 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 27:17; Proverbs 29:18; Ephesians 4:15-16.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry you've been hurt so badly — that kind of pain is real, and it's not a small thing to carry.

The books speak directly to this, and they treat forgiveness as something you do, step by step, not a feeling that just arrives. To forgive is to release all hurts, bitterness and wickedness from your heart, so that you deny the enemy access to it [1]. Concretely, that means dismissing the thorny, painful issues, giving up your claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any debt they owe you, making no more mention of the matter, stopping the resentment and the anger, and cancelling any punishment you had planned for them [1][3]. It also means walking in love and praying for your offender, as Jesus taught us to love our enemies and pray for those who despitefully use us [1].

Two things make it easier. First, analyse the offender: Jesus, as they were killing Him, said, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34) — He made excuses for His own murderers, and often the person who hurt you is sick, ignorant or confused, not fully aware of what they are doing [2]. Second, analyse your own past sins, considering yourself lest you also be tempted, and remember that you are equally in need of forgiveness from God — for if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you (Matthew 6:14) [2][3].

And do not be afraid to forgive, as though letting go means the offender gets away with it. Give place to wrath, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19) — your duty is to forgive, and God's duty is to repay [6]. If your enemy hungers, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink, for in so doing you heap coals of fire on his head [6].

If the wound is deep, know that healing has stages — shock, fear, guilt, hurt, anger, acceptance, forgiveness, then healing — and you are the key to your own recovery; whether you get healed, and how soon, depends on you [5]. The Lord heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds (Psalm 147:3), and His Spirit is like oil and balm for your wound [5]. Forgiveness is where you let go and are liberated; allow the Holy Spirit to help you [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended*, chapters 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 147:3; Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Romans 12:19-20; Ephesians 4:32; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: What does the Bible say about people who rebel against their leaders in church?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. A rebel is someone who is defiant and resistant, who openly opposes and defies the leadership, disobeys the leader's instructions, and gets into conflict and confrontation with authorities [2]. Rebellion itself is defined as defiance, an open disregard and contempt for an authority figure, resistance to a higher authority, and a group attack against authority [8].

Scripture treats it with great seriousness. In 1 Samuel 15:23, rebellion is compared to the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness to iniquity and idolatry [1][6]. Joshua 24:19 says God is a holy and jealous God who will not forgive your rebellion and your sins [6]. Proverbs 17:11 calls rebels evil men who seek only rebellion [6][8]. And Joshua 1:17-18 records that whoever rebels against the commandment and will not hearken to the words of the leader was to be put to death [2].

The books also describe what rebellion looks like and where it leads. It stems from the heart, and every rebellious child of God has rejected legitimate authority in his life [1]. It often camouflages itself as a fight for independence, though many so-called freedom fighters are actually downright rebels [1]. Those who rebel become men of darkness and secrets, full of secret meetings, secret comments, secret phone calls, and secret rendezvous, because Ephesians 5:11-13 says to have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness [4]. Rebellion is also associated with treachery and betrayal, and it causes deep emotional wounds, destroys trust, and leaves lasting pain in loved ones [6]. All rebels are headed for the same place — destruction — as the prodigal son, Judas, Absalom, Adonijah, Ahithophel, Shimei, and Lucifer all show [1].

The counsel is to reject rebels. Psalm 139:21 says to abhor those who are in rebellion against God, and the books say you must hate all forms of rebellion and have nothing to do with anyone rebelling, because if you admire a rebellious person you are in great danger of becoming a rebel yourself [3]. Romans 16:17 says to mark them which cause divisions and offences and avoid them [5]. And do not rebel against God or His servant, for many times when you are defying God's servants, you are defying God Himself [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapters 1, 2, 4 and 8 of *Those Who Rebel* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 31:27; Joshua 1:17-18; Joshua 22:19; Joshua 24:19; 1 Samuel 15:23; Ezra 4:19; Nehemiah 9:17; Job 34:37; Psalms 139:21; Proverbs 17:11 and 5 more.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
Here are the ways our books describe praying effectively.

- **Pray strategic Bible prayers.** Let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the prayers recorded in Scripture — for instance Ephesians 1:17-19, which the author prayed for himself for many years, and Ephesians 3:15-19, which grounds you in love [1]. Become a Word person and believe in the Word more than you believe in yourself [1].

- **Pray fervently.** Pray ardently, with passion and feeling — passionate, zealous, burning, eager — so that anyone watching could describe your prayer with one of those words [1]. Doodling and dawdling prayers do not show fervency [1].

Ministers who converse with the Holy Spirit are often very advanced in their walk with God [1].

items.question: What difference does it make whether I serve the Lord or not?
items.book: It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord
items.text:
Yes, there is a real difference — Scripture says you will return and see it plainly, between the one who serves God and the one who does not [1]. Here is what our books describe.

- **Your standing changes.** The son who stayed and served was a joint heir with his father, while the one who left was reduced to the rank of a servant with no rights, no money, no property and no good standing [1][3].

- **Your covering changes.** The one who left his father's house found himself in great need with no one to help him, for he had lost the covering over his defenceless head [3].

- **Your peace changes.** The son who went to the far country had no peace there — even the pigs quarrelled with him over the food — while the brother who served rode high as the only remaining heir [3][2].

- **Your prosperity changes.** The father told the serving son, "all that I have is thine," while the one who refused to serve was left with basically the clothes on his back [2].

- **How the Father relates to you changes.** To the faithful servant the father spoke his secrets — "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine" — while to the returning prodigal he simply said, "Welcome home" [2].

- **Your very life changes.** The father said of the son who would not serve in the house, "this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found" [2].

And there is this too: whatever you do, you will serve something or someone. When God offers you the chance to serve Him, He is offering you a chance to escape serving your enemy — for if you will not serve the Lord, you are handed over to serve your enemies, other gods, even wood and stone [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 10 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 28:36-37; Deuteronomy 28:47-48; Deuteronomy 28:64; Isaiah 48:18-19; Isaiah 65:12-14; Malachi 3:17-18; Luke 15:15-17; Luke 15:21; Luke 15:29; Luke 15:31-32.

items.question: How does God give revelation to people today if it's not always through visions?
items.text:
Yes, God still gives revelation today, and He does it in more ways than visions alone.

**Through real-life encounters with Him.** The apostle John's ministry was launched not by a vision but by what he had heard, seen, looked upon, and touched of the Word of life — a "real life revelation" that was just as important as the visions he had later [1].

**Through meditation on His Word.** Most of us will not receive special supernatural revelations; we depend instead on meditation, thinking deeply about God's Word, and the lack of meditation is the cause of a lack of personal conviction [6]. Someone who meditates is full of wisdom and understanding, and it is dangerous to relay others' messages without meditating for yourself, lest you become a false prophet reading out dead sermons [6].

**Through reading.** A great blessing comes by reading — "Blessed is he that readeth" (Revelation 1:3) — and Martin Luther received the greatest blessing of his life by reading the Bible, discovering in Romans, Ephesians and the Psalms that salvation comes by faith and not by works [5].

**Through believing without seeing.** Jesus said, "Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed" (John 20:29); those who accomplish great things for God without visions are even more blessed than those who have seen them, and John Wesley bore lasting fruit though his writings record no visions of Jesus [5].

**Through sharing the Word with one another.** Exhortation — sharing the Word with small groups and individuals — grounds you in the truth, helps you understand and remember it better, and grooms you for ministry [6].

And when revelation does come as visions and dreams, it is God's way of speaking to His anointed (Psalm 89:19) [4], of assuring them of His presence [2], and of preventing destruction, for "where there is no vision, the people perish" (Proverbs 29:18) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Victory Secrets*, chapter 18 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapter 30 of *How To Neutralize Curses* and chapter 6 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 3:1; Psalms 89:19; Proverbs 29:18; John 20:29; Acts 10:9-11; Ephesians 1:15-18; 1 Timothy 4:16; 1 John 1:1; 1 John 1:3; Revelation 1:3.

items.question: How do I deal with people in the church who are disloyal or stealing from the offering?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this — it's a heavy thing to face people you've served alongside and find disloyalty or theft in the house. Here is what our books say.

- **Deal with thieves firmly and practically.** Direct firmness at humbling, warning and controlling those who steal the offering [1]. Prevent the loss by monitoring who becomes an usher, keeping ushers in view at all times so none can dip fingers into the bags, and ensuring security so an intruder cannot steal [7][8]. Have two or three people count the money at the same time, never leave anyone alone with it, and use a signed form that corresponds with the bank pay-in slips [7][8]. Keep the money in a secure safe, never in the pastor's house, bank it at the very next opportunity, bank 100% of it promptly, and take nothing out before it reaches the bank — if you need petty cash, sign a cheque of a fixed amount as a petty cash imprest [7][8].

- **Recognize disloyalty as demonic activity, not just a personality clash.** If you are struggling to gain the absolute trust of your associates and elders, think of demon activity, because devils work where there is disloyalty and treachery [2]. Satan is the author of all forms of separation and disloyalty, and he comes as an angel of light, so most devils operate through nice-looking people rather than the obvious outsider [2]. The constant breaking up of your church, division and confusion is a sign of the presence and activities of devils — usually a demon gang, since evil spirits hardly work alone [2].

- **Cast out the scorner.** The biblical remedy for the scornful — those who mock you and do not believe in you — is not prayer or fasting but to cast them out, as Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease" [4][5][6]. In modern English that means to dismiss, expel, eject, banish, fire, sack, discard, unseat or lay off [4]. A scorner is worthless to the ministry and against you, so he must go away [6].

- **Dismiss those with questionable loyalties.** A leader must refuse to lead people who are mysterious, secretive and questionable in their loyalty, because failing to dismiss them lets a root of bitterness grow until many are defiled and the whole church is destroyed [5]. Questionable loyalty is diagnosed when someone makes malicious, damaging or poisonous comments; when they have a spouse or close relative who is openly disloyal; when they have friendships, alliances and close ties with an openly disloyal person; or when they are known to communicate with openly disloyal persons [5]. Absolute evidence is not needed to deal with mysterious characters —

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *A Good General*, chapter 12 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 8 of *Pillars of Loyalty*, chapter 10 of *Church Growth* and chapter 3 of *Church Administration*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 15:11; Psalms 1:1; Proverbs 22:10; Titus 1:5.
